evidence_items.summary: Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched success-failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills. Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) that converts each skill into supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction, strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex. Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents' robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics, supporting scalable agent training. Our code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex.
evidence_items.title: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively

evidence_items.summary: AI agents now browse and buy on people's behalf, and benchmarks measure how well the agents perform. Far less is known about the other side of the transaction: whether a merchant's website lets an agent in, publishes terms precise enough to decide a purchase, and leaves evidence of what was agreed. This paper presents a merchant-side benchmark built on those three questions and reports a pilot of it. The central measurement, decision sufficiency, rates each criterion of a concrete buyer mandate (total cost, cancellation or return terms, service date, variant identity) as determinate, indeterminate, or unknown from the merchant's own published evidence. Readiness scores carry their evidence coverage and missingness bounds; access is reported separately for a declared bot, a declared headless browser, and a user-present browser; and each observed term is mapped to the RAILS admissibility class of the evidence that could support it in a dispute. Four large merchants received the full assessment: three refused the declared profiles at their offer pages, and no mandate could be confirmed as met, because each merchant left a total or a refund term undetermined. An access census of 555 sites of merchants that two payment processors publicly name as clients found the home page unreadable to both declared profiles at 105 sites (18.9%). A declared assessment of 330 merchants, scored by deterministic rules without a rater, found that evidence coverage rather than the score decides who can be ranked: 115 merchants (35%) reached the ranking threshold, rankable profiles scored a median of 89 to 90, and material terms was the one pillar well below the others, because the all-in total was decidable at 18 merchants. The pilot shows that the measurements can be taken; it does not validate them or rank merchants, and the weights and the projected clearing band await validation against outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Get In, Decide, Prove: A Merchant-Side Readiness Benchmark for Agentic Commerce

evidence_items.summary: Building physical simulations from video requires coding agents to translate observations into executable models and refine them through tool use. We introduce PhysCodeGym, a benchmark for physically verifiable 4D reconstruction with $156$ tasks covering rigid-body, liquid, deformable, and wind-driven motion. Agents autonomously inspect videos, write and run Blender programs, and revise their scenes using simulation feedback. Six metrics combine rule-based measurements with rubric-based judgments to assess visual and physical reconstruction quality. Program inspection, scene measurements, and counterfactual interventions test physical consistency under original and modified conditions. Experiments with frontier coding agents reveal a tradeoff between artifact quality and completion across reasoning-effort settings, while harness comparisons and agent traces link verification behavior with reconstruction performance. Case studies show that matching visible objects and events can coexist with physical defects. Counterfactual tests further expose latent contact and support failures in reconstructions that pass ordinary physical checks, highlighting the gap between reproducing observations and building reliable physical models. Code is available at https://github.com/ShaoShuai0605/PhysCodeGym.
evidence_items.title: PhysCodeGym: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Physically Verifiable 4D Reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Static software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench suffer from three fundamental limitations: task sets are fixed and become saturated as model capabilities rapidly improve; expert construction is costly and slow; and difficulty levels cannot adapt to evolving model abilities. We present SEBGen, a self-evolving benchmark generation framework that synthesizes evaluation tasks from code repositories and continuously updates its generation strategies through an evolution loop. SEBGen introduces three key innovations: an explicit five-dimension exploration value evaluator that quantitatively scores generation strategies across quality, novelty, difficulty coverage, skill diversity, and evolution potential, replacing implicit LLM judgments; a hybrid validation pipeline combining three mechanical checks (schema, compile, functional), an LLM-based semantic assessment, and a repeated-judgment gate; and a self-evolving loop with archive-based experience accumulation, sigmoid-scaled parent selection, and LLM-driven strategy mutation. On a synthetic corpus, SEBGen achieves a 96 percent stage-level validation pass rate (E1; 48/50 stage observations) and preserves generation quality through the evolution loop while showing no measurable improvement over a budget-matched non-evolution baseline. On a real repository, it generates candidate benchmark tasks from all six tqdm commits that passed the schema and LLM-based screening stages, although the compile and functional stages could not be executed because these tasks carry no test patch. A judge-level comparison against SWE-bench Lite, partially corroborated by an independent judge from a different model family (Qwen), places generated real repository tasks below expert-constructed tasks (0.48 vs. 0.83 under deepseek-chat; 0.55 vs. 0.78 under qwen-plus, mean of two passes).
evidence_items.title: SEBGen: A Self-Evolving Benchmark Generation Framework for Software Engineering Agents

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/LatentRiskBench.
evidence_items.title: LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents
Plan-Action Consistency for Tool-Using LLM Agents: A Benchmark and a Lightweight Alignment Method

evidence_items.summary: GraphInstruct is a progressive benchmark for instruction-following graph generation by large language models. Version 1.0, on which the main experiments run, organizes 800 instructions into six constraint-type levels (L0 to L5) with 1,582 algorithmically synthesized reference solutions; version 1.1 adds 100 L5 items, for 900 instructions and 1,782 reference solutions. Outputs are scored on five dimensions with deterministic metrics, and two reference pools are included. This record holds the dataset, the raw model responses, the per-instance scores, and a snapshot of the code repository at the release commit. All archives extract into one folder and use the relative paths of the repository: GraphInstruct-1.1.0-dataset.tar.gz: the dataset alone (instructions, reference solutions, reference pools, the additional L5 items, the stress subset, the paraphrased instructions, the unchanged files of version 1.0, Croissant metadata, datasheet, data format description, data licence).- GraphInstruct-1.1.0-repository.tar.gz: every file of the repository at the release commit (dataset, evaluator, scripts, tests, per-instance quality scores, expected table fragments of the paper).- GraphInstruct-1.1.0-raw-responses-main.tar.gz: raw model responses of the 45 runs of the baseline survey as reviewed. Its four GPT-3.5 runs were served by a third-party relay and are superseded by the official GPT-3.5 runs in the next archive.- GraphInstruct-1.1.0-raw-responses-extended.tar.gz: all other raw model responses (the official GPT-3.5 runs, extended model panel, method runs and ablations, additional L5 items, paraphrased instructions, regenerated runs).- SHA256SUMS.txt and MANIFEST.tsv: checksums of the archives and of every archived file.

The dataset preserves the original 4-class annotations in the filenames while applying a custom binary relabeling scheme: Pathway 2 ( P2 ) trajectories are designated as positive (stored in good/ ), while all remaining phenotypes (Pathways 1 and 3, plus non-specific adhesion/noise) are pooled as negative (stored in bad/ ). The file good files.csv provides the reference list of 128 ground-truth positive samples for reproducibility and evaluation purposes. evidence_items.summary: This study aims to predict university students’ stress levels, risk of academic burnout, and an overall health  indicator – Health KPI – using machine learning methods based on their digital habits, academic  performance, and lifestyle-related characteristics. The study was conducted using a dataset comprising  3,000 students and 32 variables. XGBoost and the probabilistic NGBoost regression model were employed  for predictive modeling. The dataset was divided into training and test sets at an 80:20 ratio, while a 5-fold  cross-validation strategy was applied for hyperparameter optimization. Model performance was evaluated  using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and the coefficient of  determination (R²). The results showed that NGBoost outperformed XGBoost for both target variables. For  stress level prediction, NGBoost achieved MAE = 1.9339, RMSE = 2.3116, and R² = 0.3420, whereas for  burnout risk prediction, it achieved MAE = 1.9646, RMSE = 2.3321, and R² = 0.3230. In contrast, the  XGBoost model produced R² values of −0.0167 and −0.0267 for stress and burnout, respectively. Although  XGBoost achieved an R² value of 1.0000 for the formula-derived Health KPI, this result was interpreted  with caution because the exceptionally high predictive performance may be attributable to the  mathematical structure of the composite target itself. The findings indicate that probabilistic modeling  represents a promising approach for predicting student stress and academic burnout risk. They further  demonstrate that model evaluation should consider not only predictive accuracy but also the conceptual  meaning of the target variable and the method used to construct it.
evidence_items.title: PREDICTING UNIVERSITY STUDENT HEALTH KPIS  USING MACHINE LEARNING: THE IMPACT OF  DIGITAL HABITS AND LIFESTYLE ON ACADEMIC  BURNOUT

evidence_items.summary: Reliable engagement recognition is important for adaptive robot-assisted autism therapy (RAAT). However, progress remains constrained by the scarcity of publicly available benchmarks evaluated under realistic deployment conditions. Existing studies commonly adopt random train–test splits, which can inflate reported performance because recordings from the same child or therapy session may appear in both the training and test sets. To address this gap, we introduce QAMQOR, a benchmark dataset for engagement recognition collected during RAAT sessions with 34 children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), aged 3 − 12 years. The dataset includes visual engagement annotations derived from therapy session videos and feature representations extracted using two pose-estimation frameworks. The QAMQOR dataset defines four clinically relevant evaluation protocols based on Random, Child-Independent, Session-Independent, and Activity-Independent splits. These evaluation protocols assess model generalization to unseen children, therapy sessions and activity tasks. We benchmark classical machine learning classifiers together with temporal and sequence-learning baselines for both binary and multi-class engagement recognition. Experimental results show that the evaluation protocol influenced reported performance to a degree comparable to, and for fine-grained engagement classification exceeding, the influence of classifier selection: mean macro-F1 varied by 0.12 across the four protocols in the multi-class task, against 0.07 across discriminative classifiers. The Child-Independent split proved substantially more challenging than the Random split. Under the same conditions (windows, protocols, training schedule and untuned hyperparameters) a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) did not outperform the classical baselines.
evidence_items.title: QAMQOR: a benchmark dataset for engagement recognition in robot-assisted autism therapy

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Sanskrit morphology provides a setting for comparing explicit suffix rules and language-model predictions under changes in word order. This exploratory study evaluates a Python suffix classifier and supplied Gemini prediction files for 100 Bhagavad Gita entries representing 98 distinct verse identifiers. The corpus contains 614 split-token occurrences and 280 selective reference annotations. Natural and scrambled inputs preserve the same token multisets. A scoring audit identified repeated matching and unconditional credit for ambiguous outputs in the original symbolic evaluator. Using one-to-one annotation matching and candidate-set membership, the unchanged symbolic classifier achieved compatibility on 228/280 annotations (81.43%) in each order. The supplied natural and scrambled Gemini CSVs each achieved 242/280 compatible predictions (86.43%), after resolving one scrambled-token transcription mismatch by its input position. Only two of 614 paired Gemini classifications changed; neither affected the annotated score. The comparison shows no decrease in compatibility under scrambling and documents stable compatibility in this recorded comparison, alongside limitations from selective annotations, candidate ambiguity, and incomplete model metadata. The results describe robustness of these outputs under the supplied permutations rather than general word-order invariance or full morphological parsing accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Analysis of Rule Based Symbolic Logic and a Large Language Model in Sanskrit Morphological Analysis
&lt;p&gt;ScenePilot-4K: A Large-Scale First-Person Dataset and Benchmark for Vision-Language Models in Autonomous Driving&lt;/p&gt;

organizations: Texas Tech University , Lubbock, TX,
evidence_items.summary: Abstract The integration of AI into fact-checking has significantly enhanced the speed and scale of misinformation detection across digital platforms. AI-driven fact-checking systems can now access information in real-time, leveraging machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models. However, the same AI systems that enhance speed and scalability in verification also introduce new ethical and technical concerns. Biases embedded in training data, opaque algorithmic decision-making, and inconsistencies in human oversight can undermine fairness, accuracy, and accountability. Without robust safeguards, AI fact-checking may unintentionally propagate misinformation, exacerbate societal biases, and erode public trust in automated verification. This chapter examines the epistemic challenges AI fact-checking faces, namely bias, fairness, and accountability, against the backdrop of accelerating misinformation. It traces the evolution of verification technologies, evaluates the risks of static governance models, and proposes adaptive, participatory epistemic infrastructures as essential to sustaining public trust. It calls for a shift from technical optimization toward democratic and ethically anchored verification ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Fact-Checking

evidence_items.summary: LLMs are increasingly being embedded into a variety of distributed agentic systems, in the form of agents with APIs, microservices, workflows, and external tools for task completion. Systems need to be able to handle requests that are worded differently but mean the same thing, to make sure routing is consistent, caching can be reused, latency is reduced, reliability is ensured, and governance is supported. Conventional intent representations, beyond simply conveying what users want with their intent and respective slots, do not encode information about user authorization, policies with implications for execution, side effects of actions, locality of execution, and operational implications of intents. Prior work has provided frameworks for normalization, capability discovery and routing in distributed agentic systems, but all this work is done independently and thus does not provide a unified pipeline for handling requests in distributed systems. The main contribution of this paper is to propose a unified framework describing the normalization, discovery, routing, execution control and runtime feedback in distributed agentic systems. The core of this work is the introduction of a canonical representation of intent, called an intent record, which can convey all kinds of semantic information, as well as context, policy, and operational information about the system as a whole, including its uncertainty, to be used by the system’s routing layer. We also introduce a new constraint-first multi-criteria routing process. A reference architecture is also given for such sorts of systems. The architecture’s main functional components are semantic control and its decoupled, cross-governance-deterministic execution. An evaluation framework for the proposed approach in the future is also presented. This framework is not validated through implementation or benchmarking experiments. Such an empirical evaluation is left for future work.
evidence_items.title: AI-Based Intent Normalization and Service Routing in Distributed Agentic Microservices

organizations: University of East London
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models and agentic artificial intelligence provide the reasoning layer of autonomous aerial and ground robots, but the architectures remain fragmented across the two communities. This systematic review, reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 statement, searched ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, ProQuest, EBSCO, and Google Scholar from January 2020 through April 2026. Of 5298 records, 2228 remained after duplicates were removed and 124 studies were included: 67 aerial, 41 ground, and 16 on both platforms or a generic architecture. Six patterns appear, from a language model used only as a task-specific tool to an end-to-end foundation model, such as vision-language-action models. Open-loop pipelines, closed-loop pipelines, hierarchical executives, and multi-agent systems lie between those extremes. The model carries semantic reasoning, task decomposition, and tool orchestration, while classical planners and controllers retain trajectories, safety, and real-time control. Memory appears in 62 of 124 studies (50%) and function calling in 37 (30%), yet only 13 (10%) run the model onboard and 44 (35%) validate a physical robot. Aerial systems emphasize long-range vision and mission planning; ground systems emphasize local perception and interaction; both follow the same hybrid pattern. A suitability matrix shows that specialized vision models remain preferable for geometric perception. Designers should match the pattern to the task dynamics and choose the model for latency, safety, and where inference runs, rather than for benchmark score alone. Hallucination, spatial reasoning, inference latency, and the lack of standardized evaluation still limit deployment.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models and Agentic AI Architectures for Aerial and Ground Robots: A Systematic Review, Taxonomy, and Design Guidelines

organizations: Department of Software Engineering, Fatima Jinnah Women University
Department of Computer Science, Pakistan Navy Engineering College (PNEC), National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST)
Department of Computer Sciences, Quaid-i-Azam University
Department of Ocean Engineering, Harbin Institute of Technology Weihai
evidence_items.summary: Introduction Undetected calibration drift in autonomous ocean sensors corrupts temperature and salinity records underpinning climate reanalysis, seasonal forecasting, and marine ecosystem assessments. With 15–20% of active Argo floats showing meaningful drift at any time and correction workflows taking three to six months, scalable autonomous quality control is urgently needed. Methods We present DriftGuard, a five-component autonomous framework integrating a physically-informed heterogeneous sensor graph over 135 nodes, a Hybrid Temporal Transformer and Graph Attention Network (HybridTGAT), a cross-sensor consistency loss, a conformal prediction wrapper, and a LangGraph-orchestrated three-stage agentic loop supported by a 2,183-chunk RAG store. Results Evaluated on Argo float profiles (116 floats, North Atlantic, 2021–2024), NDBC buoy time series (15 stations, 2019–2024), and the expert-labelled AdapAD benchmark, DriftGuard achieves a GAT-level ROC-AUC of 0.8376, an AdapAD zero-shot AUC of 0.8423, and detects gradual drift types an average of 84.7 readings earlier than the operational Argo QC Test 16 baseline. Operational fleet evaluation across 131 sensors identifies 13 floats in a CRITICAL state requiring correction within 24 hours. Discussion DriftGuard is the first system in the marine sensor domain to unify graph-based spatial reasoning, temporal modelling, autonomous LLM-driven correction, conformal uncertainty certificates, and closed-loop retraining within a single operational pipeline, demonstrating readiness for real-world deployment.
evidence_items.title: DriftGuard: an agentic hybrid temporal transformer and graph attention network framework for autonomous calibration drift detection and correction in distributed marine sensor networks

evidence_items.summary: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
evidence_items.title: Virtual Head Attention

evidence_items.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) remains challenging for low-resource languages, where the scarcity of transcribed speech limits the development of accurate systems. This challenge is particularly acute for African languages such as Ewe, which has millions of speakers but remains underrepresented in publicly available ASR resources and benchmarks. In this work, we consolidate, normalize, and partition existing Ewe speech resources into a standardized 174-hour Ewe ASR benchmark, the largest to date to our knowledge. We fine-tune and evaluate pretrained speech models, including Whisper and AfriHuBERT, to establish strong baselines on our benchmark. Whisper-medium achieves a word error rate (WER) of 37.98%, while AfriHuBERT achieves 39.70% on the test set. We further provide a qualitative analysis of common recognition errors. We release the benchmark under the name Nufo, derived from the Ewe word for "talk", accompanied by models and evaluation resources, to facilitate future research on Ewe and other underrepresented African languages.
evidence_items.title: Nufo: A Benchmark for Ewe Automatic Speech Recognition

evidence_items.summary: Deep Research agents rely on long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool use to solve complex information-seeking tasks. However, adaptive decision-making over these trajectories remains challenging, as agents may stop prematurely when further evidence is needed, continue unnecessarily after sufficient evidence has been gathered, or fail to redirect unproductive trajectories. Existing solutions either require costly model retraining and dense turn-level supervision, or rely on heuristic control rules that are not directly optimized for downstream research utility. This motivates a lightweight, utility-aware alternative for Deep Research control. We formulate adaptive rerouting in long-horizon Deep Research as a state-conditioned trajectory correction problem. Based on this view, we introduce RIVO, a lightweight plug-in framework for adaptive trajectory correction. The agent estimates its research state from lightweight signals and determines whether trajectory redirection is needed. Once triggered, the plug-in modifies the Host token logits to steer generation toward a more promising research direction. Theoretical analysis shows that, under a value-alignment condition and bounded local curvature, a sufficiently small logit intervention can locally improve expected downstream research utility. We further construct BrowseCore, a curated dataset with a paired local corpus, for efficient and controlled Deep Research experimentation. Building on this resource, the plug-in is trained from downstream outcomes, enabling it to learn corrections that improve subsequent research and final task performance. Extensive experiments across multiple Deep Research benchmarks and control settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showing that lightweight logit intervention can improve long-horizon research without retraining the underlying Host model.
evidence_items.title: RIVO: Lightweight Adaptive Rerouting for Deep Research Agents

evidence_items.summary: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.
evidence_items.title: Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners

evidence_items.summary: A benchmark score is a measurement whose uncertainty has two sources: an aleatoric component from stochastic decoding and an epistemic component from the finite problem set. Using 16 models on 99 recent LeetCode-style problems with two prompts and five runs each (15,840 judged runs in a fully crossed design), we estimate both components and ask a design question: how much can repeated running buy? First, the pooled-binomial interval that repeated-run protocols invite answers neither question of interest---it is about $2\times$ too narrow for generalisation to new problems and $2\times$ too wide for the fixed problem set---and under correctly clustered intervals, 12 of 15 adjacent leaderboard pairs are statistically unresolved. Second, the variance ceiling $1+\mu_w/\sigma_b^2$, the largest factor by which repetition can reduce score variance, has median 1.34 across models (range 1.05--1.71), so repetition can narrow confidence intervals by at most 23% on this benchmark, and by 14% for the median model. Third, once the cost of adding verified problems is priced in, the precision-optimal repeat count is $R^{*}=\sqrt{\mu_w c_p/(\sigma_b^2 c_g)}$, and the variance curve is flat around it: on this benchmark the decisive reason to repeat is not precision but identification---two to three runs suffice to estimate the components that the ceiling and the fixed-benchmark interval require. All three are measurements of one benchmark at one decoding temperature, and we state explicitly what they do and do not license.
evidence_items.title: How Much Can Repeated Running Buy? A Measured Variance Ceiling for LLM Code Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Modern video games provide a measurable testbed for AI models, combining abilities of visual understanding, instruction decomposition, goal planning, and precise action control over multiple temporal horizons. Existing datasets and benchmarks, however, either cover a narrow range of games, lack language instructions, or rely on high-variance online rollouts. To address these challenges, we introduce GameHorizon, a unified data and evaluation suite that measures gameplay capabilities at different horizons for diverse model families. GameHorizon Suite consists of three components. First, GameHorizon-Annotator is a scalable and automated annotation pipeline for multi-horizon instructions. Second, utilizing the pipeline, we construct GameHorizon-Data, the first large-scale AAA gameplay dataset with temporally aligned videos, player actions, and multi-horizon instructions. It comprises 5,000 hours of recordings from 21 games, collected by 100 human expert players. Third, we build GameHorizon-Bench with reproducible offline and stepwise online testing. The offline track enables reproducible evaluation using thousands of standardized questions organized into three primary tasks and a series of diagnostic variants, while the online track tests whether offline scores reflect actual gameplay capabilities and localizes failures to specific steps within long-horizon gameplay. Based on our GameHorizon Suite, we evaluate 47 models through more than one million model invocations, revealing a meaningful hierarchy of task difficulty and pronounced differences in model capabilities. Our work can provide a standardized yardstick for evaluating gameplay capabilities across horizons and model families. We will release our dataset, annotator, and benchmark to facilitate future research.
evidence_items.title: GameHorizon Suite: Multi-Horizon Data and Evaluation in Gameplay

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: The proposed pipeline integrates a representation-flow convolutional neural network with a dynamics- and uncertainty-aware tree-based Gaussian Process classifier. In this framework, latent motion dynamics are exploited both as discriminative representations and as a source of input uncertainty, enhancing robustness against temporal variations and abnormal motion transitions. Compared with conventional deep learning approaches, the proposed strategy requires less training data and offers improved computational efficiency. To further improve classification performance, we introduce novel semantic-aware compound kernels that effectively capture semantic, flow, and dynamic information embedded in surgical video features. In addition, uncertainty-aware kernels are developed to strengthen the robustness and practical applicability of the compound kernel framework. The proposed method is evaluated on two benchmark datasets, namely the JIGSAWS and the Cataract-LMM (Capsulorhexis) datasets. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance across both datasets, including the LOSO and LOUO evaluation protocols on JIGSAWS, including the subject-independent LOUO protocol on JIGSAWS, on which the framework attains a mean accuracy of \ph{96.9}\%; results under the within-subject LOSO protocol are reported for comparability with prior work, achieving competitive accuracy while substantially reducing computational cost. Overall, the proposed pipeline provides an efficient and accurate framework for video-based surgical skill assessment.
evidence_items.title: Video-based Surgical Skill Assessment Using Dynamics-and-Uncertainty-Aware Tree-based Gaussian Process Classifier

evidence_items.summary: Feature engineering remains a cornerstone of tabular data analysis, and Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for its automation, giving rise to LLM-powered Automated Tabular Feature Engineering (LATTE). However, the field lacks standardized, cost-aware evaluation platforms, and the combinatorial explosion of design choices obscures true algorithmic progress. To bridge these gaps, we systematically deconstruct 15 representative LATTE methods into a unified 6-dimensional taxonomy. Based on this abstraction, we introduce LATTEArena, a standardized, modular, and extensible benchmarking framework that decouples monolithic pipelines into reusable execution blocks. By distilling the massive combinatorial space, we evaluate 24 core LATTE configurations across 7 research questions. Our head-to-head benchmarking goes beyond predictive accuracy to quantify token efficiency and execution robustness, yielding 17 empirical findings on cost-effectiveness trade-offs. Furthermore, we provide 3 concrete recommendations for optimal real-world deployment. By enabling controlled component-level comparisons, LATTEArena shifts the paradigm from ad-hoc prompt engineering to systematic context management. All code, datasets, and over 4,000 execution logs are publicly available to foster a dynamic, community-driven benchmark. Our framework, leaderboard, and all artifacts are hosted on the LATTEArena project website at https://goodenhak.github.io/LATTEArena.
evidence_items.title: LATTEArena: An Evaluation Framework for LLM-powered Tabular Feature Engineering (Extended Version)

evidence_items.summary: Parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is a cornerstone of their success, yet remains poorly understood. Existing knowledge benchmarks typically rely on predefined questions (e.g., "What is the birth date of M.L. King?"), evaluating only knowledge that benchmark designers explicitly choose to query, a problematic availability bias. In this paper, we introduce open knowledge evaluation, a new paradigm for benchmarking the stated knowledge of LLMs. Instead of asking narrow questions, it evaluates models on the knowledge they choose to surface in response to open-ended elicitation prompts (e.g., "Tell me everything you know about M.L. King"). This shifts the focus from predefined answer retrieval toward characterizing the knowledge models naturally express. We instantiate this paradigm with BeQu (Beyond Questions), a benchmark of 10,000 entities paired with reference corpora for statement verification. Using BeQu, we evaluate a broad range of language models and analyze the effects of reasoning effort, model scale, prompt format, and knowledge domain. Data and leaderboard are available on this work's GitHub repository and at ANONYMIZED.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Questions: Evaluating the Stated Knowledge of LLMs

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: Forests worldwide are increasingly threatened by climate change and disturbances such as fire, pests, and pathogens, creating a need for scalable monitoring of tree cover and tree mortality. Aerial imagery from drones and aircraft enables detailed mapping of tree crowns and mortality, but progress is limited by the lack of globally distributed, multi-biome, harmonized datasets for joint segmentation of tree cover and mortality. To address this, we introduce two open, machine-learning-ready datasets for joint segmentation of tree cover and tree mortality from centimeter-scale aerial imagery across globally distributed sites. Our training dataset, DTE-aerial-train, comprises 346K image patches of $1024 \times 1024$ pixels at spatial resolutions from 2.5 to 20\,cm, with audited pseudo-labels for tree cover and mortality and expert annotations for rare mortality sites. Our evaluation dataset, DTE-aerial-bench, is a multi-biome, multi-resolution benchmark of 25 globally distributed orthoimages (525 patches) with expert annotations for both tree cover and mortality. Both datasets span tropical, temperate, boreal, and dryland biomes and cover a wide range of forest structures and mortality patterns. Using the benchmark, we establish reference baselines for mortality and tree cover segmentation across biomes and spatial resolutions. Improvements over prior models vary by biome: they are largest in boreal and montane forests (F1 from 0.40 to 0.58) and smaller in tropical forests and drylands. For data, model and code, please visit our \href{https://ayushi-3536.github.io/deadtrees_aerial.github.io/}{project page}. An interactive visualization of the benchmark dataset is also available at \href{https://deadtrees.earth/releases/dte-aerial-bench}{our release page}.
evidence_items.title: deadtrees.earth-aerial: A Multi-Resolution Aerial Image Dataset for Tree Cover and Mortality Detection

evidence_items.summary: Deep learning underpins a wide range of applications in MRI, including reconstruction, artifact removal, and segmentation. However, progress has been driven largely by public datasets focused on brain and knee imaging, shaping how models are trained and evaluated. As a result, careful studies of the reliability of these models across diverse anatomical settings remain limited. In this work, we introduce MosaicMRI, a large and diverse collection of fully sampled raw musculoskeletal (MSK) MR measurements designed for training and evaluating machine-learning--based methods. MosaicMRI is the largest open-source raw MSK MRI dataset to date, comprising 3,150 volumes and 89,830 slices, including a 3,096-volume 1.5~T core dataset and a 54-volume 0.55~T low-field set. The dataset offers substantial diversity in volume orientation (e.g., axial, sagittal), imaging contrasts (e.g., PD, T1, T2), anatomies (e.g., spine, knee, hip, ankle, and others), numbers of acquisition coils, and field strengths. Using accelerated reconstruction as a testbed, we study scaling, robustness, and data selection under realistic MSK distribution shifts. Across E2E-VarNet, U-Net, and ViT baselines, mixed-anatomy training improves over anatomy-specific training, showing that the benefit of anatomical diversity is not architecture-specific. Zero-shot experiments on the 0.55~T low-field set highlight that using more training data improves average reconstruction under field-strength shift. Controlled subset experiments further suggest that these gains come from transferable cross-anatomy structure, rather than anatomy or contrast matching alone.
evidence_items.title: MosaicMRI: A Diverse Dataset and Benchmark for Raw Musculoskeletal MRI

evidence_items.summary: Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN, TabICL, ExaOneTabular, and Nori already produce full predictive distributions, yet prevailing regression benchmarks evaluate them almost exclusively via point-estimate metrics such as RMSE. This overlooks the distributional information these models are designed to provide. We introduce ScoringBench, an open and extensible benchmark that evaluates tabular regression models under a comprehensive suite of proper scoring rules - including (weighted) CRPS, energy scores and interval scores - alongside standard point metrics. ScoringBench covers 101 regression datasets from diverse domains, supports transparent community contributions via a git-based leaderboard, and provides two complementary ranking protocols: an ordinal Demsar/autorank approach and a magnitude-preserving $z$-score ranking approach. Our evaluation of various model types, including (fine-tuned) tabular foundation models, gradient-boosted trees, and MLPs, shows that model rankings shift depending on the chosen scoring rule. Models that perform well on point-estimate metrics can rank lower on probabilistic ones. These findings demonstrate that evaluation metric selection is a core modeling decision and a domain-specific requirement for applications where certain types of errors carry higher consequences.
evidence_items.title: ScoringBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models with Proper Scoring Rules

evidence_items.summary: Book image rectification presents unique challenges due to its complex geometric distortions from binding constraints, where left and right pages exhibit distinctly asymmetric curvature patterns. However, existing single-page document image rectification methods fail to capture the coupled geometric relationships between adjacent pages in books. In this work, we introduce BookNet, the first end-to-end deep learning framework specifically designed for dual-page book image rectification. BookNet adopts a dual-branch architecture with cross-page attention mechanisms, enabling it to estimate warping flows for both \rev{individual pages and the book spread}, explicitly modeling how left and right pages influence each other. Moreover, to address the absence of specialized datasets, we present Book3D, a large-scale synthetic dataset for training, and Book100, a comprehensive real-world benchmark for evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BookNet outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on book image rectification. \rev{Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Liu-Shaokai/BookNet.
evidence_items.title: BookNet: Book Image Rectification via Cross-Page Attention Network

evidence_items.summary: The African mining industry continues to face a serious communication gap between technical safety documentation and the language used by the workforce. Safety manuals, operating procedures, and regulatory guidance are often produced in English or French, while many workers communicate in isiZulu, chiShona, and other local languages. This mismatch is not just inconvenient; it can be dangerous in safety-critical settings where misunderstandings may contribute to preventable incidents. This paper reports on Talk MINING, a domain-adapted multilingual large language model built on InkubaLM and trained on mining-specific text, question–answer pairs, and multimodal hazard data. The model was developed using Hugging Face tools and evaluated with both quantitative and qualitative methods. Results show a marked improvement over the baseline model, with overall accuracy rising from below 50% to 82%, and strong gains across isiZulu, chiShona, and English. The project also includes a web-based prototype that allows users to take photos of mining conditions and receive guidance in a local language. This paper presents the full pipeline for Talk MINING, including document preparation, translation and localization, model training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and validation. Beyond benchmark performance, the system is designed for practical deployment in environments where connectivity is limited and literacy levels vary—supporting both text queries and image-based hazard input through a mobile-ready prototype. The work contributes a reproducible pipeline, a curated multilingual mining corpus, and an open evaluation framework that can serve as a foundation for extending domain-adapted AI to other African languages and safety-critical industries. Ultimately, Talk MINING demonstrates that closing the language gap in mining safety is not only technically feasible but achievable with relatively modest model size when domain adaptation is done rigorously.
evidence_items.title: A Domain-Adapted Multilingual Large Language Model for Mining Safety in African Languages

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed information interaction, yet their application in environmental science and engineering (ESE) is hindered by multimodal data formats, dynamic context requirements, and hallucination risks. To transition from general-purpose models to domain expert agentic systems, this Perspective introduces a three-pillar framework for ESE-LLMs: domain perception, knowledge grounding, and action capability. Implementing these capabilities introduces potential pitfalls such as geographic representation bias, catastrophic forgetting, and source authenticity vulnerabilities, which require strategic model blending and careful data curation to overcome. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation must extend beyond standard knowledge benchmarks to systematically assess factuality, fairness, consistency, and safety using both human and automated metrics. Finally, we present a decision-guided deployment workflow that helps researchers in ESE fields integrate LLMs into their workflow. Ultimately, achieving trustworthy environmental intelligence relies on continuous evaluation, robust governance, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration to safely deploy agentic ESE-LLMs for high-stakes environmental challenges.
evidence_items.title:
Putting Large Language
Models into Environmental Context

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) promises structured, traceable development of complex systems, but high modeling effort remains a key adoption barrier. The textual notation of SysML v2 turns model construction into a text-to-text generation problem, opening new avenues for large language model (LLM) automation. This paper presents AMADEUS (Agentic Model-Aided Development Engineering Utilizing SysML), a conceptual framework for integrating agentic AI into systems engineering workflows in automated driving. The AMADEUS framework comprises three contributions: (1) a work package concept that operationalizes a domain-specific Systems Engineering methodology into discrete units executable by agents and maps each section to orchestration patterns such as actor-critic validation and role-based routing, (2) two complementary architecture patterns, typed operations exposed by a dedicated model server and direct SysML v2 text editing in a Git-based workflow, with a comparative analysis, and (3) an empirical benchmark evaluating three late-2025 frontier AI agents (OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini 3 Pro, Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5) against a human expert reference on seven SysML v2 modeling tasks of varying complexity. The evaluation provides initial evidence that AI agents achieve comparable quality (average score 3.69 vs. 3.86 on a 0–4 scale) while reducing modeling time by a factor of approximately 12 and per-task execution cost by a factor of 3,500. Transformation tasks achieve average $$S {total} \ge 3.6$$ S total ≥ 3.6 out of 4, while deduction-heavy tasks reveal remaining gaps, suggesting that the engineer’s role shifts from model creator to model reviewer.
evidence_items.title: AMADEUS: A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Agentic AI into Model-Based Systems Engineering

evidence_items.summary: Phishing URL detection using machine learning has achieved near-perfect accuracy on popular benchmark datasets, but the extent to which these results generalize across datasets remains unclear. We train a Random Forest classifier on the PhiUSIIL phishing URL dataset (235,795 records) and evaluate it on the UCI Phishing Websites dataset (11,055 records), after mapping a subset of PhiUSIIL features into the UCI feature space. In-domain, our model achieves balanced accuracy of 0.9999 on a domain-separated PhiUSIIL test split and 0.9979 for a URL-lexical-feature-only variant. On the external UCI dataset, balanced accuracy drops to 0.9530 (full numeric) and 0.6753 (transfer experiment using 10 mapped features), with a generalization gap of 0.287. We further analyze 64 feature-vector groups with conflicting labels in the UCI dataset and show that a trained model is near chance-level on those rows, indicating an irreducible label-noise ceiling rather than a model deficiency. Our results argue that high in-domain performance is insufficient evidence of real-world reliability and that multi-dataset evaluation should be standard practice for phishing detectors.
evidence_items.title: Explainable and Robust Machine Learning for Phishing URL Detection: A Cross-Dataset Evaluation

The DIC technique measures the strain distribution within these minerals, offering valuable insights into their mechanical behavior and deformation characteristics in response to thermal changes. The thermal strain of both mineral grains and their boundaries is derived by averaging the thermal strain of the micro-pillars. evidence_items.summary: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
evidence_items.title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual perception and spatial reasoning, leading to growing interest in using them as high-level planners for embodied AI. However, physical tasks require models to integrate spatial information, reason over temporal states, and generate multi-step plans under various constraints, raising the question of whether current VLMs can reliably support such reasoning and planning independently of execution. We introduce Plan-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating the high-level reasoning and multi-step planning capabilities of VLMs relevant to embodied worlds, while isolating the influence of action execution. It covers three complementary dimensions, spanning 16 subclasses and 699 curated samples. Extensive evaluation of 28 VLMs reveals room for improvement, with even the strongest model achieving only 75.0% accuracy. We further find that model scaling generally improves these capabilities. Ablation studies also indicate larger models show increasing potential as high-level planners. Overall, Plan-Bench provides a lightweight probe for evaluating VLMs' reasoning and planning capabilities relevant to embodied environments and assessing their potential as decision makers for physical tasks. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/MinneFeng/Plan-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Plan-Bench: Can Existing VLMs Go Well Beyond Perception to Reason and Plan in Embodied Worlds?

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.
evidence_items.title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly generate Solidity smart contracts that, once deployed, can never be patched, making a single latent fault permanent and exploitable. Yet current evaluations mostly ask only whether generated code compiles. We introduce SolBehave, a benchmark for evaluating the correctness of model-generated contracts at scale, moving beyond ad hoc unit tests. Across 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts, we apply three complementary tests of behavioural fidelity: differential fuzzing, historical-transaction replay, and, as our core contribution, synthetic-transaction replay guided by a Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graph that enumerates the space of legitimate function-call sequences. Differential fuzzing compares each generated function with the original on automatically generated inputs; historical replay compares the whole contract on the transactions it actually received on-chain; DCR-guided replay compares it on sequences of calls that follow its intended usage, including orderings that never occurred on-chain. We evaluate seven state-of-the-art open-weight models after one round of automated repair. Compilation success ranges from 26.4% to 92.7%, but under differential fuzzing only 31.4% of all generated function bodies that compile, pooled over models and samples, are equivalent to the original. Divergence at the contract level is the norm rather than the exception: for six of the seven models, between 13% and 31% of the generated contracts that compile diverge from the original under historical replay, and between 13% and 44% under DCR-guided replay; only Gemma-4-31B stays below 3% on both. Compilation is therefore a necessary condition for correctness and far from a sufficient one.
evidence_items.title: SolBehave: Evaluating the Behavioural Correctness of LLM-Generated Smart Contracts

evidence_items.summary: 3D semantic occupancy prediction is crucial for autonomous driving, but camera-based methods degrade in low-light conditions and LiDAR-based methods are sensitive to adverse weather. 4D radar is more robust, yet its sparsity and the high cost of radar tensor processing limit its use. We propose Radar Geometric-Semantic Occupancy Prediction (RadarGSOcc), an efficient framework that directly processes 4D radar tensors by separately extracting geometric and semantic features, including Doppler information, with a deformable attention-based geometric refinement module as its key component. We also introduce the K-Radar 3DSemOcc benchmark, the first large-scale benchmark for 3D semantic occupancy prediction using 4D radar tensors, built on the K-Radar dataset with refined LiDAR-based annotations. RadarGSOcc predicts 15 classes within a 51.2m range and achieves 38.2% IoU, 7.6% mIoU, and 25.5% weighted mIoU, outperforming RadarOcc by 17% relative (25.5 vs. 21.9) in weighted mIoU while using fewer parameters and lower computation. It substantially improves truck prediction while trading off car accuracy, outperforms camera-based approaches, and narrows the gap with LiDAR-based methods. To assess robustness without per-frame ground truth in adverse weather, we further propose a novel proxy metric, Environment-Based KL Divergence (EBKL), under which 4D radar proves a reliable and efficient modality for 3D semantic occupancy prediction. The dataset and code will be publicly available.
evidence_items.title: RadarGSOcc: Doppler-Aware 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction Using 4D Radar Tensor with Geometric-Semantic Feature Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Audio memory must recognise recurring sources across acoustic changes while keeping their attributes up to date. Overall accuracy does not reveal how these demands interact. We introduce Audio Memory Operations (AMemOps), a benchmark for latest-attribute retrieval, preservation of unchanged attributes and absent-source rejection in long audio streams. Paired controls vary recordings, training identities and earlier events to examine their effects on updating. Training on other recordings of the test instruments increases a reference delta-rule memory's update advantage over matched attention by 13.4 percentage points. At retrieval delays of 120\,s, matched histories separate benefits of consistent repetition from costs of conflicting earlier values, while additive-memory controls identify benefits of erasure.
evidence_items.title: AMemOps: Evaluating Memory Updates in Long Audio Streams

evidence_items.summary: AI-based cellular perturbation prediction is essential to accelerate drug discovery and therapeutic identification. However, perturbation-specific signals are generally obscured by cellular complexity, making it difficult for existing methods to correctly capture perturbation effects. To address this problem, we propose PerturbEnergy, which introduces a conditional energy-based prior over perturbation representations. It assigns lower energy (higher probability) to representations compatible with the given perturbation and higher energy to others, thereby explicitly tilting the latent space toward perturbation-preferred regions. Besides, PerturbEnergy can be integrated into autoencoder architectures as we find its Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is equivalent to the ELBO of the complete autoencoder. We further prove that optimizing PerturbEnergy increases the lower bound on the conditional mutual information between representation and perturbation. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our PerturbEnergy: it improves perturbation recognition especially in latent space with improvement of up to 83.2\%; It also achieves state-of-the-art performance for predicting top-50/100/200 differentially expressed gene(DEG) response and remaining competitive on highly variable gene(HVG) prediction. The code is provided: https://github.com/BlueWhaleLab/PerturbEnergy
evidence_items.title: Learning Perturbation-Specific Representations through Conditional Energy Prior for Cellular Response Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) have significantly promoted using text-to-image (T2I) models to generate images with specific affective intentions. However, the emotional effects conveyed by generated images frequently deviate from target expectations, and it remains unclear whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reliably interpret the emotion of AI-generated visual content. Existing affective benchmarks are predominantly built on natural images, while affective studies of generated images have largely focused on emotions expressed in portraits, lacking a unified benchmark for studying the emotions expressed and evoked by generated images. We therefore introduce EmoGenie, a benchmark of emotion for AI-generated images that evaluates capabilities in T2I generation and MLLM understanding across expressed and evoked emotions. It comprises 6,400 images generated by eight T2I models using 800 emotion-targeted prompts, annotated with question-answer (QA) pairs, termed EmoGenie-QA, and continuous human ratings, termed EmoGenie-Assess. EmoGenie-QA contains 90,000 closed-set questions in single-image and image-pair settings, as well as 1,057 open-ended questions for emotion description. EmoGenie-Assess benchmarks continuous affective and aesthetic prediction using 13,175 mean opinion scores (MOSs) aggregated from human ratings in terms of valence, arousal, dominance, and aesthetic quality. We further develop EmoProbe, which combines emotion question answering with response-aligned, dimension-specific regression heads for continuous score prediction. Experimental results show that EmoProbe achieves superior results on emotion-related QA tasks, while its affective and aesthetic predictions correlate better with human ratings, demonstrating its state-of-the-art capabilities of unified coarse-to-fine affective understanding for AI-generated images.
evidence_items.title: EmoGenie: Benchmarking and Evaluating Expressed and Evoked Emotion in T2I Generation with MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Virtual footwear try-on (VFTON), a critical yet underexplored area in virtual try-on (VTON), aims to synthesize faithful try-on results given diverse footwear and model images while maintaining 3D consistency and texture authenticity. Unlike conventional garment-focused VTON methods, VFTON presents unique challenges due to (1) Data Scarcity, which arises from the difficulty of perfectly matching product shoes with models wearing the identical ones, (2) Viewpoint Misalignment, where the target foot pose and source shoe views are always misaligned, leading to incomplete texture information and detail distortion, and (3) Background-induced Color Distortion, where complex material of footwear interacts with environmental lighting, causing unintended color contamination. To address these challenges, we introduce MVShoes, a multi-view shoe try-on dataset consisting of 7305 well-annotated image triplets, covering diverse footwear categories and challenging try-on scenarios. Furthermore, we propose a dual-stream DiT architecture, ShoeFit, designed to mitigate viewpoint misalignment through Multi-View Conditioning with 3D Rotary Position Embedding, and alleviate background-induced distortion using the LayeredRefAttention which leverages background features to modulate footwear latents. The proposed framework effectively decouples shoe appearance from environmental interferences while preserving high-quality texture detail through decoupled denoising and conditioning branches. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method substantially improves rendering fidelity and robustness under challenging real-world product shoes, establishing a new benchmark in high-fidelity footwear try-on synthesis.
evidence_items.title: ShoeFit: A New Dataset and Dual-image-stream DiT Framework for Virtual Footwear Try-On

evidence_items.summary: Reward models are central to preference alignment for legal tasks, yet existing reward model benchmarks are still primarily centered on general-domain preferences. In this work, we introduce LegalRewardBench, the first human-verified benchmark for evaluating reward models in the legal domain. The benchmark organizes legal preference evaluation into five capability levels: knowledge, understanding, analysis, decision, and writing, and preference examples are constructed through rubric-guided automatic judging combined with human verification. We evaluate three families of judges, covering both general and fine-tuned models, and generative and discriminative architectures. Experimental results show that strong general-purpose generative models are currently the most robust legal reward models, while existing fine-tuned reward models transfer less reliably to legal preference evaluation. We also conduct detailed comparisons of input organizations and training strategies.
evidence_items.title: LegalRewardBench: Benchmarking Reward Models for Legal Preference Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks are essential for evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs). Yet many widely used benchmarks are redundant, making evaluation unnecessarily expensive. Benchmark compression lowers this cost by estimating full-benchmark scores and rankings from a partial evaluation. Research in this area has grown rapidly since 2024, but to our knowledge no survey has systematically organized its methods and findings. We review 119 papers to explain how methods choose what to evaluate, recover full-benchmark results, and verify their reliability. From this analysis, we develop a taxonomy covering compression within individual benchmarks, across benchmark suites, and during adaptive evaluation, together with work on redundancy and reliability. We compare their information needs, total costs, reliability checks, and limitations. Methods reduce evaluation costs by selecting representative subsets, using cheaper or reusable information, and testing adaptively, but risk poor coverage, inaccurate estimates, and sequential delays. The resulting taxonomy and practical guide help researchers choose, validate, and deploy methods for more efficient and reliable LLM evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Are We Testing Too Much? A Survey of Benchmark Compression for Efficient Evaluation of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Task-oriented dialogue understanding remains underexplored for Bangla, particularly in multilingual settings involving English and romanized Bangla (Banglish). We introduce BanglaTOD, a parallel tri-lingual benchmark comprising 209 multi-turn dialogues across nine Bangladesh-specific service domains and 64 intents. Each conversational turn is aligned across Bangla, English, and Banglish, yielding 4,689 language-specific turn records annotated with intents, token-level slots, state updates, and accumulated dialogue states. We establish context-aware baselines for joint intent classification and slot filling using mBERT, BERT-base-uncased, and BanglaBERT. Cross-language analysis reveals substantial performance differences across models and linguistic representations, while removing dialogue history reduces intent accuracy by 19.0--25.7 percentage points. BanglaTOD provides a foundation for multilingual dialogue understanding and future dialogue state tracking research in Bangladesh-specific conversational applications. The dataset is publicly available at \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/afri7here/BanglaTOD}{Hugging Face}.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Bangla Task-Oriented Dialogue Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is an important image/video processing problem for reliable visual systems under poor illumination, yet it remains challenging due to the strong coupling among insufficient illumination, noise amplification, and structural degradation. Existing methods typically rely on sophisticated network architectures or engineered objective functions. While effective, the former increases model complexity and deployment burden, whereas the latter relies on empirically tuned loss weights. We revisit supervised LLIE from a training-dynamics perspective and observe that brightness-related errors tend to converge early, while residual noise and structural artifacts often remain insufficiently optimized in later stages. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Interpolation Training-only Module (DITM), which introduces no additional learnable parameters and adaptively reshapes the model prediction for supervised feed-forward LLIE training. Specifically, DITM employs brightness-aware interpolation, in which the model prediction is combined with a mean brightness-aligned image constructed by rescaling the model prediction according to the mean brightness of the ground-truth image. By reducing the relative dominance of global brightness discrepancy, DITM makes residual local errors more influential during backpropagation after global luminance has largely stabilized, thereby facilitating artifact suppression and fine-detail restoration in later training stages. DITM is used only during training and is fully removed at inference, introducing no additional inference cost. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and CNN-, Transformer-, and Mamba-based LLIE backbones show that DITM consistently improves fidelity and perceptual quality while preserving the inference-time architecture and introducing no additional inference-time computation.
evidence_items.title: Dynamic Interpolation for Training-Time Prediction Reshaping in Low-Light Image Enhancement

evidence_items.summary: Recovering high-quality images from degraded underwater observations is crucial for underwater exploration. Polarization observations show promise as an effective source of complementary physical cues for recovering target radiance under clear-water conditions. However, existing methods have yet to jointly model raw intensity information and polarization cues to enable image restoration driven by an understanding of mixed degradations (color casts, haze, and low light). To overcome these limitations, we propose PolUR, a unified multimodal language-driven framework that jointly uses polarization and RGB information to identify degradation types and severity levels through structured semantic instructions and enhances joint restoration representations under the guidance of degradation-aware semantic features to improve restoration robustness under mixed degradations. We further construct a new benchmark named MixPolar, which contains underwater images exhibiting real-world degradations and their corresponding degradation descriptions. MixPolar supports systematic evaluation of degradation perception, image restoration, and performance on downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PolUR effectively integrates polarization and RGB information, achieving competitive performance in degradation perception and image restoration, while also demonstrating generalization capability and utility for downstream tasks.
evidence_items.title: PolUR: Polarization Aware Multimodal Degradation Perception for Underwater Image Restoration

evidence_items.summary: We present Swiss4Arg, a multilingual dataset for argument mining based on official Swiss voting brochures, covering all four national languages: German, French, Italian, and Romansh (a Romance minority language exclusively spoken in Switzerland). The brochures contain explicitly formulated arguments systematically organized into pro and con sections, resulting in a cross-lingually aligned resource with balanced argumentative stance. We create a dataset that comprises 53 federal voting issues collected between 2019 and 2025, annotated for argument components (major claims, claims, premises, and non-argumentative units) and relations (support and attack) by three native speakers per language. Inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) reaches 0.548 for component classification and 0.623 for relation and target classification, computed jointly across all annotators on the parallel data. We release both adjudicated labels and individual annotator annotations, enabling analyses of disagreement and cross-linguistic variation, and provide baseline results using GPT-5.4 and SwissBERT. Swiss4Arg establishes a novel benchmark for multilingual argument mining, with a particular focus on cross-lingual comparability and low-resource settings such as Romansh. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://anonymous-hf.up.railway.app/a/gozw0nion72y/ (HuggingFace) and https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MultiVote-03BD/ (GitHub).
evidence_items.title: Swiss4Arg: A Parallel Dataset for Multilingual Argument Mining across Swiss National Languages

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to discover scientific equations from experimental data. Such a discovery system has two parts that must work together: a library of executable computational tools and the model's tool-use policy. The tools supply the solving capability, from diagnosing structure in the data to fitting candidate equations; the policy plans and orchestrates their use. Yet existing systems adapt only one part, keeping either the toolset or the model fixed, which leaves the corresponding failures uncorrectable. We develop a coupled evolution framework that improves both parts from the same verifiable fit-error signal. In the tool-evolution phase, an agent grows an executable tool library from a small set of generic numerical operations by diagnosing its own failures: it authors a new tool when a capability is missing and revises its selection rules when the right tool went unused. In the policy-evolution phase, a small open model (roughly 3B active parameters) is fine-tuned on successful tool-use trajectories collected with the frozen library, on training formulas screened to be disjoint from all evaluation benchmarks. Ablations show the two phases are complementary: with no tool library at all the same model solves almost nothing, the tools account for most of the gain, and trajectory training adds a further gain that is largest on the most difficult problems. The full system solves 79.1/71.3\% of LSR-Synth problems at fit tolerances $10^{-2}$/$10^{-3}$, reaches 63.8\% pooled accuracy on the distributionally different SRSD-Feynman panel, and obtains a normalized CP3-28 aggregate of $-7.27$. These results suggest a broader recipe for scientific agents: let the model and its instruments improve each other under verifiable feedback.
evidence_items.title: Coupled Harness--Model Evolution for Scientific Equation Discovery

evidence_items.summary: End-to-end (E2E) full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) enable simutanous listening and speaking continously, requiring models to take appropriate interaction actions as conversations unfold. However, existing benchmarks lack a structured action-level formulation, often evaluate action occurrence rather than success, and provide limited coverage of diverse real-world conversations. We introduce DuplexAct, a benchmark for evaluating interaction action taking in E2E FD-SLMs. DuplexAct defines a three-level action taxonomy spanning eight interaction actions and 24 corresponding interaction conditions. We further characterize successful action-taking through immediate execution and subsequent follow-through, and develop action-specific evaluation metrics for both. DuplexAct contains 4,691 test instances spanning casual conversation, meetings, customer service, and interviews, including 2,531 instances derived from real-world conversational recordings. Together, DuplexAct provides a structured and real-world-grounded framework for systematically assessing how E2E FD-SLMs participate in ongoing spoken interaction.
evidence_items.title: DuplexAct: How Interactive Are Frontier Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models?
