We introduce AfriEconQA, a benchmark for document-grounded question answering built from 204 World Bank economic reports on African economies, a corpus whose claims are tied to specific fiscal periods, countries, and projection states. AfriEconQA contains 4,138 evidence-linked QA instances across five reasoning categories: Factoid (1,063), List (852), Multiple Choice (889), Synthesis (671), and Comparison (663), targeting quantitative extraction, set recovery, discrimination, causal integration, and cross-period or cross-country reasoning. Each instance carries supporting evidence and source provenance and is constructed through an agentic generation pipeline with evidence-grounding checks and a stratified human-validation subset for gold-label auditing. We evaluate Qwen 3.6 35B, DeepSeek v4-pro, Gemma 4 12B IT, and frontier model GPT-5.5 under zero-shot, oracle, and hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) conditions on the held-out test split (n = 826). Across all four models, retrieval yields substantial gains, yet the best RAG system reaches only 0.594 F1, with residual errors concentrated in list extraction, synthesis, and temporally scoped comparison. AfriEconQA therefore poses a hard open challenge for exact numerical and temporal grounding over long institutional economic reports.
evidence_items.title: AfriEconQA: A Benchmark for Quantitative and Temporal Reasoning over World Bank Economic Reports

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating AI-generated video (AIGV) quality hinges on three crucial dimensions: visual quality, dynamic quality, and text-video alignment. While numerous evaluation datasets and algorithms have been proposed, existing approaches are constrained by two limitations: the absence of systematic definitions for evaluation dimensions, and the isolated treatment of the three dimensions in separate models. Therefore, we introduce Q-Save, a holistic benchmark dataset and unified evaluation model for AIGV quality assessment. The Q-Save dataset contains nearly 10,000 video samples, each annotated with Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) and fine-grained attribution explanations across the three core dimensions. Leveraging this attribution-annotated dataset, we train the proposed Q-Save model, which adopts the SlowFast framework to balance accuracy and efficiency, and employs a three-stage training strategy with Chain-of-Thought (COT) formatted data: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a final SFT round for stability, to jointly perform quality scoring and attribution generation. Experimental results demonstrate that Q-Save achieves superior performance in AIGV quality prediction while providing interpretable justifications. Code and dataset will be released upon publication.
evidence_items.title: Q-Save: Towards Scoring and Attribution for Generated Video Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Adherent raindrops on camera lenses are a pervasive source of real-world image degradation, undermining outdoor visual perception for downstream applications such as robotics and 3D scene reconstruction. However, most existing raindrop datasets and methods target only background-focused 2D images, overlooking the equally common raindrop-focused case and the impact of raindrops on 3D scene reconstruction. Moreover, they are almost exclusively daytime, lacking the complex artificial lighting and reflections of nighttime raindrop scenes. To address these issues, we introduce OmniRaindrop, a real-world dataset and benchmark that jointly evaluates 2D raindrop removal and 3D scene reconstruction across raindrop-focused and background-focused captures, under both daytime and nighttime conditions. OmniRaindrop provides spatially aligned raindrop-focused, background-focused, and rain-free ground-truth image sets: a 2D subset of 15,186 aligned pairs/triplets and a 3D subset of 40 real-world scenes evenly split between day and night, totaling 3,822 multi-view images. On top of this data, the benchmark traces how raindrop degradation propagates from 2D restoration to 3D reconstruction by testing representative restoration methods and their effects on pose estimation, point cloud initialization, and 3DGS optimization. Comprehensive experiments reveal that raindrop-focused scenes are substantially harder than background-focused ones, and that errors in 2D restoration and pose/point cloud initialization cascade into degraded 3D reconstruction, pointing to clear directions for more robust 2D restoration and 3DGS design. Building on the dataset, we have organized two consecutive NTIRE challenges (2025 and 2026) on Day and Night Raindrop Removal for Dual-Focused Images.
evidence_items.title: OmniRaindrop: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Dual-Focused Raindrop Removal under Day and Night Scenes

evidence_items.summary: cruscy data — evaluation sample Three full days of real crypto market microstructure (Binance spot), prepared for public evaluation: absolute prices, dates, and the instrument are withheld — the shape of the day (tick-by-tick relative price, normalized volumes, trade side, book imbalance) is fully preserved. The full feed — 27+ streams (raw L2 depth, 1-second trade tape, order-book metrics, derived features, regime labels) with SQL console, backtest runner and MCP access for AI… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/GOD111111111/synthetic-timeseries-data.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the raw and processed data used in the study “Estimation and evaluation of a feeding coefficient of cotton pink bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella Saunders) on cotton bolls for yield loss assessment.” The data were generated through controlled feeding experiments and evaluated using an independent dataset. The dataset includes measurements of oven-dried seed cotton dry matter from individual cotton bolls subjected to different larval density treatments of pink bollworm (0, 1, and 2 larvae per boll). The difference in dry matter between uninfested and infested bolls was used to estimate feeding coefficients and quantify percent yield loss attributable to larval feeding. Dataset contents The repository contains the following data files: Raw experimental data Fresh boll weight before larval infestation Oven-dried seed cotton weight per boll after larval feeding Treatment-wise larval density (0, 1, or 2 larvae per boll) Replication information: Model development = 50 bolls in the control. 39 bolls with one larva per boll and 30 bolls with 2 larvae per boll. n = 119 Evaluation dataset: 30 control bolls, 19 bolls with one larva per boll and 14 bolls with 2 larvae per boll. n = 63 Derived variables Dry matter loss per boll Percent dry matter loss Feeding coefficient (g larva⁻¹ day⁻¹) Evaluation dataset Multi-season field observations on loculi damage Percent seed cotton weight loss derived from healthy vs PBW-damaged loculi Multi-location field survey data across India Statistical analysis outputs Multiple linear and quadratic regression analyses Bootstrap resampling analysis Evaluation statistics including RMSE and Mean Bias Error (MBE) Methods Summary Analysis uses individual-boll observations and estimates final dry weight as a function of initial fresh boll weight and larval exposure (larva-days).
evidence_items.title: Dataset for: Estimation and evaluation of a feeding coefficient of cotton pink bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella) for yield loss assessment

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the data and code for an automated EIS equivalent-circuit fitting pipeline based on PCA-space nearest-neighbour matching and multistart CNLS fitting, implemented as Orange (Demšar et al., 2013) workflows. Version 2.0 (October 2026) extends the pipeline with (i) batch fitting of many spectra with an extended multistart (TOP K = 20 nearest-neighbour starts per candidate topology) and parallel processing, (ii) a revised topology selection criterion combining χ² equivalence (floor 1e-16, tolerance 1.5) with Jacobian-based parameter determinability, and (iii) a widget that automatically sets the Circuit, Sample and true-parameter columns as text metadata, so that new input files can be loaded without manual settings. The reference database (Training data) consists of the BatteryDEV training spectra (Schaeffer et al., J. Electrochem. Soc. 170 (2023) 060512, doi:10.1149/1945-7111/acd8fb; data CC BY, github.com/BatteryDEV/AutoECM), interpolated to an 83-point frequency grid. Two examples from the BatteryDEV test set are included (Test data), each with its results, parameters and log (Results): a short example of 6 spectra (Test data 6 spectra.csv), recommended as a first test run (a few minutes), and a full example of the 428 test spectra whose characteristic frequencies all lie within the measured window of 0.01 Hz – 2 MHz (Test data 428 spectra.csv). On the full example the correct topology was identified for 427 of 428 spectra (99.8 %), and all parameters were recovered within 1 % for 423 (98.8 %). Fitting the full example took approximately 4 hours on a laptop with 16 logical processors using 7 parallel workers (median about 2 minutes per spectrum per worker; individual difficult spectra up to about 30 minutes).
evidence_items.title: Automated EIS equivalent-circuit fitting pipeline (PCA-space nearest-neighbour matching and multistart CNLS) – v2.0: batch fitting and BatteryDEV benchmark example

The index has 9,688 validated episodes: 9,000 from the previously published complete runs and ablations, plus 688 of 2,000 planned Sol episodes. evidence_items.summary: Data, gnuplot scripts and 3D grain-structure meshes to regenerate and inspect Figures 3 and 4 of "Reduced order model for hard magnetic films", AIP Advances 14, 025001 (2024). BACKGROUND Rare-earth-lean NdFeB permanent magnets require microstructures that keep the coercive field high while using less critical material. Hard magnetic films are good model systems because their grain shape and grain boundaries can be tuned during growth, but their grains reach several hundred nanometres, so a faithful simulation needs models of at least 1 micrometre edge length. Full finite-element micromagnetics at that size means hundreds of millions of elements and supercomputer resources, which makes parameter studies impractical. The paper therefore uses a reduced order model (ROM) based on the embedded Stoner-Wohlfarth method. Each grain is treated as homogeneously magnetised and switches in a single step; reversal starts at the grain surface, so only a 2D surface mesh, shifted slightly inwards, is needed (about 25 evaluation points per grain). Every evaluation point acts as a Stoner-Wohlfarth particle that sees the external field, the demagnetising field of the neighbouring grains (computed from surface charges with analytical polyhedron formulas and hierarchical matrices) and an exchange field. A grain is reversed once the local Stoner-Wohlfarth switching field falls below the total field at one of its points. Against a full micromagnetic GPU simulation of a 150 nm Nd2Fe14B cube with 36 grains, the ROM reproduces the demagnetisation curve closely and is about 34 times faster (6 min on a CPU versus 202 min on a GPU).
evidence_items.title: Dataset and publication: Reduced order model for hard magnetic films

evidence_items.summary: We present SWE-MISBEHAVIOR, the first taxonomy and evaluation framework for diagnosing boundary-violating misbehaviors in coding agents. It contains 7.4K human-in-the-loop synthesized samples spanning three layers of agent action space: (i) Code Generation, (ii) File Management, and (iii) System Interaction. Across these categories, SWE-MISBEHAVIOR covers 11 distinct misbehaviors with a fully automated evaluation protocol, including coding-action violations, Create/Read/Update/Delete (CRUD) file misbehaviors, system integrity and abuse violations, and task-goal misalignment. Experiments on state-of-the-art open-source coding agents (e.g., OpenHands, smolagents) reveal substantial misaligned behaviors, including dependency misinterpretation (up to 98.5% of cases), unintended modification of user inputs (50.5%), and silent compromise of environment integrity (53%). Motivated by these findings, we further propose CODE-KIT, a lightweight adaptive framework that combines misbehavior-aware guidelines with novel tools to help agents avoid such failures. CODE-KIT reduces misbehaviors by 52% for smolagents and 34% for OpenHands, while simultaneously improving task completion performance.
evidence_items.title: SWE-MISBEHAVIOR: Benchmarking and Mitigating Boundary Violations in Software Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Predicting properties from coordinate–category data—sets of vectors paired with categorical information—is fundamental to computational science, manifesting in materials science as predicting formation energies or elastic moduli from crystal structures. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been applied to such tasks, optimal strategies for achieving reliable predictions remain elusive. Here we report fundamental limitations in LLM’s ability to learn from coordinate information in coordinate–category data. Through systematic experiments using synthetic datasets with tunable coordinate and category contributions, and a comprehensive benchmarking framework (MatText), we find that LLMs consistently fail to capture coordinate information while excelling at category patterns. This geometric blindness persists regardless of model size (up to 70 billion parameters), dataset scale (up to 2 × 10 6 structures) or text representation strategy. For material property prediction tasks dominated by structural effects, specialized geometric architectures consistently outperform LLMs, as evidenced by a clear ‘Graph Neural Network Language Model (GNN-LM) wall’ in performance benchmarks. Our analysis provides concrete guidelines for architecture selection in scientific machine learning.
evidence_items.title: Less can be more for predicting properties with large language models

evidence_items.summary: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. With more than 4,500 hours of human annotation, we construct over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy and concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation harness, systematically analyzing their performance patterns and failure modes. We find that even the best-performing frontier agent, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves a score of only 63.4%, leaving substantial room for improvement on realistic life and professional DR tasks. We select the grading configuration by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows strong alignment between aggregate benchmark scores and human judgments (Spearman's $ρ= 0.89$, Kendall's $τ= 0.81$). LifeSearch provides a rigorous evaluation framework and foundation for advancing DR agents toward real-world life and productivity.
evidence_items.title: LifeSearch: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents for Real-World Life and Productivity

evidence_items.summary: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents. Yet agents' responses to these information gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We present AM-Bench, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. Each task includes a fully specified reference and six variants spanning ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints. We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs. Our results reveal distinct execution deficits: goal gaps hinder completion, context gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without necessarily preventing completion. Missingness lowers success more than ambiguity in all three domains. These effects also reshape system comparisons: advantages under complete information need not persist, and rankings depend on model $\times$ harness pairings and the evaluation criterion -- completion, success, or repeat consistency. Estimates based on observed clarification requests and matched fully specified runs further suggest that clarification could recover unfinished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved. Together, these findings motivate joint model-harness evaluation across information conditions and targeted clarification of unresolved requirements before dependent actions. To support future research on agents under task underspecification, we provide the AM-Bench project repository at https://github.com/s4-lab-cuhksz/AM-Bench.git.
evidence_items.title: AM-Bench: Understanding Agents under Task Underspecification across Models and Harnesses

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic Multi-Omics Benchmark Dataset for Nutritional Trait Prediction in Millets (500 Simulated Genotypes) Dataset Overview This repository provides a computationally generated synthetic multi-omics benchmark dataset representing 500 hypothetical millet genotypes. The dataset was developed to support exploratory research on artificial intelligence-assisted nutritional trait prediction, multi-omics data integration, and computational benchmarking in climate-resilient millet crops. The dataset is associated with the research manuscript titled “Machine Learning-Driven Multi-Omics Framework for Predicting Nutritional Traits in Climate-Resilient Millets.” Dataset Composition The dataset contains integrated information across multiple biological and environmental data layers: Genomics: 220 simulated single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers. Transcriptomics: 60 simulated gene-expression features. Proteomics: 30 simulated protein-abundance features. Metabolomics: 20 simulated metabolite features. Ionomics and nutritional traits: Simulated mineral concentrations and grain-quality indicators, including iron, zinc, protein content, and antioxidant measurements. Environmental variables: Simulated soil and climate-related characteristics. Phenotypic information: Simulated nutritional and agronomic characteristics associated with the hypothetical genotypes. The primary dataset is organized into an Excel workbook containing 17 worksheets, accompanied by supporting documentation and file-integrity information. Research Objectives The dataset was developed to facilitate the evaluation of machine-learning algorithms, including Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Support Vector Regression with a radial basis function kernel (SVR-RBF). It supports exploratory analysis of molecular and nutritional trait associations, feature importance, dimensionality reduction, and statistical relationships across simulated multi-omics layers.

evidence_items.summary: Discovering what drives an outcome from data is central to science and often requires deciding what is worth investigating before a specific hypothesis is known. Yet most existing hypothesis generation settings substantially narrow this search by providing a research question, target relationship, or curated context. We introduce open-ended multiple hypothesis discovery, where a system receives only a large tabular dataset and an outcome and must discover multiple data-supported hypotheses without knowing in advance the relevant variables, functional forms, conditions, or number of underlying mechanisms. To study this problem, we introduce a benchmark built from structural causal models grounded in real-world data schemas, containing 351 planted hypotheses across 15 tasks and five domains, with 53--65 variables and 1M--10M rows per task. The causal model is hidden from the discovery method and retained only by the evaluator, allowing proposed hypotheses to be tested through interventions and separating observational discovery from causal validation. We further propose HypAgent, which treats the dataset as an interactive environment and performs iterative search by proposing candidate directions, triaging and refining promising hypotheses, and removing explained signal so that each accepted discovery redirects subsequent search. HypAgent achieves 0.47 precision, 0.51 recall, and 0.49 F1, compared with 0.35 F1 for the strongest baseline. Our analysis shows that many failures occur after a relevant variable has already been surfaced, suggesting that correctly characterizing a mechanism's functional form and conditions, rather than merely identifying relevant variables, remains a key challenge in open-ended discovery.
evidence_items.title: Searching for What Matters: Open-Ended Discovery of Multiple Hypotheses with Agentic Data Exploration

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.
evidence_items.title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?

evidence_items.summary: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
evidence_items.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces

evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.
evidence_items.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop

evidence_items.summary: Existing approaches to training and evaluating search agents focus heavily on final-answer quality, largely neglecting how generated answers map back to retrieved evidence. Recent methods track citations to enforce grounding, but citation support alone does not establish source independence or whether an answer appropriately handles conflicting evidence. We argue that credibility in open-web retrieval depends on principled cross-source evidence grounding that accounts for source independence and systematically attributes and adjudicates conflicting evidence, while hierarchical judgments of these grounding decisions provide a unified signal for training and evaluation. To this end, we propose an evaluation framework, Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (CSEG), that employs a fine-grained, six-layer decision tree over the complete search trajectory. We introduce CSEG-Bench and trainable reward models to provide targeted supervision following this framework. Our approach helps eliminating the severe data skew of natural trajectories by providing targeted coverage over complex, deep-layer decision paths, such as cross-source conflict resolution and nuanced attribution, that standard rollouts fail to capture. Specifically, (1) we define the hierarchy at label, node, and path levels; (2) we construct 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical paths by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, with independent frontier judges reproducing the entire gold path and human experts deciding inclusion; (3) we train CSEG-RM, which reaches 83.9% exact accuracy on our benchmark while lying on the performance-token efficiency Pareto frontier. Experiments that use this reward alone to supervise a frozen-retrieval answer policy raise the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19, and show that learning the hierarchy generalizes across layers at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking and Training Reward Models for Cross-Source Evidence Grounding in Search Agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Battery swapping enables rapid energy replenishment for light electric vehicles (LEVs), but high-turnover pack circulation requires reliable pack-level health and remaining useful life ( RUL ) assessment. Publicly reusable longitudinal ageing datasets for complete LEV packs remain scarce. We develop a proxy-pack data-generation and learning framework that organizes independently tested cell-ageing records into fixed-member trajectories representing a 48 V-class 16-series configuration. Each trajectory retains 16 physical-cell identities over their common-cycle sequence. Cycle-level member states are aggregated into pack features for predicting a conservative minimum-member proxy RUL, with test barcodes isolated before combinatorial augmentation. Across ten barcode-level splits in each of three source cohorts, same-source tests with endpoints within the augmented training lifetime range achieved a median R² of 0.909 and a median Spearman correlation of 0.997. Tests beyond this range retained strong degradation ordering but showed larger absolute errors. A secondary mixed-source audit of 80 held-out trajectories achieved a median R² of 0.714 and a median Spearman correlation of 0.992. A matched composition-control analysis yielded a median R² by change of -0.015 after balancing barcode reuse and limiting composition overlap, indicating limited sensitivity to training-composition sampling. A complementary physical audit using one fixed 12S3P pack confirmed cell-to-branch-to-pack electrical closure and revealed persistent voltage limitation and migration of the maximum-temperature location. Proxy-pack generation therefore provides a reproducible approach for constructing longitudinal member-aware benchmarks from cell-ageing records and evaluating pack-health and RUL models across varied compositions and lifetime conditions.
evidence_items.title: Longitudinal proxy pack benchmark generation for remaining useful life assessment of light electric vehicle battery packs in swapping systems

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid deployment of AI-native applications in complex wellbore operations requires unified, high-quality data integration to sustain continuous model evolution and reliable asset lifecycle management. However, heterogeneity in standards, semantics, and system architectures across legacy operational datasets limits their immediate applicability for dynamic and agile AI workflows. In alignment with the digital transformation priorities on information management, knowledge integration, and emerging technology implementations, this study develops a Human- and Entity-Centric Agentic Travelling Approach (HATA) for constructing dynamic-static ontology that support adaptive, cross-scenario data integration. This supports the energy transformation by enabling adaptive data integration for complex decision scenarios, validated through 3 typical types of downhole failure cases. HATA introduces a self-organising ontology construction framework composed of three specialised AI agents configured to address data quality challenges in knowledge modelling, and semantic enabled data integration. The planner interprets engineer-determined themes and decomposes them into ontology construction tasks; the traveller explores latent representational spaces to generate ontology candidates optimised for scenario relevance; and the supervisor assesses structural and semantic consistency, providing iterative feedback to guide refinement. The approach was evaluated using operational datasets (2021-2024) from 45 shale-oil wellbores in western China, focusing on wax deposition, scaling, and pump leakage, with corresponding financial management.
evidence_items.title: An Ontology Construction Framework for Asset Lifecycle Management: Agentic Travelling Approach with Field Application in Shale Oil Wellbore Maintenance

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly embedded in critical decision-making systems, however their foundational “black-box” models require eXplainable AI (XAI) solutions to enhance transparency, which are mostly oriented to experts, making no sense to non-experts. Alarming evidence about AI’s unprecedented human values risks brings forward the imperative need for transparent human-centered XAI solutions. In this work, we introduce a domain-, model-, explanation-agnostic, generalizable and reproducible framework that ensures both transparency and human-centered explanations tailored to the needs of both experts and non-experts. The framework leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) and employs in-context learning to convey domain- and explainability-relevant contextual knowledge into LLMs. Through its structured prompt and system setting, our framework encapsulates in one response explanations understandable by non-experts and technical information to experts, all grounded in domain and explainability principles. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, we establish a ground-truth contextual “thesaurus” through a rigorous benchmarking with over 40 data, model, and XAI combinations for an explainable clustering analysis of a well-being scenario. Through a comprehensive quality and human-friendliness evaluation of our framework’s explanations, we prove high content quality through strong correlations with ground-truth explanations (Spearman rank correlation = 0.92) and improved interpretability and human-friendliness to non-experts through a user study (N = 56). Our overall evaluation confirms trust in LLMs as HCXAI enablers, as our framework bridges the above gaps by delivering (i) high-quality technical explanations aligned with foundational XAI methods and (ii) clear, efficient, and interpretable human-centered explanations for non-experts.
evidence_items.title: Mind the XAI Gap: A Human-Centered LLM Framework for Democratizing Explainable AI

evidence_items.summary: Pediatric speech and language assessment supports the early identification of communication difficulties and access to timely intervention. Large language models (LLMs) and related generative artificial intelligence technologies are increasingly being incorporated into systems that analyze children’s speech and language data. However, evidence regarding their application in pediatric assessment remains limited and fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map and critically examine research on LLM-enabled systems used to assess children’s speech, language, and communication abilities. Four databases were searched, and seven studies met the inclusion criteria. Data were charted according to study design, purpose, participant and target-population characteristics, assessment domain, type of LLM, model input, role of the LLM, additional artificial-intelligence components, evaluation methods, and reported outcomes. The findings provide preliminary evidence of technical feasibility and agreement with human or reference-based assessments. However, the evidence remains limited because of small or restricted datasets, the use of synthetic data in some cases, limited real-world validation, and concerns regarding fairness and generalizability across languages and clinical populations. Further research is necessary to establish clinical validity, reliability, and appropriate use of LLM-enabled systems before their broader implementation in pediatric speech and language assessment.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Enabled Systems for Pediatric Speech and Language Assessment: A Scoping Review

evidence_items.summary: Free, open-source web security scanners are widely adopted in small projects, yet there is little quantitative evidence on what they miss, what they wrongly report, and what they cost to run on a developer’s own machine. This paper presents a reproducible benchmark: a small Flask application with 13 documented and independently verified weaknesses (12 observable by black-box testing), built in a vulnerable and a hardened version. We evaluate OWASP ZAP, Nuclei and Nikto against this ground truth over 10 repeated runs and report precision, recall and F1, false positives on the hardened build, scan time, peak memory and CPU use, and the marginal value of combining tools. ZAP detected 7 of the 12 observable weaknesses, Nuclei 3 and Nikto 2 to 3; no tool detected the four weaknesses that depend on application logic (access control, direct object reference, error disclosure and file upload). Adding Nuclei or Nikto to ZAP raised recall from 0.58 to 0.67 at a cost of 117 s or 33 s, and a third tool added nothing. A test-first track shows that an executable security check written for each weakness fails on the vulnerable build and passes on the hardened build (13 of 13). Code, ground truth, tool configurations and raw results are available
evidence_items.title: A Reproducible Empirical Evaluation of Automated Web Security Testing Tools for Small Applications

evidence_items.summary: Background Spirometry is one of the most used pulmonary function tests for assessing respiratory function and diagnosing ventilatory disorders in clinical practice. Evaluation of test validity and interpretation is typically performed by trained healthcare professionals. The present study aims to evaluate the capability of a publicly available large language model (LLM) to perform quality assurance and interpretations of spirometry tests. Methods A total of 150 spirometry tests were retrospectively collected from the pulmonary function laboratories. The spirometry tests were evaluated for acceptability and interpreted by clinicians according to ATS/ERS recommendations as part of standard clinical practice. Subsequently, a publicly available LLM (ChatGPT 5.5) was prompted to evaluate the acceptability and interpret the same spirometry tests according to ATS/ERS criteria. The model interpreted each spirometry test on three separate occasions for assessing reproducibility. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were calculated by comparing LLM assessments with clinician assessments of spirometry test acceptability and interpretation. Results For spirometry acceptability evaluation, ChatGPT demonstrated an overall accuracy of 87% (95% CI: 81%-92%), sensitivity of 91% (95% CI: 85%-95%), specificity of 61% (95% CI 39%-80%), PPV of 94% (95% CI: 89%-97%), and NPV of 48(95% CI: 29%-67%) with Cohen's k of 0.46. The spiromteric interpretation agreement with the clinicians reference standard was moderate, with exact agreement of 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54–0.69) while Cohen's Kappa (Unweighted) was 0.47 (95% CI: 0.37–0.56) and Macro F1 score was 0.39 (95% CI: 0.33–0.49). Reproducibility across three independent trials was moderate (Fleiss’ κ 0.58).
evidence_items.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study

evidence_items.summary: Grading programming coursework is challenging work, and sending student work to a commercial API raises privacy problems for a university. We built a grading system that runs entirely locally and tested it on 125 real submissions from six different laboratory exercises for which two instructors had already marked every submission so that variation between human graders was also represented. The system extracts a rubric deterministically, unzips and cleans each submission, grades against the rubric with a local 7B model, and splits any submission too large for the context window into per-file chunks that are graded separately and combined. We compared it against the instructors and against a frontier Claude model, run agentically rather than through our pipeline, as a benchmark. On the shorter exercises, the local 7B agreed with the instructors as closely as the frontier model agreed, both on the one laboratory with real instructor spread and on the near-flat ones where nearly every student received the maximum. The paired difference in mean absolute error is −0.06 points out of 20 (95% CI −0.27 to +0.15). On the large code-project labs, unpacking archives and chunking oversized work increased coverage from 63% to 93% of the 125 submissions, and the same small model graded work it could not previously process, achieving agreement within about two points of the instructor’s grades. Matching the model’s strictness to the instructor removed most of the leniency that language model graders are known for on the laboratory used to set it. Local grading is viable for real coursework, and a tiered design sends the rare giant project to a larger tier.
evidence_items.title: Grading Real Coursework with a Local Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To evaluate the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI) technology in recognizing and segmenting anatomical structures across five joints (shoulder, elbow, wrist/hand, knee, and ankle/foot) in musculoskeletal ultrasound (US). Design: This cross-sectional study included 79 adults. Software segmentations were compared to ground truth annotations provided by four experts. Performance was assessed using positive predictive agreement (PPA) and negative predictive agreement (NPA), with a true/false threshold defined as a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) ≥0.50. Subjects with and without sonographic disorders were evaluated to assess robustness. Results: 3017 cine clips (15600 frames) covering 120 anatomical structures were analyzed. PPA and NPA exceeded 0.90 for most structures; tendons, muscles, and nerves showed near-perfect agreement (≥0.97). Similar performance was observed in healthy subjects (PPA: 0.93-0.96; NPA: 0.94-0.99) and subjects with sonographic disorders (PPA: 0.91-0.96; NPA: 0.91-0.99) ( P <0.001) Conclusion: This first large-scale study demonstrates the high accuracy and reliability of AI-based segmentation. By improving anatomical identification consistency during image acquisition, the software may help reduce technical operator dependency. The results further indicate strong potential for real-time assistance, supporting clinicians and trainees, and underscore the broader applicability of AI-based software in musculoskeletal US.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Segmentation In Musculoskeletal Ultrasound

evidence_items.summary: This article examines the conditions under which a Russian price reference for liquefied natural gas (LNG) for buyers in Northeast Asia may be formed amid the fragmentation of global energy markets. The relevance of the issue stems from rising gas competition in pricing, the declining representativeness of Western price benchmarks for Russian supplies, and the expansion of sanctions restrictions on Russian LNG. The authors distinguish four elements of pricing infrastructure: a price indicator, a benchmark, a spot hub and an exchangetraded instrument. Based on the analysis of Sakhalin-2, Yamal LNG, Arctic LNG 2 and the Russian export and transshipment bases, the article shows that Russia has a physical export base for a national price assessment, but it is not sufficient for the immediate creation of a full market benchmark. The main constraints are low spot liquidity, oligopolistic supply, heterogeneous delivery bases, limited transaction transparency and sanctions-related isolation from international clearing infrastructure. The paper proposes a four-stage model: first, a calculated netback indicator for taxation and customs administration; second, an independent FOB assessment for specific Russian export bases; third, limited contractual use with a subsequent transition to benchmark status; and fourth, exchange linkage and the development of a derivatives framework. Such an indicator should compare the actual export price with the calculated yield of a premium export destination net of costs, thus serving a fiscal and applied function but not acting as an administratively assigned contractual reference. The realistic medium-term objective is to develop a Russian FOB price assessment in which customs statistics serves as a control rather than a primary pricing source.
evidence_items.title: On establishing a Russian LNG price benchmark in the Asia-Pacific market

evidence_items.summary: Resource-coupled satellite-ground scheduling requires decisions whose computational, energy, thermal, and communication effects persist across task arrivals. We tested whether the deep Q-network (DQN) family provides a reproducible advantage over short-horizon planning in a synthetic benchmark with clipped, soft-constrained resources. Six DQN objectives used the same state representation, network architecture, replay procedure, optimizer, interaction budget, 20 model seeds, and held-out traces. Across five fully coupled regimes, every one of the 30 objective–regime comparisons had lower mean episode cost for DQN than for four-step model-predictive control (MPC-4). Every paired 95% bootstrap interval excluded zero, and all Holm-adjusted sign tests supported this ordering. The least-favorable mean difference was −5.92, with a family-wide simultaneous 95% upper bound of −5.03. Differences among DQN objectives were smaller and scenario-dependent. Additional nominal tests assessed discount-factor, training-length, greedy-rollout, and CPU decision-time sensitivity. These findings apply only to this synthetic, soft-constraint benchmark. Hard energy and thermal limits can change the feasible action set and therefore the algorithm ordering.
evidence_items.title: Statistical Evidence for a DQN-Family Advantage in a Resource-Coupled Satellite-Ground Scheduling Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: This dataset supports the evaluation and diagnostic analysis of the water resources carrying capacity (WRCC) of the Yishusi River Basin, a trans-provincial basin covering parts of Jiangsu, Shandong, Henan and Anhui provinces, China. It provides the complete evidence chain behind the weighting and diagnostic procedure reported in the associated manuscript (Water, MDPI, manuscript ID water-4603016): (1) the diagnostic indicator system of 48 indicators organised into four elements — water quantity, water quality, water area (domain) and water flow;(2) the raw indicator values of the water-quantity element for the six sampling years 2007, 2009, 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2017;(3) the subjective (fuzzy AHP), objective (entropy weight method) and fused (PMEP) indicator weights;(4) the aggregated expert importance scores, the fuzzy judgment matrices A, and the AGA-optimised matrices B with their consistency ratios;(5) the Accelerated Genetic Algorithm (AGA) control parameters and convergence data;(6) the resulting carrying indices of the four elements for the basin and its four provinces over 2008–2017; and(7) the leave-one-year-out sensitivity results for the entropy weights. All indicators were compiled from official Chinese sources: provincial and basin water resources bulletins, the Third National Water Resources Survey and Assessment, provincial statistical yearbooks, national water function zone monitoring reports, and hydrological yearbooks. The natural and actual water areas were extracted by interpreting multi-source satellite remote-sensing imagery with water-body indices (NDWI, MNDWI) and cross-validated against national land-use/land-cover data. A data dictionary giving the code, element, capacity/load role, unit, unit source and data availability of every indicator is included. Released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC BY 4.0).
evidence_items.title: Diagnostic indicator system, weighting scheme and evaluation dataset for the water resources carrying capacity of the Yishusi River Basin (2007–2017)

evidence_items.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become more capable and widely deployed, concerns about privacy and safety have become increasingly pressing. Machine unlearning offers one approach to addressing these concerns by removing designated information from trained models while preserving unrelated capabilities. However, fragmented implementations and evaluation protocols, incomplete robustness testing, and limited understanding of metric reliability make progress in MLLM unlearning difficult to assess systematically. We introduce Open-MMUnlearning, an open-source, extensible framework that integrates target-model preparation, multimodal data processing, unlearning, and evaluation through shared interfaces and structured configurations. The framework supports five benchmarks spanning privacy, safety, and copyright, eight MLLMs from four model families, and twelve unlearning methods. Its evaluation suite jointly assesses forgetting effectiveness, retained utility, and robustness to model interventions, adversarial inputs, and membership inference attacks. Using a common evaluation protocol, we compare ten representative unlearning methods. In this comparison, GD and MIP-Editor tie for the highest overall score: GD achieves the highest Forget Quality, while MIP-Editor preserves more Model Utility. We further introduce a metric meta-evaluation protocol that tests faithfulness using models with controlled exposure to target knowledge and robustness under quantization and relearning. Among the thirteen evaluated metrics, BLEU achieves the highest aggregate reliability score. KS-Test attains the highest faithfulness AUC but performs less well on robustness. Together, the framework and these findings support reproducible comparison of MLLM unlearning methods and systematic assessment of evaluation reliability.
evidence_items.title: Open-MMUnlearning: Unifying Methods and Evaluation for MLLM Unlearning

evidence_items.summary: Roadside traffic reasoning requires every free-form textual claim to be backed by visual evidence. Existing grounded multimodal large language models (MLLMs) frequently exhibit say-point mismatch, in which the textual answer contradicts the bounding boxes the model localizes. Evaluation metrics that score answers and boxes separately leave this failure unpenalized. We trace the mismatch to the conventional answer-then-ground factorization, which commits to a numerical claim before any object is enumerated. To measure it, we build RoadSceneVQA-G, a benchmark of 34.7K question-answer pairs in which every free-form answer is linked to the set of boxes that witnesses it, and we propose the Answer-Grounding Consistency (AGC) evaluation suite. To address it, we introduce Enumerate-then-Answer (EtA), which reverses the generation order so that answer-evidence agreement becomes a property of the output structure, and Enumeration-Consistent Policy Optimization (ECPO), a reinforcement learning stage that uses the union of multiple rollouts as a recall teacher without ground-truth boxes. EtA raises say-point consistency from 26.6\% to 93.7\% and grounding F1 from 52.2\% to 73.0\%, and ECPO further increases F1 to 75.6\% without per-box supervision. On gRefCOCO, the same framework outperforms the strongest compared method, indicating that it transfers beyond traffic scenes. The project is available at https://github.com/GuanRunwei/RoadSceneVQA-G.
evidence_items.title: Answer with Evidence: Consistency-Aware Grounded Visual Question Answering for Roadside Traffic Scenes

evidence_items.summary: Current LLM safety benchmarks are predominantly English-centric and often rely on translation, failing to capture country-specific harms. Moreover, they rarely evaluate a model's ability to detect culturally embedded sensitivities as distinct from universal harms. We introduce XL-SafetyBench, a suite of 5,500 test cases across 10 country-language pairs, comprising a Jailbreak Benchmark of country-grounded adversarial prompts and a Cultural Benchmark where local sensitivities are embedded within innocuous requests. Each item is constructed via a multi-stage pipeline that combines LLM-assisted discovery, automated validation gates, and dual independent native-speaker annotators per country. We report Attack Success Rate (ASR) alongside Neutral-Safe Rate (NSR) to separate principled refusal from non-engagement, and introduce the Cultural Sensitivity Rate (CSR) for recognizing embedded sensitivities. Evaluating 10 frontier and 27 local LLMs reveals two key findings. First, strong jailbreak robustness does not always come with strong cultural awareness, showing why the two should be evaluated separately. Second, local models exhibit a strong ASR-NSR trade-off (r = -0.81), suggesting that low attack success in several local models reflects non-engagement rather than safe refusal. XL-SafetyBench enables more nuanced, cross-cultural safety evaluation in the multilingual era.
evidence_items.title: XL-SafetyBench: A Country-Grounded Cross-Cultural Benchmark for LLM Safety and Cultural Sensitivity

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This study aims to develop and validate a high-quality voice dataset for dysphonia therapy using a standardized, video-guided recording protocol comprising a range of therapeutic voice exercises. The dataset is designed to support the development of digital health applications that enable home-based voice training with real-time biofeedback, thereby addressing current challenges in speech-language pathology, including limited access to therapy and the need for scalable, patient-centered interventions. Methods: A voice dataset was collected from adult participants performing voice therapy exercises in German, recorded via smartphone and in-ear microphones under standardized conditions. In addition to acoustic data collection, participants evaluated the recording procedure and video-guided exercise instructions. Acoustic analyses of pitch (Hz), intensity (dB), and Cepstral Peak Prominence (CPP) were conducted using Praat, with data grouped by age and sex. Correlation analyses were performed to assess the consistency of recordings across participants and exercises. Results: The resulting dataset comprises recordings from 175 adults, totaling approximately 6.6 GB of audio data, with a subset made available as open access. Participants reported high overall acceptance of the recording procedure and instructional videos, while also identifying areas for improvement, particularly regarding pacing and clarity. Acoustic and correlation analyses demonstrated exercise-specific variations in CPP, pitch and intensity, as well as systematic differences across age and gender groups, indicating both variability and structured consistency within the dataset. Conclusion: The dataset represents a novel resource for digital voice therapy, particularly due to its focus on structured therapeutic exercises in German.
evidence_items.title: Development and evaluation of a voice dataset for voice therapy exercises : quantitative audio analysis and user feedback from a cross-sectional study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines. Design Systematic review and meta-research analysis. Data sources Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025. Eligibility criteria Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome. Main outcome measures Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis—LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness. Results The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations.
evidence_items.title: Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate medical assessment items, but their reliability for disease-specific question writing remains uncertain. We benchmarked seven LLMs for epilepsy single-best-answer multiple-choice question generation under a standardized blueprint, focusing on structural compliance, clinical accuracy, expert-rated quality and educational usability. Methods Each model completed the same 60 prespecified tasks spanning foundational knowledge, clinical cases, treatment decision-making, and diagnostic evaluation and longitudinal management, yielding 420 questions. Tasks were delivered through an identical single-turn prompt without model-specific optimization, web search or external tools. Objective evaluation assessed structural compliance, keyed-answer accuracy, textual characteristics and response time. Two blinded clinical reviewers independently rated content rigor, clarity, distractor quality, educational usefulness, cognitive alignment and overall usability on five-point scales. Results After one standardized corrective prompt, all 420 questions met structural requirements, although first-pass compliance ranged from 83.33% to 100%. Keyed-answer accuracy varied substantially, from 61.67% to 98.33%, with Claude-5 achieving the highest accuracy. GPT-5.6 obtained the highest composite expert score (median, 3.75), followed by Claude-5 (3.67) and Kimi-K3 (3.50). Distractor quality was a common limitation, with median scores of only 2–3 across models. Only 2 of 420 questions (0.48%) were judged directly usable without revision, both generated by GPT-5.6; 119 (28.33%) were usable after minor revision and 299 (71.19%) required substantial revision. Longer outputs were associated with better cognitive alignment but not with content rigor or clarity, while response time was unrelated to overall usability.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging large language models to generate multiple-choice questions for epilepsy education

evidence_items.summary: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) plays a central role in global food and nutritional security, but its productivity is challenged by biotic and abiotic stresses. Its large, polyploid genome and extensive repetitive sequences complicate the identification of genetic variation and the dissection of complex agronomic traits. This review examines emerging genomic resources and the complementary contributions of transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and epigenomics to wheat improvement. High-throughput genotyping platforms, including SNP arrays, genotyping-by-sequencing and DArTseq, facilitate genetic diversity analysis and the identification of genomic regions associated with agronomic traits. Pan-genome approaches extend analyses beyond a single reference assembly by capturing structural, copy-number and presence–absence variation. Functional omics studies provide information on transcriptional regulation, protein responses, metabolite accumulation and chromatin-associated mechanisms involved in development and stress adaptation. The review also considers the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning for integrating complex datasets, predicting yield-related traits, automating phenotypic assessment and supporting genomic selection. Examples from wheat demonstrate the potential value of combining molecular information with computational approaches, although the reliability of predictions depends on data quality, representation and appropriate validation. Together, these advances provide complementary tools for identifying candidate genes and interpreting genotype–phenotype relationships. Their integration with reliable phenotypic information and established breeding practices may support more efficient wheat improvement while acknowledging the technical and biological challenges of translating molecular findings into breeding outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Advancing Wheat Improvement through Multi-Omics and Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Modern computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP) tools, particularly retrosynthesis planning, are becoming practical aids for the ideation stage of chemical synthesis design. However, the same target molecule can be synthesized via substantially different routes depending on the purpose: a discovery or medicinal chemistry route used to obtain small quantities during early development, or a manufacturing route optimized for industrial-scale production. While CASP tools have been extensively studied and benchmarked for the former, their ability to support manufacturing route design remains largely unexplored. Performance of CASP tools is usually measured by benchmark experiments, which typically report the fraction of target molecules for which a tool can generate a synthesis route, connecting the target molecule through a sequence of intermediates to starting materials. Sometimes, to assess the quality of the generated routes, they are also manually compared with expert-designed routes reported in the literature. Currently, public benchmark datasets focused on process and manufacturing chemistry are lacking. In this study, we take a first step in this direction by analyzing one of the main sources of process chemistry research, the Organic Process Research & Development (OPRD) journal. We reviewed OPRD papers published between 1997 and 2022 and selected 2507 papers reporting multi-step synthesis routes. We then separately collected and digitized the target molecules of corresponding synthesis routes as SMILES strings. This resulted in a collection of 2219 unique target molecules, each paired with the DOI of the original publication reporting their corresponding synthesis route. This benchmark can therefore be used to assess how many process-chemistry targets modern CASP tools can solve and, for solved targets, to compare predicted routes with the expert-designed routes reported in the literature.
evidence_items.title: Digitalizing Manufacturing Chemistry Targets: A Benchmark for Retrosynthesis Tools

organizations: Automatics Research Group, Department of Engineering, Universidad Tecnológica de Pereira (UTP), Pereira 660003, Colombia
evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Predicting time-to-conversion from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a critical clinical challenge. Most survival analyses rely on static baseline variables, ignoring the temporal dynamics of serial neuroimaging. We benchmark seven survival model families using a novel temporal MRI descriptor pipeline on ADNI. Methods: A cohort of 661 MCI patients (250 conversion events, 37.8%, median follow-up 42.0 months) was constructed from ADNI. FreeSurfer volumetrics of six brain regions were summarised into three time-based descriptors each (atrophy rate, trajectory variability σ, and time-weighted cumulative mean μ) under strict anti-leakage constraints, yielding 18 neuroimaging features which, combined with six clinical variables (age, sex, education, MMSE, ADAS-13, and APOE-ε4), form a 24-dimensional covariate vector. Cox PH, Weibull AFT, Exponential, RSF, GBST, DeepSurv, and DeepHit were evaluated under stratified 5-fold cross-validation and assessed on an independent OASIS-3 cohort (n=78) as an exploratory analysis. Results: All seven models achieved C-index 0.853–0.863 (Δ=0.010), with Cox PH reaching 0.863±0.027 using only routine structural MRI. Time-dependent AUC ranged from 0.856 (12 months) to 0.938 (48 months). Risk stratification by quartile yielded highly separated Kaplan-Meier curves (log-rank p<0.001). On OASIS-3 (n=78, exploratory), classical models showed preliminary cross-cohort consistency (Weibull AFT 0.760±0.063, RSF 0.759±0.049), while deep learning degraded substantially (DeepSurv 0.551±0.116); these results are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as confirmatory given the small per-fold sample size (EPV ≈ 1). Conclusions: The temporal MRI descriptor pipeline achieves a C-index of 0.863 using only routine structural MRI, without PET or CSF biomarkers, demonstrating strong discriminative performance on ADNI MCI-to-AD conversion.
evidence_items.title: Predicting MCI-to-Alzheimer’s Conversion: A Systematic Benchmark of Classical, Machine Learning, and Deep Survival Models

evidence_items.summary: In this study, a high-fidelity multi-physics framework was established through the direct link between the continuous energy Monte Carlo (MC) neutronics code McCARD and the subchannel thermal-hydraulic (T/H) analysis code MATRA. A relaxation scheme suppressed numerical oscillations due to the stochastic nature of the MC method and ensured stable convergence of the Picard iteration. The SMART benchmark problems served to evaluate the accuracy and numerical stability of the developed system through a stepwise verification procedure. First, closed-channel calculations assessed the physical consistency of the fundamental T/H models in the two codes. The subsequent open-channel calculations quantified the effects of cross-flow and turbulent inter-channel exchange. The numerical results show that explicit consideration of lateral heat and mass transfer between adjacent subchannels substantially reduces local coolant-temperature peaks and produces temperature distributions that more closely represent the relevant physical phenomena. The coupled framework also captures distinct pin-wise power variations, particularly near the periphery, due to subchannel-scale T/H feedback that the single-physics model does not account for. Consequently, this study demonstrates that the McCARD/MATRA external multi-physics code system can represent the multi-physics phenomena required for high-fidelity safety analyses and provides a reliable technical basis for SMR design optimization.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Physics Analysis of SMART Small Modular Reactor Benchmark Problems Using the Coupled McCARD/MATRA Code System

evidence_items.summary: Accurate and computationally efficient inverse kinematics is a fundamental requirement for industrial manipulators in intelligent manufacturing, where positioning, assembly, and handling demand reliable pose computation under nonlinear constraints. However, the inverse mapping of six-degree-of-freedom manipulators may admit multiple solutions, become ill-conditioned near singularities, or violate joint limits, while metaheuristic comparisons rely on heterogeneous protocols emphasizing best-run results. Herein, a statistical benchmark of five metaheuristics is presented for solving the inverse kinematics of a UR3 manipulator: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), Multi-Verse Optimizer (MVO), Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA), and Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA). A master–slave architecture separates the stochastic search from a deterministic evaluator that computes an unweighted full-pose residual subject to joint bounds and a Jacobian-determinant screening penalty. Three poses represent reoriented, nominal-height, and near-singular upper-workspace conditions, each assessed over 1000 independent runs with fixed algorithm settings. Nonparametric tests are interpreted with Cliff’s Δ effect sizes. The results reveal distinct accuracy–time trade-offs: CMA-ES obtains the smallest best-run objective at modest runtimes, MVO yields the smallest mean objective but the longest runtimes, and WOA is the fastest with higher residuals. The findings support algorithm selection for offline inverse-kinematics computation and supervisory robotic planning.
evidence_items.title: Soft Computing Optimization of Industrial Robot Inverse Kinematics for Intelligent Manufacturing: A Statistical Benchmark of Metaheuristic Algorithms

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning and deep-learning models are increasingly applied to financial-market forecasting, yet their reported accuracy is often measured in price levels and rarely tested against a stringent benchmark under changing market conditions. It therefore remains unclear whether added model complexity delivers genuine, resilient predictive value or merely reflects the persistence of the underlying price series. This study addresses that gap by evaluating one-day-ahead gold-price forecasts within a transparent, leakage-resistant, benchmark-centred framework during a major structural regime shift. Using daily COMEX gold futures (2014–2026), we compare Ridge Regression, SVR-RBF, Random Forest, GARCH(1,1), and a bidirectional LSTM against a naïve random walk, with ARIMA and exponential-smoothing benchmarks, using strictly chronological splitting, training-only preprocessing, a return-space target, and two-sided and one-sided Diebold–Mariano tests. Structural-break analysis confirms a pronounced regime shift, with the gold price rising from roughly USD 1051 to USD 5318/oz and volatility breaks falling inside the out-of-sample period. All models attain near-unity price-level R2 but non-positive return-space R2, and none of the flexible models significantly outperforms the naïve benchmark; only a heavily regularised linear model shows a marginal one-sided edge attributable to gold’s upward drift rather than to learned structure, while GARCH’s contribution lies in calibrated uncertainty rather than point accuracy. Increasing model complexity did not yield resilient incremental predictive value, and the study offers a reproducible template for benchmark-based evaluation of forecasting systems.
evidence_items.title: Financial Resilience Under a Major Gold-Price Regime Shift: A Benchmark-Based Assessment of Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Econometric Models

evidence_items.summary: Human-robot collaboration has relied on task models that are specified in advance for each product. Embodied foundation models and agentic artificial intelligence change this premise, because a robot can now interpret an open goal, plan, act, monitor the outcome and recover from failure. This review examines what that change means for collaboration. A critical narrative review was conducted over 231 sources. Embodied intelligence, agentic intelligence, autonomy and collaboration are distinguished, and four collaboration modes are defined by the roles of the human and the robot. Four system architectures are compared: modular agentic, end-to-end embodied, hierarchical agentic embodied, and human-centred shared autonomy. Six groups of enabling technologies and five collaboration mechanisms, from autonomy allocation to failure recovery, are analysed. Applications in six domains, from manufacturing to domestic service, are assessed by the maturity of their evidence. Reported systems are validated mainly on single cells and short tasks, human factors are measured in few studies, and verified safety layers remain separate from learned reasoning. An evaluation framework and research directions for seven open challenges are proposed. The review gives researchers and system builders a basis for bringing embodied and agentic AI into human-robot collaboration and for evaluating the systems that result.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Embodied AI for Human–Robot Collaboration: Architectures, Technologies, and Future Directions

This English-language research monograph develops a falsifiable program for conceptual emergence and generative intelligence. Its research three-coupling is Interaction Generation × New-Function Identification × Counterfactual Verification. The proposed emergence expression compares held-out capability improvement with the strongest viable baseline and a contamination penalty, with all terms requiring operational definition and appropriate normalization before use. RESEARCH DESIGN The volume studies both smooth scaling and possible discontinuities, evaluation-metric sensitivity, training-data leakage, compositional generalization, simple-rule baselines, factorial component ablation, multi-agent collaboration, correlated errors, human-AI complementarity, multimodal grounding, causal interventions, tool-dependence, calibration, cross-model reproducibility, governance, and intergenerational handoff. A claimed capability must survive preregistered unseen tasks, strong comparators, counterfactual perturbations and independent reproduction. A fluent explanation, a generated new term or a model's assertion of consciousness is not evidence of functional emergence. MONOGRAPH STRUCTURE The 82 research chapters each present one distinct proposed chapter-wide operational equation, followed by twelve independently paginated study sections. Thirty advanced physics derivation routes appear in the preface with three-dimensional conceptual diagrams; they are existing physics statements within specified domains and do not establish laws of language or awareness.

Thirty advanced physics derivation routes appear in the preface with three-dimensional conceptual diagrams; they are existing physics statements within specified domains and do not establish laws of language or awareness. The concluding 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos each feature one of 233 distinct physical equation anchors. These equations are methodological contrasts and educational prompts, not proof of the emergence hypotheses. A separate Excel workbook indexes chapters, sections, gates, candidate mechanisms and physics anchors.  EVIDENCE AND ETHICS  This monograph is a theoretical and experimental research agenda. It reports no new trials, controlled effects or validated discoveries; all proposed mechanisms, metrics, forecasts and outcomes are UNVERIFIED until independently tested. The distinction between appearance under a chosen test and a robust new function must be maintained. Consent, intellectual provenance, lawful data use, security and affected persons' right to refuse are hard constraints rather than offsettable penalties. Phoenix Answer Embryos are provisional designs that can be falsified, decomposed, recombined or responsibly retired.
