evidence_items.summary: As AI agents increasingly act through external tools, tool results are no longer simple outputs but execution artifacts that must remain correctly associated with the context that produced them. Yet as results persist across caches, recovery mechanisms, and shared runtime state, this association can break, causing a real and unmodified result to be consumed in an incompatible execution context and lead the agent to an unsafe action. We characterize this failure as tool-result misbinding. To systematically study this failure, we introduce ReplayBench, a benchmark that uses controlled tool-result replay to evaluate misbinding across 19 representative agent scenarios, 4 failure properties, and 3 replay mechanisms. Across eight LLMs, three agent frameworks, and diverse stateful workflows, we find widespread replay-induced failures, with a mean Final-State Error Rate of 0.649 under cross-task replay. Stage-wise analysis localizes these failures to model-side action generation. Further analyses show that replay susceptibility varies with task similarity, shows little dependence on object similarity, and remains high under result staleness and implicit environment changes. These findings motivate runtime validity mechanisms that eliminate final-state errors in our evaluated settings while preserving legitimate recovery. The results call for explicit contextual binding in tool-using agent runtimes. Our work is public at https://github.com/Phitooo/Replaybench.
evidence_items.title: TRAP: Tool-result Replay Attack for Probing Misbinding in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents are emerging as an important new class of users of desktop applications. However, existing desktop interfaces were designed for human end users or application developers, leaving agents to interpret visual controls or discover and compose low-level software operations. This mismatch can hinder even capable agents, yet it remains unclear what interface properties make desktop software easier for agents to use. To study this question, we treat software evolution as a natural source of interface variation and introduce DeskIF-Bench, a benchmark of 255 artifact-verified tasks across six desktop applications. By holding the task, agent, and verifier fixed while varying the software release, we measure how interface changes affect agent performance. Across two models and six applications, the newest release consistently outperforms the oldest. Trajectory analysis identifies three relevant interface properties: discoverability, granularity, and observability. Guided by these properties, we develop ANIS, a framework that synthesizes agent-native interfaces from the capabilities of installed applications. On an expanded evaluation of 368 tasks across eight applications, atomic interfaces improve success over native SDK use by 3.8 and 3.5 percentage points with DeepSeek V4 Flash and Claude Haiku 4.5, respectively, while reducing online token usage by approximately 73%. Goal-level commands further raise success to 74.5% and 67.4%, respectively.
evidence_items.title: A Decade in a Day: Synthesizing Agent-Native Interfaces from Human-Oriented Software Evolution

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are increasingly evolving beyond reproducing what a world looks like toward constructing executable worlds that capture how a world works. This shift calls for executable world modeling, which integrates two core capabilities: world understanding, reasoning about the underlying structural, mechanical, and causal principles of a world, and executable realization, translating that understanding into a code-based system whose behavior emerges from physical interactions. However, existing benchmarks provide only fragmented evaluations centered on physical reasoning, visual fidelity, or behavioral correctness, leaving the integration of these capabilities insufficiently assessed. To bridge this gap, we introduce ExeWorldBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark to comprehensively evaluate world understanding and executable realization through code-based 3D world construction. ExeWorldBench comprises three progressively challenging tasks: Mechanism Executability, which evaluates the realization of individual mechanisms from visual observations; Compositional Executability, which extends to multi-stage systems with spatial, mechanical, and causal dependencies; and Intent-Driven Executable World Synthesis, which requires constructing executable worlds from high-level goals and physical requirements. Extensive experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in executable world modeling, offering insights into the development of more physically grounded and causally coherent world construction systems.
evidence_items.title: ExeWorldBench: Benchmarking Code-Based Executable 3D World Modeling

evidence_items.summary: As the production of software passes into the hands of software itself, coding agents are increasingly commissioned to build agents fitted to their users' own workflows. This delegation carries a quiet assumption, that the delivered agent will faithfully serve the requirement it was built for, rather than merely appear to. No existing benchmark tests that assumption. We introduce AgentSWE, a benchmark for agent software engineering spanning three stages of the agent development lifecycle: Creation of a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, Editing of production agent codebases, and Optimization toward a measurable target. Each of its 25 tasks is framed as a commission rather than an exam: the builder iterates against a handful of illustrative cases, while acceptance exercises the frozen submission on held-out cases designed to span the full requirement, grading behavior against requirement-derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates or, for Optimization, against the source benchmark's own objective. Evaluating a range of coding agents across models and harnesses, we find that none comes close to delivering what a requirement asks for: the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm, not the corner case. An accompanying empirical analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring failure modes, among them overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion, each a signal by which coding agents can learn to build the agents they are asked for.
evidence_items.title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?

evidence_items.summary: Terminal agents are moving beyond local operations toward completing real-world professional tasks. Short trajectories can demonstrate commands and tool calls, but they do not fully show how agents accumulate evidence through exploration, use it to inform judgments, continually adjust strategies based on feedback, and turn intermediate results into final deliverables. High-quality long-horizon trajectories capture these agentic behavioral patterns and their connections within a single problem-solving process, providing richer experience for sustained autonomous work. However, environment synthesis may complete or simplify the key work underlying these patterns in advance and thus remove the need for exploration, implementation, and verification that the agent was meant to perform. To address this, we introduce TerminalHorizon, a fully automated data synthesis engine for long-horizon terminal agents. Starting from real-world professional work, it uses independent execution to identify key work omitted during construction and uses the resulting evidence to guide environment reconstruction. To extend these patterns across stages, it progressively expands tasks under the same goal, introducing new requirements that build on prior results and call for further exploration and improvement. Using this engine, we construct 1.5K task environments and perform supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B on the resulting dataset to obtain TerminalHorizon-27B. We achieve substantial performance gains on all 12 benchmarks spanning coding-agent tasks, agentic tasks in real-world production settings, and general reasoning. Multiple RSI case studies, each with a 12-hour research budget, further demonstrate the model's ability to continue experimenting beyond an initial solution, improve its methods based on feedback, and retain effective improvements in its final deliverables.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Agentic Data for Long-Horizon Terminal Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with spatial, embodied, physical, and temporal reasoning. We hypothesize that these failures reflect a shared deficit in visual transition reasoning, and test whether this capability can serve as a shared training primitive, one that different models can learn from different supervision sources and reuse across different tasks, with a systematic training recipe. Existing benchmarks document these deficits separately but do not support controlled comparisons across scenes, actions, and reasoning operations. We therefore introduce WOVEN, a training source and benchmark for visual transition reasoning that organizes transition supervision by scene, action, and reasoning type, using diverse, realistic rollouts from video-pretrained generative models: 36,076 examples across 20 scene types, 5 action types, and 8 reasoning types. We first evaluate 38 frontier MLLMs (e.g., GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B) and find a substantial and systematic deficit: even the strongest models fall far below humans, and the failures recur across model families and persist with scale. We then train MLLMs at multiple scales on WOVEN and find that they learn a shared capability that transfers broadly: training subsets of only about 2,000 items each collectively improve 22 of 26 external benchmarks by up to 27.3 percentage points, and WOVEN data can replace 30-50% of a task's own training data with comparable accuracy. Controlled comparisons further yield a training recipe for visual world modeling, validated prospectively on held-out benchmarks: select supervision by the reasoning operation it teaches rather than by the actions, scenes, or domains it shows, and prefer larger changes to the visual state for robustness. Our work establishes visual transition reasoning as a reusable foundation for systematic visual world-model training in MLLMs.
evidence_items.title: WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Precise grounding matters. It specifies which object is the target and where that object is, even in clutter and for tiny objects, and it has to be fast enough for closed-loop control. Yet vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) take perception from general-purpose vision-language and video-generation backbones, which still fail in these settings. We introduce GroundingPI, a 4B grounding foundation model that generates points and boxes as quantized coordinates in a shared vocabulary. Training combines multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO, using supervision from public datasets and dedicated data engines. Against 44 baselines across 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, GroundingPI establishes a new state of the art, averaging 73.68%, above the larger GPT-6 Astra (71.54%). As a downstream visual backbone, GroundingPI improves performance on robotic manipulation and autonomous driving. On RoboTwin 2.0, it outperforms every mainstream backbone we evaluate in all four out-of-distribution settings, by up to 24.8% relative to the strongest backbone. On RoboCasa-GR1, GroundingPI trained with 50% of the demonstrations outperforms those baselines trained with 75%. On nuScenes, used as the visual backbone, GroundingPI attains an average open-loop L2 error of 0.296 m. We systematically analyze GroundingPI's pretraining in scale and data composition. Downstream autonomous driving and robotic manipulation improve as the pretraining is scaled. Analyzing the data recipe across these 11 perceptual capabilities shows dense grounding's substantial benefits for both, and OCR's potential as a catalyst for perceptual learning. These results support grounding as a perceptual foundation, and dedicated perceptual pretraining as a promising direction for foundation models of physical intelligence.
evidence_items.title: GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model towards Physical Intelligence with Visual Primitives

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating the physical consistency of generated videos remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches rely on off-the-shelf vision-language models, which can often be myopic to physical dynamics, or fine-tuned evaluators trained on human annotations, which overfit to dataset-specific cues and fail to generalize. A key challenge is that existing supervision sources provide either relative ordering or absolute scores, but not both reliably and consistently across varied settings. To this end, we introduce PhyProbe, an evaluator that extracts features from a frozen pretrained spatio-temporal encoder and maps them to a scalar physical consistency violation score via a lightweight scoring head. PhyProbe is trained through a unified objective combining pairwise ranking, regression on noisy scalar annotations, and anchor-based calibration over a curated set of heterogeneous supervision sources. Experiments show that PhyProbe outperforms prior methods on most pairwise benchmarks spanning real-generated and generated-generated pairs under varying correspondence, with the largest gains in no-correspondence and generated-generated settings where existing fine-tuned evaluators degrade sharply. PhyProbe achieves strong correlation with human judgments, with close agreement between rank-based and linear metrics, indicating that scores are both well ordered and anchored to a stable [0, 1] scale. Further, despite being trained on supervision indicative of physical consistency, without explicit general-preference labels, PhyProbe also performs competitively on human preference benchmarks: consistent with the observation that physics violations are entangled with broader quality degradations.
evidence_items.title: PhyProbe: Rethinking Physical Consistency Evaluation in Generated Videos

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating recommender systems before deployment requires simulators that remain realistic over long, closed-loop interaction cycles. Current LLM-based agents generally function as surface imitators that generate realistic short-term responses but fail to capture the underlying user dynamics such as fatigue, affect, and shifting preferences. We propose PsyBer-Agent, a psychology-inspired simulator that models these dynamics through its Psy-Engine. This engine represents each user with three evolving, model-defined latent states. To calibrate simulated behavior against real interaction logs, we align log-conditioned reference trajectories with simulator-generated latent-state trajectories via Unbalanced Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport. This approach provides structured supervision for a lightweight policy without the computational burden of fine-tuning the backbone LLM. We also introduce WebSim and the PsyBer Benchmark, which encompass multimodal scenarios and seven recommender backbones. Our framework evaluates behavioral fidelity, latent-state consistency, robustness, and responses to social-cue perturbations. On the tested horizons, PsyBer-Agent shows lower behavioral discrepancy than the prompt-only simulators while maintaining stable performance under large-scale concurrent simulation for up to 5M queued simulation tasks under bounded concurrency. Code is available in the supplementary material and at: PsyBer-Agent: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CC66F/, WebSim Platform: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/D8EAX/.
evidence_items.title: PsyBer-Agent: A Psychology-Driven User Agent for Recommender Systems

evidence_items.summary: The growing popularity of large language models (LLMs) over the last five years has produced a large amount of technical documentation and research that are published almost exclusively in English. For low-resource languages such as Bulgarian this creates a twofold gap: a lack of accessible, systematic descriptions of the LLMs in Bulgarian, and a lack of an agreed terminology for the fundamental technical concepts. These gaps impede AI literacy, regulatory compliance under the EU AI-related legislation, and hinder the explainability and understanding of AI concepts by the wider public in general. This paper presents an integrated resource that aims to make the first steps towards addressing these gaps for Bulgarian. The first component is a structured database of LLM descriptions (currently, 424 from more than 30 families), covering open-weight, proprietary, and Bulgarian, Slavic and Balkan oriented models. The description is organised in a Neo4j graph database with information on architecture, training data, training methods, benchmarks, licensing, access conditions. The second component is a bilingual English–Bulgarian terminology dictionary of LLM-related concepts (currently comprising 251 verified entries, of which 94 attested in Bulgarian, and 157 newly proposed) across nine thematic domains. The two components are linked as descriptive nodes in the graph of LLM descriptions carry Bulgarian labels drawn from the dictionary, and any revision of terminology propagates through the database. The resources are released under CC-BY-4.0 license with a web interface in Bulgarian for search and filtering of LLMs. The intended use of the resources is to support research, education, and public engagement with AI in Bulgaria.
evidence_items.title: System for Describing Large Language Models in Bulgarian

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucination and knowledge staleness in large language models (LLMs) by injecting external knowledge into the context window, yet its effectiveness is rigidly constrained by attention dilution and inference cost. Existing knowledge-graph-enhanced methods follow a sequential “retrieve-then-compress” paradigm in which retrieval and compression are optimized independently, preventing the compressor from rectifying redundancy and noise introduced during retrieval and making it difficult to achieve globally efficient information allocation under a limited token budget. To address this paradigm-level limitation, we propose LOKG (LLM-Oriented Knowledge Graph), a high-information-density knowledge graph retrieval augmentation framework that uses token-level information density maximization as a shared design objective across schema compression, subgraph retrieval, and triple encoding. LOKG comprises three synergistic modules: Semantic Compression of Ontology Schema (SCOS) offline merges semantically overlapping relations by fusing normalized mutual information, Jaccard co-occurrence, and TransE embedding similarity under a conditional-entropy-based adaptive threshold; Topology-Aware Indexing and Multi-granularity Retrieval (TAIMR) computes topology-aware multi-hop path scores using relation-aware graph attention and node information gain, then applies late query–answer semantic re-ranking in the E5 space; Information-Theoretic Triple Compression (ITTC) formulates granularity assignment as a multiple-choice knapsack problem, adaptively allocating compact, balanced, or verbose representations to candidate triples to maximize injected information under the budget constraint. Experiments on four KGQA evaluation settings from three benchmark families (CWQ, WebQSP, PathQuestion-2hop, and PathQuestion-3hop) demonstrate that under a single-LLM-call constraint, LOKG achieves a superior accuracy–efficiency trade-off.
evidence_items.title: High-Information-Density Knowledge Graph Retrieval Augmentation for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) path planning is widely applied in fields such as Internet of Things (IoT) environmental monitoring, intelligent transportation, low-altitude logistics, and autonomous inspection. With the rapid development of UAV intelligence, natural language task planning powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising research hotspot. However, in safety-critical flight missions, LLMs suffer from issues such as unstable structured outputs, insufficient understanding of complex constraints, and unreliable responses to dangerous inputs, which can jeopardize the safety and robustness of UAV path planning. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an LLM-based hierarchical safe and robust UAV path planning framework to achieve co-optimization of natural language task understanding and deterministic path search. We design a Prompt–RAG–Validator safety enhancement mechanism that improves the LLM’s safety decision-making capabilities through prompt constraints, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and rule validation, while constructing a structured constraint representation to convert natural language requirements into parsable planning constraints. Furthermore, we combine a grid cost map with the A algorithm to achieve autonomous obstacle avoidance and safe grid-path generation. In addition, a two-stage evaluation system targeting both the constraint generation layer and the path-planning layer is constructed to verify model output reliability and actual planning performance. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed method across various complex scenarios, including multi-constraint tasks, risk-zone planning, incomplete input information, and prompt injection attacks. Notably, on the current template-derived benchmark, the deterministic regex/slot parser provided a stronger baseline with no dangerous outputs, whereas the LLM-based pipeline offers greater flexibility in handling diverse linguistic expressions.
evidence_items.title: Hierarchical Safe and Robust UAV Path Planning Based on Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Layout evaluation in early-stage building design often relies on manual inspection to verify compliance with spatial requirements such as adjacency, accessibility, capacity, and programme-specific constraints. As programmes grow in size and interdependency, review becomes time-consuming, inconsistent across reviewers, and difficult to integrate into rapid iteration. This paper proposes an automated method to identify and repair non-compliant spatial layouts represented as graphs, while preserving interpretability and limiting unnecessary changes to designer intent. A candidate layout is encoded as an attributed, weighted graph, and requirements are formalised as a target benchmark graph specifying expected spaces, relations, and admissible attribute ranges. Structured compliance checking aligns candidate and benchmark graphs to detect structural violations, including missing or redundant spaces and incomplete connectivity, and attribute violations, including incorrect capacities, distances, edge weights, or constraint-relevant labels. The method then applies modular repair operators, including node insertion or deletion, edge completion, weight correction, and constraint-aware attribute adjustment, to produce a revised graph with improved benchmark conformity. Each edit is logged with its triggering violation, the operation applied, and the resulting change in compliance metrics, enabling transparent auditing and traceability. Experiments across multiple scenarios and benchmark configurations show consistent gains after repair, reducing detected violations and increasing overall benchmark alignment. The resulting logs provide actionable evidence for automated pipelines and human review, positioning graph repair as a practical quality-assurance layer for compliance-oriented generative layout workflows. Future work will scale to larger and noisier benchmarks and incorporate designer preferences and multi-objective trade-offs.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-Guided Graph Repair for Compliance-Oriented Spatial Layout Networks

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid development of computer vision and industrial manufacturing has brought 3D Anomaly Detection (3D-AD) wide attention in recent years. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive review of computer vision based 3D anomaly detection techniques from the perspectives of multimodal 3D-AD, point cloud 3D-AD, pose-agnostic 3D-AD, dataset, and benchmarks. In addi- tion, we highlight several inherent or emerging challenges in 3D anomaly detection. The advantages and disadvantages of representative network archi- tectures for different tasks are discussed. Finally, we summarize the research results and point out future research directions. For more resources, please visit https://github.com/M-3LAB/awesome-3d-anomaly-detection.
evidence_items.title: 3D Anomaly Detection: Approaches, Benchmark, Challenges, and Prospects for Intelligent Manufacturing

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Machine-learning studies of autism spectrum disorder from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging routinely report near-perfect accuracy, yet the models rarely transfer to an unseen scanner. We audited a pipeline of the kind this literature builds, which reported an accuracy of 0.999, and traced that number to five data-leakage pathways. Methods: Under a nested leave-one-site-out protocol on 871 participants from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange, in which the held-out site influenced nothing but model selection, the threshold, the combiner, or the site correction, we closed every pathway, priced each by reopening it, and validated on a locked external cohort. Results: With all five pathways closed, the graph attention network reached an area under the curve of 0.648 and did not outperform a support vector machine on the same connectivity (0.679; p = 0.009). Decision-level fusion added nothing detectable (0.682, p = 0.72). A network identified its training participants better than it detected autism (0.710 versus 0.610); both questionnaire benchmarks proved label-tautological, and performance held on the external cohort. Conclusions: Reported gains in this literature should be read as claims about evaluation protocols until shown otherwise on an untouched acquisition site; all predictions, models, and code are released.
evidence_items.title: A Reproducible Benchmark for Leakage-Resistant Machine Learning on Multi-Site Brain Connectivity Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Agent frameworks expose tools, delegation, memory and human approval, yet the controls attached to a request (identity, tenant, scopes, budgets, deadlines, rate limits, fail behavior) are routinely lost at execution boundaries: delegation, threads, streaming, resume, caching, retrieval and adapter exports. We present Agent Foundry, an open-source Python platform whose architecture is organized around one principle: every control is a property of the request’s execution scope, not an argument that each layer must remember to pass. We formalize this as the Governed Execution Contract (GEC), a meet-semilattice of control scopes with seven invariants, and prove that delegation can only attenuate authority, that deny rules can only tighten resolution, that per-principal rate limits are exact under arbi-trary thread interleavings, that every call yields exactly one audited decision even when the policy source is unreachable, and that admission partitions by principal without cross-shard coordination. On AgentGovBench, a public 48-scenario gov-ernance benchmark, Agent Foundry passes 48/48 in 10 of 10 repetitions, against 46/48 for the best published governed configuration and 13/48 for each of 7 pub-lished framework-native runners; run through the same harness, Microsoft’s Agent Governance Toolkit scores at most 46/48 and Bounded Agents 36/48, and on a 24-scenario suite authored blind to our code Agent Foundry scores 24/24 against 17 and 8. A set of 13 single-control ablations attributes 35 of the 48 scenarios to specific mechanisms and exposes a measurement problem: a runner that denies every call scores 31/48, above the audit-only reference, and two controls can be re-moved without losing an official point. Eight supplemental discriminating scenar-ios and three anti-vacuity checks close that gap.
evidence_items.title: Agent Foundry: A Boundary-Preserving Architecture for Governed Agentic Platforms

organizations: Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, Nigeria.
evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This article develops a Human Governed Agentic Project Management (HG-APM) model for integrating autonomous AI capabilities with human project management authority. Design/methodology/approach: An integrative conceptual synthesis combines four literature streams: AI-enabled project management, autonomous Manager Agents, human oversight governance, and human–AI teaming. Source supported findings are separated from conceptual inferences, and the resulting architecture is expressed as a closed-loop model. Findings: The model comprises Sense, Understand, Diagnose, Predict, Plan, Evaluate, Authorize, Act, Monitor, Learn and Replan. It proposes a consequence sensitive, graduated autonomy rather than a single autonomy level. Routine and reversible actions may be automated within predefined boundaries, whereas consequential financial, contractual, scope, safety, stakeholder, reputational and strategic decisions require stronger authority from the designated human or organizational decisionmaker. Originality: The model integrates project-management intelligence, human–AI teaming and governance into one operational architecture. It contributes to a project specific decision boundary and testable propositions for evaluating whether governed agentic AI improves project outcomes without weakening human control.
evidence_items.title: Designing A Human-Governed Agentic Project Management  Model: A Closed-Loop Architecture for Autonomous Project  Intelligence, Decision Control and Human–AI Teaming

evidence_items.summary: To measure the success of a research and development project and assess its impact, an evaluation methodology has to be established. The proposed methodology in the NextETRUCK project follows best practices in validation and draws on insights from previous support projects such as CONVERGE and FESTA. It outlines a set of research hypotheses and associated goals for different innovation aspects of the project, forming the basis for evaluation. Key elements of this evaluation plan include defining Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). A total of 28 KPIs have been identified, covering areas such as vehicle and charging performance, digital tools, driver/fleet operator experiences, and market/ total cost of ownership considerations. These KPIs can be measured during the demonstration and digital twin operations, using both quantitative and qualitative measures. Objective data, subjective evaluations, and inputs such as vehicle data, questionnaires, and driver interviews can all contribute to the assessment. The evaluation plan takes a structured approach, detailing each KPI’s description, assessment methods, parameters, and necessary information to address potential risks and challenges during the evaluation phase.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation Framework of Next Generation Electric Trucks

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid advancement of materials science and engineering has increased the demand for technical personnel with practical skills in material characterization, quality control, and research and development (R&D). Therefore, application-oriented learning models that meet industrial needs are essential for improving vocational education and training. This study proposes a project-based education model integrating analytical and characterization techniques used in polymer and composite materials technologies into vocational education. Students will investigate the structural, thermal, and morphological properties of materials using techniques such as Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). They will interpret experimental results, evaluate material properties, and prepare scientific and technical reports. These activities aim to develop competencies in laboratory safety, experimental planning, quality control, data interpretation, and problem-solving. Sector-specific case studies covering packaging, agriculture, food, manufacturing, polymer processing, and composite materials will connect theoretical knowledge with industrial practice. Through these applications, students will gain experience in identifying and addressing real-world production and material-related challenges. The proposed model aims to integrate R&D centers into vocational education, improve practice-oriented learning, and train qualified technical personnel in line with industrial requirements. It also seeks to strengthen university–industry collaboration and facilitate the transfer of advanced materials technologies into educational settings. Ultimately, the model offers a practical framework for transforming vocational education through project-based learning, laboratory applications, and the effective use of R&D infrastructure.
evidence_items.title: Research and Development Centers and Project-Based Education Model for Training Qualified Technical Personnel for Industry

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Photovoltaic (PV) systems have transformed from traditional energy production infrastructures to data-intensive and cyber-physical systems; this transformation has increased the need for qualified technical personnel who can not only install systems but also monitor real-time data, evaluate performance, diagnose faults, and optimize system efficiency. This study proposes an AI-supported integrated training model to support the digital transformation of photovoltaic laboratories in vocational and technical education. The proposed model integrates the physical laboratory infrastructure, consisting of PV panels, inverters, batteries, charge controllers, loads, and measurement units, with an ESP32-based data acquisition system, Internet of Things (IoT)-supported real-time monitoring, Python and pvlib -based data analysis, TensorFlow -based generation forecasting, and a digital twin environment. This aims to develop students' competencies not only in installation skills but also in data analysis, performance interpretation, fault diagnosis, and technical decision-making. The theoretical framework of the study is based on current research published between 2023 and 2026 in the fields of digital twins, AI-based fault diagnosis, real-time production forecasting, intelligent monitoring systems, and digital vocational training. A quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test control group research design was proposed to evaluate the educational impact of the model; student achievement, fault diagnosis performance, PV data literacy, and laboratory self-efficacy were determined as the key evaluation criteria. In conclusion, the study presents a low-cost, scalable, and applicable smart laboratory model for renewable energy education that is compatible with Industry 4.0 requirements and applicable in various vocational training institutions.
evidence_items.title: Vocational In education Artificial Intelligence Supported Photovoltaic System Education Model: Real Timed Performance Analysis and Digital Twin Approach

The archive contains Python software, a local browser interface, tests, processing protocols, R/Python analysis scripts and selected historical numerical results. evidence_items.summary: Background: Surgical skill assessment in orthopaedic trauma surgery still relies on subjective expert ratings, which limits consistency and scalability. While digitalization offers a path toward objective and scalable assessment, the highly manual and haptic nature of surgery makes tool use difficult to capture digitally, keeping such approaches underdeveloped. This study introduces a digital assessment framework for orthopaedic trauma training that derives digital behavioral metrics (DBM) from tracked surgical tool motion. Specifically, it investigates (1) which DBM indicate technical proficiency and (2) to what extent these DBM are capable of predicting expert-rated surgical performance. Methods: Twenty-eight participants performed 3 standardized fracture fixations on synthetic bone models of the radius, ulna, and fibula. Tool motion was captured and transformed into a digital twin from which metrics such as path length, smoothness, and task duration were derived. These metrics were statistically compared with the average Global Rating Scale (GRS) obtained from 4 experts who rated each surgical performance. (1) Correlation analysis identified skill-relevant metrics and (2) a predictive model was trained to estimate performance from DBM evaluating its accuracy against the individual expert ratings. Results: (1) Several DBM were found to be indicative of surgical performance. Measures based on tool path length and time per activity showed strong correlations with expert ratings, reaching coefficients of up to 0.6. Correlation strength varied across tools and procedures. (2) The predictive model achieved a mean absolute difference of 3.8 points from the average GRS score (scale range: 28-70), outperforming the mean interexpert difference of 4.6 points. Conclusion: DBM were identified as valid indicators of surgical skill.
evidence_items.title: Assessing Surgical Skill in Orthopedic Trauma Surgery Training: Behavioral Metrics for Digital Performance Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of the modern information environment. Libraries are also experiencing changes as AI-based tools are increasingly used for information searching, reference services, content organisation, and research support. Students and researchers use generative AI tools to find information, generate ideas, summarise documents, and understand difficult topics. These tools can provide useful support, but they also raise concerns related to accuracy, bias, privacy, copyright, misinformation, and academic integrity. In this changing environment, digital literacy needs to go beyond the basic ability to use computers and digital resources. Users need to understand how AI-generated information is produced, how its accuracy can be evaluated, and when information should be verified through reliable and authoritative sources. Critical AI use is therefore becoming an important part of modern information literacy. Librarians can guide users in understanding both the benefits and limitations of AI and encourage them to use these tools responsibly. This paper discusses digital literacy and the responsible use of AI in libraries. It focuses on the changing information environment, the use of AI in library services, the critical evaluation of AI-generated information, ethical concerns, and the changing role of librarians. The paper highlights that AI can be a useful tool for learning and research when it is used with human judgement, critical thinking, and ethical responsibility.
evidence_items.title: DIGITAL LITERACY AND CRITICAL AI USE IN LIBRARIES: NAVIGATING THE HUMAN AND ETHICAL DIMENSIONS IN THE AI ERA

evidence_items.summary: This dataset constitutes part of the dataset used in the manuscript: Greggio N., Giambastiani B.M.S., Moretti G., Valenti J., Dinelli E. 2026. Geochemical fingerprints of modern and relict sands along the Northern Adriatic coast: tracing natural processes and anthropogenic sediment redistribution. Physics and Chemistry of the Earth. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pce.2026.104905  The dataset contains the geochemical composition of 43 beach sand samples collected along the Emilia-Romagna coast (Northern Adriatic Sea, Italy) during two regional monitoring campaigns carried out in 2006 (n = 20) and 2020 (n = 23). Each record corresponds to one composite beach sediment sample and includes the sample identifier, sampling campaign, SICELL coastal sedimentary cell, geographic coordinates (WGS84, EPSG:4326), major element composition (wt.%), trace element concentrations (mg/kg), loss on ignition (LOI), and derived elemental ratios (Al-, Mn- and P-normalized ratios and selected trace element ratios). Samples were collected from the upper 20–30 cm of beach sediment; at each site, sediments from 5–6 points within an area of approximately 100 m were combined and homogenized to obtain a representative bulk sample. Geochemical analyses were performed by Wavelength Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence (WDXRF) on pressed powder pellets using a Panalytical Axios 4000 spectrometer. The dataset complements previously published regional geochemical datasets and provides open access to beach sediment data that have not been presented in dedicated scientific publications. These data can be used for studies on sediment provenance, coastal sediment dynamics, heavy mineral distribution, geochemical mapping, environmental monitoring, and assessment of beach nourishment effects on sediment composition.
evidence_items.title: Beach Sand Geochemical Dataset (Emilia-Romagna Coast, Italy) — 2006 and 2020 monitoring campaigns

evidence_items.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is one of the most widely used imaging techniques in medical imaging with better capability for soft tissues imaging. It is very appropriate for brain imaging, for early detection and diagnosis of brain tumors, treatment monitoring and, other brain abnormalities. Even though it’s providing high-quality information, images may be corrupted by the different types of noises during acquisition and transmission. However, the incorporated noise during MRI image acquisition and transmission process makes it difficult for human interpretation as well as computer-aided analysis of the images. The Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) images are generally prone to noises such as Gaussian noise, Rician noise, Salt and Pepper noise (impulse noise) and speckle noise. A more precise brain MR image is essential for further analysis process. In this proposed experimentation five different filters such as Median filter, Adaptive Median filter, Gaussian filter, Wiener filter and Average (mean) filter are used to remove the additive noises present in the MRI images. The additive noises used to test filters are Gaussian, Salt and pepper, Rician and speckle noises. The additive noise of varying density was step by step added to MRI image from 10% to 90% to evaluate performance of the denoising filters by qualitative and quantitative evaluation. The performances analyses of these denoising filtering techniques are evaluated by observing the statistical parameters such as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Normalized Mean Squared Error (NRMSE).
evidence_items.title: Investigational Analysis of Denoising Filters on Brain MR Images using Image Quality Assessment Performance Measurements

evidence_items.summary: Reducing of pollutants with simultaneous increase of the gas turbine power, is always a fundamental aim of the Turbine technology. New developed structures and operating systems in the turbine production have been established. In the meanwhile, burning instabilities are still appearing in these systems during a Cross-ignition process (CI), creating pollutants due to high flame temperatures, and are not yet completely investigated.The phenomena of a CI is taking place during operation of malty-burner combustion chambers, when one burner is extinguished and a particular volume of combustible mixture is formed in the distance between this burner and the adjacent lightened one, which considered to be as an ignition path. Cross ignition process should be performed along the ignition path in a particularly controlled small time.So that, no excessive quantities of combustible mixtures will be injected during this time in the combustion chamber. Otherwise, burning instabilities and mechanical wear will be occurred. Depending on this illustration, the Cross Ignition Time (CIT) of an extinguished burner, that will be considered as the evaluation measure for the entire cross-ignition process, should be Possibly as low as its normal ignition time.The main objective of this project is to reproduce constructive criteria for controlling of cross ignition process by influencing the mixing process and heat flux in a defined mixing zone existing along the ignition path.
evidence_items.title: Design Criteria for Optimization of the Cross Ignition Process in Gasturbine-Engines

evidence_items.summary: Plants and plant-derived materials play an immensely vital role in disease management and health care programs. Essential oil from wood chips of Himalayan Cedar, Cedrus deodara (Roxburgh) family: Pinaceae ), was obtained by hydrodistillation. The cedar wood oil at various test doses of 250mg/kg, 500mg/kg, and 1000mg/kg was evaluated for various activities like liver function tests, lipid profile, and renal function tests by using the in vivo mice model. The study’s bioassay results revealed the potential of cedar oil for its use in health management and its efficacy in treating high levels of Total Cholesterol (TC), Triglyceride (TG), Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL), High-Density Lipoprotein (HDL), Very Low-Density Lipoprotein (VLDL), ALP, AST, ALT, Bilirubin, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), Urea (U) and Creatinine. In conclusion, Cedar wood oil can be an effective therapeutic agent against hepatotoxicity, renal toxicity, and hyperlipidemia. Furthermore, the detailed analysis of cedar wood oil will further explore the formulation of new medicinal plant-based drugs. published by the International Journal of Biosciences | IJB
evidence_items.title: In-vivo study of cedar wood oil on the protective effects of hepatotoxicity, renal toxicity and hyperlipidemia

evidence_items.summary: Understanding the predictors of plant diversity gradients remains a major challenge in biogeography, particularly in understudied arid ecosystems where water availability is highly constrained. Coastal lomas—isolated, fog-fed vegetation oases distributed across the Peruvian and Chilean coastal deserts of South America–provide a unique system for examining how climate, topography, and geography shape plant diversity under extreme aridity. Here, we evaluated the geographic variation and predictors of the taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity of seed plants in these environments. We compiled the most comprehensive data set to date of 71 coastal lomas and used generalized linear models to assess latitudinal diversity gradients. We also evaluated the relative importance of environmental, topographic, and geographic predictors of plant taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity. We found that mean phylogenetic distance (MPD) exhibited non-linear relationships with latitude, and standardized phylogenetic diversity (PD) showed a weak variation with latitude, with both peaking in the hyper-arid core of the Atacama Desert. In contrast, standardized mean nearest taxon distance (MNTD) and species richness (adjusted by area) showed no significant association with latitude. Our results suggest that current climate, environmental heterogeneity, and geographical factors are the primary predictors of seed plant diversity in these regions. Plant species richness (adjusted by area) increased with aridity and cloud cover, while standardized PD decreased with aridity and distance to the coast while increasing with human footprint and northness. Standardized MNTD also increased with human footprint and northness, and decreased with increasing aridity and temperature. Standardized MPD increased with slope, temperature, northness, and aridity, and decreased with cloud cover, isothermality, and distance to the coast.
evidence_items.title: Environmental and geographic predictors of seed plant diversity across South American terrestrial coastal lomas

evidence_items.summary: Reliable individual identification is fundamental to ecological and behavioural studies, yet many marking techniques are invasive and may affect animal behaviour or survival. Biometric identification approaches offer a non-invasive alternative for individual recognition using phenotypic traits. In amphibians, body patterns, especially colouration, have been used to identify individuals, but species lacking permanent body patterns require alternative traits. This study evaluated whether iris patterns could serve as a marker for individual recognition in the treefrog Osteocephalus oophagus . A capture-recapture study was conducted over three breeding seasons (2021–2023) in French Guiana. At each encounter, eye photographs were compared with an image library to identify individuals without handling. Manual identifications were independently verified using Wild-ID software. Across 392 capture events involving 103 individuals, iris patterns were highly distinctive among individuals and enabled repeated identification across encounters. Within-season recapture rates ranged from 56% to 80%, indicating that iris patterns remained sufficiently stable for short-term monitoring. However, only three individuals were re-identified across years, preventing a robust assessment of long-term pattern stability. As these individuals showed no substantial alteration in iris patterns, the low interannual recapture rate was more likely explained by population turnover or emigration than by changes in iris morphology. The findings suggest that iris recognition provides an effective, non-invasive method for short-term individual identification in O. oophagus , reducing the need for repeated handling and supporting ethical wildlife research. Further studies are needed to assess the long-term stability of iris patterns and evaluate the applicability of this method to other amphibian species.
evidence_items.title: Iris pattern recognition as a non-invasive method for individual identification in Osteocephalus oophagus (Hylidae)

evidence_items.summary: As coastal ecosystems and their services face intensifying cumulative human pressures that degrade habitats and alter community structure and functioning, understanding ecosystem recovery capacity is essential. This is particularly true in the Black Sea, which is vulnerable to these impacts due to its oceanographic and hydrological characteristics, and its historical susceptibility to severe eutrophication. This study analyzes long-term marine monitoring data from the LTER-BG site Sozopol-Black Sea (LTER EU BG 06) to track macrobenthic community recovery following the closure of an untreated sewage outfall - a major point source of anthropogenic eutrophication in the area. Samples were collected annually from 2014 to 2026, spanning the periods before and after outfall closure in 2016. We measured macroinvertebrate richness, abundance, and biomass, as well as sediment parameters (grain size, total organic matter) and water column variables (temperature, salinity, nutrients, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll, suspended matter, and transparency). Macroinvertebrate community structure, compositional shifts, and recovery trajectories were evaluated using alpha diversity metrics (species richness, specific abundance, and biomass per m2), biodiversity indices (Shannon index H', effective number of taxa), and ecological state indicators (M-AMBI n (Sigovini et al. 2013), ecological group proportions). While water physical and chemical parameters in the study area returned to good ecological state within one year post-closure, macrobenthic communities required more time to recover, showing multi-year fluctuations in biodiversity, ecological state, and ecological group composition. Notably, since 2021–2022, seagrass beds have recolonized the former outfall site, supporting rich and abundant invertebrate communities.
evidence_items.title: Recovery of coastal benthic ecosystems from human pressure: a ten-year case study in the Black Sea

evidence_items.summary: Emerging Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has revolutionized and pervaded various sectors, organizational systems and activities including Knowledge Management (KM). In the knowledge domain, AI holds great promise in transferring tacit knowledge in useful explicit form. AI offers powerful tools for automating tasks, analyzing vast datasets, and extracting valuable insights. However, integrating AI into knowledge management systems introduces new cyber security challenges. This research article explores the interplay between AI and knowledge management, analyzing the influence of AI on knowledge management strategies and the cyber security risks associated with such integration. This paper explores case studies that illustrate the impact of AI on knowledge management practices and discusses real-world examples of cyber security incidents related to AIpowered knowledge management systems.
evidence_items.title: ROLE OF DELNET IN ENHANCING SCHOLARLY COMMUNICATION SERVICES IN ACADEMIC LIBRARIES : AN ASSESSMENT

evidence_items.summary: This study explores whether participation in short food supply chains (SFSCs) reduces perception gaps and cognitive biases in farmers’ evaluation of financial performance in post-pandemic conditions. Research design and methods: survey data from 76 SFSC and 95 non-SFSC-farms in Poland were compared with actual data from the FADN system to assess accuracy in estimating production, income, and cost changes. Findings: SFSC farmers demonstrated more accurate and optimistic assessments of economic indicators, particularly for production and income, compared to non-SFSC peers. Differences were statistically significant, suggesting better perception and reduced bias. Implications and recommendations: encouraging SFSC participation and offering training in accounting and financial literacy may help farmers make more informed decisions and reduce cognitive distortions. Contribution and value added: by applying behavioural economics, Sustainable Systems Theory, and Social–Ecological Systems Theory, the study highlights SFSCs as tools for increasing farmers’ adaptive capacity, market awareness, and resilience in uncertain conditions.
evidence_items.title: Farmers' perception of post-pandemic economic performance: do short food supply chains reduce cognitive biases?

evidence_items.summary: Freshwater ecosystems are among the most sensitive indicators of global environmental change because they integrate the effects of climate variability, atmospheric deposition, watershed processes, and human pressures. Detecting and understanding these changes requires observation systems capable of capturing ecosystem dynamics across multiple temporal scales, from short-lived events to long-term trends. Long-Term Ecological Research (LTER) provides the instrument to distinguish natural variability from monotonic, directional environmental change and to identify the mechanisms driving ecosystem transformations. The European eLTER Research Infrastructure further promotes harmonized and integrated observations across environmental spheres, supporting the assessment of ecosystem responses to climate change, biodiversity loss, and other major sustainability challenges. Lake Maggiore, one of Europe's largest and deepest subalpine lakes, is a core site of the Italian and European LTER networks since their establishment and represents a unique freshwater observatory for studying both global and local change. Continuous limnological observations since the 1980s, funded by the International Commission for the Protection of Swiss-Italian waters (CIPAIS), have produced one of the longest and most comprehensive datasets available for southern European lakes. These records documented the lake's recovery from eutrophication following nutrient reduction measure implementation and subsequently revealed the emergence of climate change as the current dominant driver of ecosystem dynamics (Rogora et al. 2021). To strengthen its observational capacity, Lake Maggiore has recently integrated high-frequency monitoring into its long-term research framework through the deployment of two automated limnological buoys, located in different sub-basins of the lake.
evidence_items.title: Lake Maggiore: a long-term Observatory for Global Environmental Change

evidence_items.summary: Modern computing and human-machine systems are increasingly throttled by the "phase change bottleneck"—a systemic failure that occurs when high-density, high-velocity data streams encounter a localized, bandwidth-constrained processing boundary. Whether this boundary is biological (human cognitive workload), computational (Large Language Model context windows), or infrastructural (edge-mesh network constraints), standard mitigation strategies rely on lossy filtering or rigid, reactive alerting mechanisms that inherently exacerbate systemic load during crises.    This paper introduces the Thermodynamic Data Paradigm (TDP), a novel, unified architectural framework that treats digital information as a multi-state fluid. By deploying a low-latency, closed-loop state engine—termed the Phase Governor—the system dynamically modulates information density across three distinct operational modalities based on shifting real-time constraints: Explicit Static (Ice), Structured Kinetic (Liquid), and Attenuated Latent (Steam). The framework continuously evaluates a composite state index derived from external systemic pressure and internal consumer absorption capacity. When critical thresholds are breached, the engine executes non-linear "flash-boil" transitions to bypass conscious linguistic or computational overhead, utilizing a mathematical hysteresis curve to safely manage the subsequent condensation phase as equilibrium returns.
evidence_items.title: The Thermodynamic Data Paradigm: A Unified Architectural Framework for Closed-Loop Adaptive State Transitions Across Asynchronous Bottlenecks

evidence_items.summary: Processed multisensor feature dataset from an instrumented laboratory-scale belt conveyor of the GAMHE 5.0 pilot line at the Centre for Automation and Robotics (CAR, CSIC-UPM). The conveyor is driven by a Maxon 148867 DC motor through a planetary gearbox and a pulley transmission. Its adjustable mechanisms were used to set nominal configurations and to introduce controlled changes in belt tension, pulley tension, roller alignment and gearbox adjustment. The campaign comprises eight experiments, each provided as one CSV file: •              A, B and C: nominal references for the motor alone, the motor with gearbox and the complete conveyor, at setpoints 10–100. •              D, E and F: graded belt-tension, pulley-tension and roller-alignment levels, without and with an additional 10 kg load. •              G: a return to the C, B and A configurations. •              H: graded gearbox adjustment. Recordings took place in two sessions: A–C on 6–7 October 2025, and D–H between 19 January and 9 February 2026. The data contain 90,112 one-second observations from 154 acquisition executions. Each observation has 284 sensor features (120 vibration, 114 electrical, 48 acoustic, 2 temperature/humidity) and the experimental context: sub-stage identifier, speed setpoint, mechanical configuration, adjustment levels and, for D–H, motor speed.
evidence_items.title: Multisensor Conveyor Belt Dataset from the GAMHE 5.0 pilot line.

evidence_items.summary: This reproducibility package accompanies the manuscript “Finite-Memory Predictive Closure in Low-Dimensional Physical Reservoirs” by Chikoo Oosawa. The study formulates finite-memory predictive closure as a task-conditioned trade-off between simultaneous state information and temporal memory. The central quantity is the excess predictive log loss incurred when prediction is based on a finite observation history rather than a richer reference information set. The framework separates a recoverable finite-memory deficit from an irreducible observation deficit , thereby distinguishing information that can be compensated by temporal history from information that is permanently lost through the observation map. This archive contains the source code, generated numerical tables, figure files, software-environment information, and checkpoint-free run logs used to reproduce the numerical results reported in the manuscript. The included calculations cover: exact linear-Gaussian predictive-closure calculations and state-memory frontiers; Mori–Zwanzig memory-kernel and decay-rate diagnostics; a nonlinear driven-pendulum benchmark using finite delayed observations; held-out probabilistic prediction scores; matched sensor-delay budget comparisons; and supplementary KNN robustness checks. The principal numerical results can be regenerated with: python scripts/run prc mz1.py --fresh The archive is intended as a reproducibility object accompanying the manuscript rather than as a replacement for the article. It provides the numerical material needed to inspect and regenerate the reported figures and quantitative comparisons. Author: Chikoo Oosawa Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Systems Engineering, Kyushu Institute of Technology ORCID: 0009-0007-8824-5465 Version: 1.0.0 License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23357199

evidence_items.summary: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from π_{0.5} and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.
evidence_items.title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics

evidence_items.summary: Test-time scaling has enabled LLMs to solve increasingly complex reasoning, discovery, and optimization tasks. However, existing approaches often gather observations while seeking evidence for current hypotheses, then generate new hypotheses conditioned on those hypotheses and their associated evidence. This couples observation discovery to existing hypotheses, favoring local refinements over exploration of unknown hypotheses regions. Inspired by the hypothetico-deductive method (Hempel, 1945) and dual-space models of scientific discovery (Klahr & Dunbar, 1988), we introduce SHELDON, a scientific reasoning harness that separately represents and jointly explores hypothesis and observation spaces. By actively seeking new observations along with new hypotheses, SHELDON can discover observations that its current hypotheses do not explain. These unexplained observations expose gaps in its understanding, motivate new investigations, and guide the generation of hypotheses beyond refinements of existing ones. Across diagnosis, abstract reasoning, and optimization benchmarks, SHELDON outperforms evaluated baselines by up to 26.7 points. Additional analysis shows that SHELDON generates up to 4.5x more novel solutions.
evidence_items.title: SHELDON: Reasoning through Dual Search over Hypothesis and Observation Spaces

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have substantially improved the capabilities of GUI agents, while memory augmentation has emerged as a promising approach for reusing knowledge from past interactions. However, existing memory augmented GUI agents typically adopt a fixed representation strategy, providing retrieved experience as a static modality. It remains unclear whether a single memory modality is consistently optimal, or how modality preference changes across interaction steps. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of memory modality in VLM based GUI agents. Across GUI benchmarks, we find that the preferred memory representation is strongly step dependent. Motivated by the finding, we introduce SwitchMem, a routing framework that dynamically selects between textual and visual memory representations at each step. Across three GUI benchmarks, SwitchMem outperforms memory augmented baselines that rely on static memory representations. Our findings validate our claim that memory modality is a step dependent decision rather than a fixed design choice. Code and project resources are available at https://txxnrd.github.io/switchmem
evidence_items.title: Learning How to Remember: Memory Modality Selection for GUI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
evidence_items.title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards

evidence_items.summary: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
evidence_items.title: TacitVLA: Reasoning Vision-Language-Action Models Without Reasoning Latency

evidence_items.summary: Rubric-based reward models (RMs) evaluate responses against explicit criteria. However, existing methods often derive criteria from observed response candidates, introducing response-induced bias that may limit rubric generalizability. Their judges also struggle with mechanical constraints when relying on reading alone, and commonly used pairwise judges provide only relative preferences, complicating their direct use for policy optimization. We propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM that derives hard rules and graded principles by reasoning about the instruction alone and evaluates responses independently through tool-augmented judging. Both components are trained through label-blind distillation, in which preference labels only filter a teacher's outputs, yielding ReVeR-Traces, a large-scale dataset of rubric-reasoning and judging trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that ReVeR outperforms pairwise rubric RMs in average preference accuracy, most clearly on instruction following, as well as in test-time scaling and downstream policy optimization. We further find that generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and that higher preference accuracy does not necessarily translate into better downstream policies. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties, shedding light on future RM research.
evidence_items.title: Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence: Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges

evidence_items.summary: Learning humanoid loco-manipulation from human demonstrations rests on observing how locomotion, posture, and object interaction evolve together as tasks unfold. Scaling collection across diverse environments, in turn, favors lightweight, portable capture systems. Yet, existing datasets provide only partial views of this coordination. Thus, we introduce EgoExplorer, a 100-hour vision-motion-touch observatory of human loco-manipulation built with a wearable system. With an emphasis on professional activities, its continuous recordings align egocentric video with reconstructed whole-body motion, fine-grained finger articulation, and tactile observations, accompanied by step-level descriptions. To achieve this coverage with sparse body sensing, we develop the Calibrate-Complete-Constrain pipeline. Concretely, reusable calibration fixes participant geometry and sensor attachments before motion inference to disentangle mounting offsets from articulation. A temporal prior then completes unobserved joint motion, while layered constraints promote measurement agreement, temporal continuity, and geometric consistency, properties that motion plausibility alone does not guarantee. Against tracker-fitted references, the method reduces body-point error by 71.9% relative to the strongest baseline; matched evaluations also show gains in hand stability and contact estimation. Preliminary studies explore multimodal generation and conditioning alongside humanoid retargeting with whole-body control in simulation.
evidence_items.title: EgoExplorer: A Vision-Motion-Touch Observatory for Human Loco-Manipulation In Situ

evidence_items.summary: Offline benchmarks for microservice root cause analysis (RCA) rank methods by a score pooled over several applications, and a pooled lead leaves two things unstated: on which of the systems it holds, and how the score was produced. We audit both on three public benchmark families (OpenRCA, RCAEval, and PetShop), running the released implementations of 16 methods under recorded configurations on 11 subsystems and on a second release of three of the applications. Whether a pooled lead between published methods holds on every subsystem is decided by a quantity the leaderboard withholds, the spread of the lead across subsystems: of 15 leads whose margin exceeds this spread, 14 hold everywhere; of the 8 whose margin is below it, 6 reverse. The per-fault and per-scenario tables that the benchmark papers publish split the same way, and every error of a ranking computed without one subsystem falls on a lead of the second kind. On the second release a third of the comparisons change sign, most through one method's response to the metric kinds it records, and on several subsystems a simple probe or a shipped baseline beats every published method. How the score was produced matters as much: the input table that one released runner reads is not the one its documentation describes, and this choice alone reverses a comparison between published methods with intervals excluding zero both ways; an unpinned dependency and a duplicated column header each make a method return its input column order without an error. Of 23 RCA papers we examined, none releases the per-case outputs needed to check either premise. We recommend that a pooled comparison state the subsystems it covers and its spread across them, the input table, the handling of failed outputs, and the denominator, and be accompanied by per-case outputs, as ours are in our replication package.
evidence_items.title: What a Pooled Leaderboard Does Not Say: Auditing the Scope and Provenance of Method Comparisons in Microservice RCA Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Abstract A persistent gap separates academic research priorities from the operational challenges faced by manufacturing firms. Established identification methods, among them Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) workshops, Lean audits and consultant engagements, are episodic, bounded by participant expertise and organised along departmental lines, which makes cross-departmental issues hard to surface. Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) have meanwhile shown collaborative problem-solving ability in software engineering and, more recently, in shopfloor scheduling and supply chain coordination. This article is a Perspective. It develops a framework and a research agenda; implementation and empirical evaluation fall outside its scope and are set out as its first research priorities. Three contributions are offered. The first is a synthesis of literature from industrial problem identification, LLM-based autonomous agents and manufacturing AI, which positions the proposal against existing industrial LLM agent work. The second is a framework in which six domain-specialised agents (production, quality, maintenance, supply chain, safety, energy) would collaborate through a five-phase protocol: worker-driven discovery, cross-departmental analysis, candidate-relationship detection, consensus-based financial assessment and debate-driven prioritisation. The prioritisation procedure is fully specified, including the normalisation of financial estimates, a measure of estimate dispersion, the derivation of criteria weights, a non-compensatory gate for safety-critical items and a mandatory human verification step. The third is a worked calculation on a hypothetical steel manufacturing vignette, included so that the procedure can be reproduced and scrutinised rather than as evidence of effectiveness. A preliminary qualitative readiness assessment and a three-horizon agenda of fourteen research questions complete the paper.
evidence_items.title: Large language model multiagent systems for industrial problem discovery and prioritization

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in decision-support systems because of their ability to interpret complex queries, synthesize information, and generate contextually relevant responses. However, their use in reliability sensitive settings remains challenging because LLMs can produce incorrect or unsupported outputs while expressing a high degree of linguistic confidence. This paper presents a confidence aware explainable AI framework for improving the reliability of LLM-based decision support. The proposed approach combines model confidence, semantic consistency across multiple stochastic generations, and explanation support to construct a composite reliability score. A selective decision module then uses this score to determine whether a generated response should be accepted, flagged for review, or withheld through abstention. The framework is evaluated across factual, commonsense, and multi-step reasoning tasks using multiple open-weight LLMs. Performance is assessed in terms of answer accuracy, expected calibration error, failure-detection AUROC, selective accuracy, and response coverage. The evaluation investigates whether combining complementary reliability signals provides a more informative assessment of response correctness than self-reported confidence, model confidence, or semantic consistency alone. The proposed framework provides a practical reliability layer for LLM-based decision-support systems by jointly communicating confidence, explanation support, and an actionable response decision, thereby helping distinguish sufficiently reliable outputs from those requiring further verification or abstention.
evidence_items.title: Confidence-Aware Explainable AI for Reliable Large Language Model Decision Support
