evidence_items.summary: Electroencephalography analysis typically requires multistage processing pipelines for which configuration depends on recording characteristics and the intended analytical objective. Although automated pipelines improve reproducibility, they generally implement predefined processing sequences. We present an agentic framework in which a large language model (LLM) orchestrator synthesizes and executes task-specific EEG processing workflows by selecting, parameterizing, and ordering established signal processing components accessed through Model Context Protocol interfaces. Computational EEG processing and analysis operations are performed using established EEGLAB (version 2026.0.0) implementations running in MATLAB (R2026a) , while structured execution results and quality control information are returned to the orchestrator to support adaptation during execution. The framework is evaluated by examining tool-layer execution fidelity, independent pipeline synthesis, and the quality of the resulting EEG output relative to the established DISCOVER-EEG workflow. In an evaluation using eight resting state EEG recordings from four participants, mean epoch retention was 0.845 for the agent-generated pipeline and 0.843 for DISCOVER-EEG, while mean spectral entropy was 4.87 and 4.84 bits, respectively. Mean signal-to-noise ratio was 13.92 dB for the agent-generated pipeline and 11.14 dB for DISCOVER-EEG; however, this difference should be interpreted cautiously because the pipelines used different upper filter boundaries. A secondary analysis examined whether EEG processed using the generated pipeline retained features relevant to Alzheimer’s disease versus healthy control classification. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of coupling LLM-based orchestration with EEG processing software to generate executable task-specific workflows with structured execution records and provenance.
evidence_items.title: Agentic EEG Pipeline Synthesis Using Large Language Models and the Model Context Protocol

organizations: The University of Sheffield , ,
evidence_items.summary: Purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) can be helpful for literature search and summarization but retracted articles can confuse them. It is therefore important to know how aware LLMs are of retractions. Design/methodology/approach Three open-weight (offline) LLMs were asked whether 161 high-profile retracted articles had been retracted, with a similar check for a benchmark multidisciplinary set of 34,070 non-retracted articles. Findings From titles and abstracts, in over 80% of cases the LLMs claimed that a retracted article had not been retracted (GPT OSS 120 B: 82%; Gemma 3 27 B: 84%; DeepSeek R1 72 B: 88%). Reasons for a correct retraction declaration were often wrong. For the benchmark test, there were only 55 false retraction claims from 34,070 non-retracted full-text articles, and 28 false claims when only the title and abstract were entered, suggesting that there is only a small chance that LLMs discount valid studies. When retractions are erroneously claimed, this does not seem to be due to mistakes in the article. Originality/value The results confirm for the first time that offline LLMs have little ability to distinguish between valid and retracted studies, unless they are allowed to, and do, check online. The results therefore give new evidence, based on LLM knowledge of retractions, to be cautious about LLM claims about academic findings.
evidence_items.title: Do large language models know which published articles have been retracted?

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in education, but evidence on their performance comes mainly from high-resource languages. We evaluated five commercial LLMs in Kazakh in a zero-shot setting: sentiment classification on 300 class-balanced KazSAnDRA reviews and question answering (QA) on the same 300 randomly sampled KazQAD questions with and without the gold supporting passage. Exact McNemar tests with Holm correction found no significant pairwise differences on sentiment classification, one with supporting context, and nine without context under the Containment criterion. For OpenAI and Anthropic, the higher-tier model had a larger advantage over its lower-tier counterpart when the supporting passage was removed (tier-by-regime interaction: OR = 1.92, 95% CI [1.52, 2.43]). Closed-book scores were affected by output format, inflectional morphology, and answer length. Human evaluation of 500 QA responses showed that string-based metrics substantially underestimated closed-book accuracy (0.55 by human judgement versus 0.26 by Containment). Under human judgement, the three higher-scoring models did not differ significantly from one another. Access to a relevant passage narrowed differences between models, although this oracle-context condition did not test a retrieval system. These findings support task-specific evaluation of Kazakh-language educational assistants and the use of answer-matching criteria checked against human judgement.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Kazakh-Language Educational Assistants: Sentiment Classification and Question Answering with and Without Context

evidence_items.summary: Background: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is a common entrapment neuropathy, and as patients increasingly seek health information online, the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in providing accurate medical advice is gaining attention. This study evaluates the responses of two large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Google Gemini, regarding CTS management, comparing their outputs to established clinical practice guidelines in terms of accuracy, completeness, and readability. Methods: Seven questions related to CTS treatment were developed and posed to both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The generated responses were assessed by eight fellowship-trained hand surgeons, who independently classified each answer as “appropriate,” “appropriate but incomplete,” or “inappropriate.” Readability was determined as grade level using a standardized online calculator that assessed multiple readability formulas. Results: Out of 112 total responses evaluated, 76 were deemed appropriate, with ChatGPT providing 46 appropriate responses compared with 30 from Gemini. Readability analysis indicated that ChatGPT’s responses averaged at a 12th-grade reading level, while Gemini’s averaged a 10th-grade level. Notably, 24 responses were graded as “appropriate but incomplete,” emphasizing the need for comprehensive information. Conclusion: This study demonstrates the potential of AI-driven platforms in enhancing patient education on CTS management. ChatGPT outperformed Gemini in accuracy, but both models showed limitations in completeness. The findings highlight the importance of ensuring that AI-generated health information is not only accurate but also accessible to patient populations. Future research should focus on improving the integration of AI with health care provider insights and quality resources to enhance patient outcomes and understanding.
evidence_items.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome: Do large language models utilize the clinical practice guidelines?

evidence_items.summary: The objective of this chapter is to determine the implications of Artificial Intelligence in doctoral education to integrate it as a priority form of literacy at this educational level. In the case of doctoral education, the integration of AI is the main challenge because these future researchers will be the generators of scientific and technological knowledge who will face the challenges of an AI-influenced world. The chapter is structured in three parts. The first presents a theoretical framework focused on the characteristics of doctoral training in universities, mentioning its relevance and the different types of doctorates (research-oriented and professional). The second part discusses the concepts and dimensions of artificial intelligence literacy through an organized review of articles. The third part addresses doctoral training in the context of AI, specifically the proposed conceptual model based on student acceptance and evaluation, institutional policies, and hybrid writing-AI process.
evidence_items.title: Implications of Artificial Intelligence in Doctoral Education

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often presented as a sequence of increasingly capable tools, yet educational outcomes do not rise automatically with model capability. This narrative review argues that the decisive variable is alignment: AI produces durable educational value when its affordances are aligned with pedagogy, assessment, educator agency, and institutional governance. The review traces the field from automation and learning analytics through adaptive support and generative co-production to an emerging model of responsible augmentation. Recent meta-analyses, controlled studies, systematic reviews, policy documents, and selected empirical studies were critically compared across three interdependent domains: resources and learning environments; teaching and learning; and management, assessment, and evaluation. The synthesis explains why apparently contradictory findings coexist. Structured, curriculum-aligned AI tutoring can improve immediate learning, whereas unconstrained answer generation can raise supported performance while weakening independent performance. Likewise, automated assessment can improve feedback speed but becomes educationally unsafe when opaque scores or unreliable detectors are treated as final decisions. Evidence concerning international and multilingual learners further shows that language, culture, affect, and data representation are not peripheral variables. The review proposes a responsible-augmentation framework in which alignment, agency, equity, and accountability operate across all three domains. It concludes with a research agenda prioritising longitudinal transfer, calibrated human–AI collaboration, subgroup validity, transparent governance, and institution-level implementation studies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education From Automation to Responsible Augmentation

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Construction delays remain a challenge in projects, often resulting in cost overruns, disputes, productivity losses, and schedule inefficiencies. Growing project complexity has increased the need for data-driven approaches to delay analysis and management. This study reviews the application of artificial intelligence in construction delay analysis and management by examining application areas, techniques, project contexts, implementation maturity, and research gaps. Methods A structured literature review was conducted using a PRISMA-guided search and screening process. Scopus and Web of Science were searched for studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following database filtering, title and abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment, 42 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. Results The reviewed studies applied artificial intelligence to delay prediction, delay-cause identification, risk prioritisation, progress monitoring, schedule recovery, and optimisation using machine learning, deep learning, ensemble learning, and hybrid modelling approaches. Several studies reported predictive accuracy above 90%, particularly for artificial neural networks, ensemble techniques, and hybrid optimisation models. However, evidence remains constrained by limited datasets, project-specific applications, weak real-time data integration, and insufficient consideration of contractual and external factors. Discussion The reviewed studies indicate that Artificial Intelligence (AI) models have improved predictive capability in construction delay management. However, practical implementation remains limited by data availability, model interpretability, and weak integration with project decision-making processes. Conclusion Artificial intelligence can improve construction delay management through transparent and data-driven approaches.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Construction Delay Analysis and Management: A Review

evidence_items.summary: Educators and researchers increasingly recognize the importance of Artificial Intelligence literacy. Despite the growing body of related literature, the challenges and enabling factors for its integration into preschool education remain insufficiently explored and theoretically documented. It is crucial to understand both the difficulties and the conditions that influence its promotion, as well as the perceptions formed in kindergartens, so that these can become subjects of further investigation and evaluation. The present study aims to capture teachers’ views on the importance of Artificial Intelligence literacy in preschool education, as well as to highlight the challenges and factors that influence its implementation. The data were collected from 97 educators through a structured digital questionnaire.
evidence_items.title: Kindergarten teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence in early childhood education.

evidence_items.summary: Background: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly growing in the field of dental medicine and in oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMS). The aim of the present review is to assess current applications of AI in OMS, to evaluate their advantages and limitations, and to identify areas requiring further research. Materials and Methods: A comprehensive search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, with targeted keywords including “artificial intelligence,” “deep learning,” “machine learning,” “oral surgery,” “maxillofacial surgery,” and “diagnosis “Artificial Intelligence” OR “Machine Learning” OR “Deep Learning” AND “Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery” OR “Oral Surgery” OR “Maxillofacial Surgery” AND “Diagnosis”. Of 308 identified studies, 37 met the inclusion criteria focusing on AI-assisted detection interpretation and surgical planning in OMS. Results: AI is effective in identifying anatomical landmarks, evaluating lesions and cysts, diagnosing bone disease like medication-related osteonecrosis of jaws (MRONJ), planning dental implants, and aiding in the classification of fractures and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders. AI can match or outperform human experts in various diagnostic tasks, particularly in panoramic and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) image analysis. AI shows promise in early detection of impacted and supernumerary teeth, maxillofacial pathologies, neoplastic conditions, and soft tissue calcifications. Limitations: However, substantial methodological heterogeneity, inconsistent reporting of AI performance metrics, and limited external validation across the included studies constrain direct comparison of results and assessment of the generalizability of reported AI performance. Conclusions: AI may assist clinicians in diagnostic and treatment-related decision-making, but current evidence does not support its use as a replacement for comprehensive clinical assessment and professional judgment.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery—A Narrative Review

evidence_items.summary: (1) Background: The aim of this study was to analyze how teacher trainees and teachers relate to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education across socio-emotional, attitudinal, competency-based, and ethical dimensions, considering the influence of personal, academic, and professional variables. The study was conceptually framed by the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (AI CFT), complemented by DigCompEdu as a broader reference for teacher digital competence. (2) Methods: A quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive, cross-sectional design was developed with a sample of 1292 participants from Andalusia, consisting mainly of university students, along with teachers. The ACISE-IA scale, consisting of 39 items developed by Serrano-García et al. (2026), was used for data collection. (3) Results: The results showed that age and teaching experience are negatively associated with favorable attitudes and digital competence, while academic performance is positively related to greater openness, critical reflection, and perception of competence. Likewise, significant differences were identified according to the branch of knowledge, employment status, and academic year, with more positive assessments among students and in social science areas. (4) Conclusions: Overall, the findings show that the relationship with AI is not homogeneous, but rather modulated by educational and professional trajectories, underscoring the need to design flexible teacher training models that integrate technological development with pedagogical, emotional, and ethical reflection. These findings also contribute to educational sustainability by highlighting the importance of developing teacher training strategies that support the responsible and sustained integration of AI into educational systems.
evidence_items.title: Personal and Academic Factors in Teachers’ Perceptions of Educational Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Spaceflight instruments must undergo electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) testing under strict contamination-control requirements. In this context, local RF-transparent protective covers may be considered when the test facility cannot provide the required cleanliness conditions around the hardware. This work presents an application-oriented electromagnetic assessment of candidate RF-transparent protective covers for contamination-sensitive EMC testing. Several candidate materials are characterized using the open-ended coaxial probe (OECP) technique over the 2–20 GHz band to determine their effective dielectric properties and estimate their normal-incidence flat-wall transmission coefficients. Full-cover transfer-function (TF) measurements are then performed at INTA’s BIANCHA free-space anechoic facility over the 4.5–8 GHz band, using two receiving antennas with complementary radiation characteristics: a pyramidal horn and a top-hat bicone. Hemispherical covers fabricated with five candidate materials are first assessed, including repeatability and time-domain gating analyses. An alternative cubic cover is then evaluated to study the influence of cover geometry, angular incidence and edge/corner effects. An additional S 11 based mismatch assessment is also performed to distinguish antenna input-matching effects from broader system-level antenna–cover interactions. The results show that low-loss dielectric covers can introduce limited TF perturbations within the tested free-space configuration, while also demonstrating that cover geometry has a significant impact on the angular stability of the measured response. The conclusions are therefore restricted to the experimentally validated 4.5–8 GHz BIANCHA configuration.
evidence_items.title: Electromagnetic assessment of RF-transparent protective covers for contamination-sensitive EMC testing

evidence_items.summary: This study assessed the physicochemical parameters and heavy metal (Pb, Cd, Cr, Ni, Cu, Zn) concentrations in surface water of Mgbuodahia River, Niger Delta, Nigeria, for six months (May– October 2025) across four stations (ST1–ST4). Physicochemical parameters were measured in situ, heavy metals were quantified by atomic absorption spectrophotometry, and data were evaluated using a General Linear Model ANOVA with Tukey’s pairwise comparison. Dissolved oxygen was low (0.62±0.12 mg/L) and biochemical oxygen demand elevated (8.41±4.20 mg/L), indicating organic pollution. Lead (0.33±0.10 mg/L) and cadmium (0.10±0.06 mg/L) exceeded WHO permissible limits (0.01 and 0.003 mg/L respectively) at every station and month. ANOVA showed significant monthly variation for pH, conductivity, temperature and most heavy metals, while chromium showed no significant station or month effect, suggesting a diffuse rather than point-source origin. Nickel showed a pronounced June peak roughly double every other month's mean, indicating an episodic input event. These concentrations are higher than values reported for several other Niger Delta water bodies, indicating that Mgbuodahia River is affected by lead and cadmium inputs. The study concludes that Mgbuodahia River is impacted by organic and heavy metal pollution and recommends continuous monitoring and regulation of discharge into the river.
evidence_items.title: Physicochemical Parameters and Heavy Metal Contamination of Surface Water of Mgbuodahia River, Niger Delta, Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: Wheat pests and diseases threaten food security, but field management still lacks intelligent systems that can connect visual diagnosis with executable treatment recommendations. This study proposes WDPG, a knowledge-enhanced multi-agent framework that integrates a three-layer heterogeneous knowledge graph with a source-traceable prescription knowledge base, and combines DSPy-based diagnostic prompt optimization, DeepResearch-based evidence completion, and agentic prescription verification. The system takes wheat images or symptom descriptions as input and coordinates Diagnostic, Prescription, and Critic agents to generate structured prescriptions with traceable evidence, dosage, application method, and pre-harvest interval. On a 601-sample held-out test set, the integrated WDPG system achieved an end-to-end full-prescription accuracy of 0.9218 and demonstrated better overall performance than GPT-5.5 and GLM-4.6V for wheat pest and disease diagnosis and prescription generation. These results support the effectiveness of the integrated WDPG framework for structured and source-grounded wheat pest and disease diagnosis and prescription generation.
evidence_items.title: WDPG: An Integrated Agentic Framework for Wheat Pest and Disease Diagnosis and Prescription Generation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Age-related molecular heterogeneity in breast cancer complicates the prioritization of reproducible research candidates across heterogeneous molecular resources. We developed a bounded agentic in silico framework integrating curated ageing genes, The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA-BRCA), the independent GSE42568 cohort, STRING protein-protein associations, and Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment. Of 307 curated human ageing-related genes, 292 were expression-testable in 1,079 TCGA-BRCA primary tumors. Continuous-age screening identified 126 genes at a false discovery rate below 0.05, and 80 remained significant after adjustment for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2, and pathological stage. Among 40 prespecified candidates tested in GSE42568, eight replicated directionally; IL7R, SQSTM1, EGR1, and IGF1 were both cross-cohort replicated and robust across estrogen-receptor strata. Stratified age-label permutation supported the overall discovery signal (empirical P = 0.001996). STRING hub rankings were stable across interaction-confidence thresholds (Spearman rho = 0.81–0.90), and 514 significant functional terms were reduced to 30 representative modules. A 760-scenario process-aware benchmark compared static, goal-planning, adaptive, and bounded controllers. The bounded controller achieved 1.000 for policy conformance, feasible-goal completion, action appropriateness, safety conformance, provenance conformance, and escalation conformance, with resource stewardship of 0.988. The framework provides a reproducible computational route for molecular candidate prioritization and hypothesis generation while explicitly excluding autonomous diagnosis, prognosis, treatment recommendation, and clinical biomarker declaration.
evidence_items.title: A Bounded Agentic In Silico Framework for Age-Aware Molecular Candidate Prioritization in Breast Cancer

evidence_items.summary: Utilising language models (LLMs) to prepare STEM activities can reduce lesson-planning time, but speed does not ensure quality. A standalone model may introduce factual errors or misconceptions, use language unsuitable for children's age, or suggest unsafe materials. This paper presents a theoretical and methodological framework that treats AI as an agentic system. Models with distinct roles cross-check one another and ground their work through RAG in an expert-reviewed, curated knowledge base. The knowledge base is locally owned and human-readable, with each note recording its source and review status. The system may use local models or privacy-protecting, low-cost services. It is paired with a TPACK-based professional development programme. Prompting matters, but teachers remain responsible for evaluating the evidence and deciding whether a draft suits their context. Four conditions are proposed: ordinary generation, RAG, matched self-review, and a reviewer-agent workflow. The framework has been partially implemented as an operational alpha but has not yet been formally evaluated.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing Teacher Professional Development for Preschool and Early STEM Education Through RAG and a Knowledge-Grounded Agentic System

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents can control robots through visual feedback and action primitives, but repeated LLM calls and redundant observations incur substantial token overhead. We introduce PyRUA-Lean, an interactive code-execution framework in which the agent composes robot primitives, including vision-language-action (VLA) policies, into Python cells that check and retry locally and return only the images and state they request. Across 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, it raises success from 63.1% to 71.7% over tool calling with the same GPT-6 Astra planner and primitives, using 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens on jointly solved instances. On RoboDojo, without any VLA policy or privileged information, it reaches 51.6% average success rate (Score 58.2), 19.4 points above the top entry of the public leaderboard. Based on the PyRUA-Lean framework, we train PyRUA-Lean Coder v0.1-4B, an open 4B model, with GRPO on 45 LIBERO-PRO instances; it improves from 18.8% to 44.1% on unseen task instances, surpassing the Qwen3.5-27B base model.
evidence_items.title: Fewer Tokens, Better Action: GPT-6 Astra Robot Agents with 14% Higher Success Rate but 65% Fewer Tokens

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in scientific writing, yet they can fabricate citation-shaped references that appear plausible but fail bibliographic verification. Existing detectors often reduce verification to binary found/not-found decisions and rely on brittle parsing or incomplete retrieval, offering little field-level signal to auditors. We reframe citation hallucination detection as taxonomy-aligned field-level adjudication and introduce a 12-code taxonomy spanning Real, Potential, and Hallucinated citations. Based on this taxonomy, we build CiteTracer, a cascading multi-agent detector that extracts structured citations from PDF and BibTeX, retrieves evidence through cache lookup, URL fetch, scholar connectors, and web search, applies deterministic field matching, and routes ambiguous cases to class-specialist judgers. We release a benchmark of 2,450 synthetic citations built from real seeds with controlled LLM mutations, paired with 957 real-world fabricated citations drawn from desk-rejected submissions at ICLR 2026 and an anonymous conference. CiteTracer reaches 97.1% accuracy on the synthetic benchmark, with class-level F1 scores of 97.0, 95.8, and 98.5 for Real, Potential, and Hallucinated, respectively, and detects 97.1% of fabrications on the real-world set without abstaining. Code: https://github.com/aaFrostnova/CiteTracer.
evidence_items.title: Source or It Didn't Happen: A Multi-Agent Framework for Citation Hallucination Detection

evidence_items.summary: Robust depth completion is fundamental to real-world 3D scene understanding, yet existing RGB--LiDAR fusion methods degrade significantly under adverse weather, where both camera images and LiDAR measurements suffer from weather-induced corruption. In this paper, we introduce AURORA-KITTI, the first large-scale, physics-consistent synthetic RGB-LiDAR benchmark for any-weather depth completion and denoising. We further formulate Depth Completion and Denoising~(DCD) as a unified task that reconstructs clean dense metric depth from weather-corrupted RGB images and sparse LiDAR inputs while suppressing weather-induced noise. AURORA-KITTI contains over 82K weather-consistent RGB--LiDAR pairs with metric depth supervision, spanning diverse weather types, three severity levels, day/night scenes, paired clean references, lens occlusion conditions, and textual descriptions.Moreover, we provide DDCD as a strong and efficient distillation-based reference baseline. DDCD is trained on AURORA-KITTI using a frozen teacher applied to paired clean RGB images only during training; at inference, it uses weather-corrupted RGB and sparse LiDAR. Experiments on AURORA-KITTI and the real-world DENSE benchmark show that existing depth completion and foundation depth models remain vulnerable under severe weather, while DDCD improves over weather-aware retraining. Controlled experiments further show that physics-consistent adverse-weather data is the dominant driver of robustness, with clean-prior distillation providing complementary gains. Comparisons with off-the-shelf zero-shot methods use different training protocols; same-data retraining and component ablations separately quantify the contributions of weather-aware data and DDCD. Github: https://github.com/Warwick-Jocelyn/AURORA-KITTI.
evidence_items.title: AURORA-KITTI: Any-Weather Depth Completion and Denoising

evidence_items.summary: As coding agents become more capable, tests remain the primary evidence for judging whether their code is correct. Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification. Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.
evidence_items.title: SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications?

evidence_items.summary: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.
evidence_items.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training

evidence_items.summary: Existing benchmarks for GUI agents primarily focus on increasing task difficulty by extending task horizons. Besides, enabling agents to explore unfamiliar environments and successfully complete tasks within them is also a critical yet challenging problem. We introduce LatentGUIWorld, a benchmark of six tasks in three matched pairs organized by the evidence needed for control: $I 0$ uses prior knowledge and available observations, $I 1$ requires interaction that directly reveals hidden semantics, and $I 2$ identifies dynamics from action-response relationships. Frontier models struggle especially on $I 2$ tasks. We introduce MOVE, which separates movement from button events and exposes intermediate visual feedback, together with demonstrations of iterative exploration and control. Ablations show that both action granularity and multi-step demonstrations improve performance. After SFT, LatentLearner-9B achieves 50.0% overall success on LatentGUIWorld, comparable to several frontier models. Joint RL further raises egocentric Drag and Ten-Choice success to 92.0% and 75.3%. Behavioral analysis reveals multi-step exploration. In egocentric Drag, RL increases Pearson correlation between error-normalized commands and ideal gain compensation from 0.610 to 0.803. Together, these behaviors show that models learn to explore through interaction and adapt their control to environment dynamics. The same format improves GUI grounding after RL, reaching 67.37% mean accuracy across five benchmarks versus 66.72% for conventional RL.
evidence_items.title: Learn from Move: the Next Step for GUI Agents

evidence_items.summary: PLANETARY AND EXTREME-ENVIRONMENT QUANTUM–NANO OBSERVATORY NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance This exploratory research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for quantum-enabled and classical sensor networks operating in extreme terrestrial and possible off-world environments. It asks how a distributed observatory can remain scientifically useful under contact loss, power scarcity, reference aging, thermal and radiation stress, material degradation, ambiguous physical changes, delayed commands and difficult maintenance. The central criterion is not uninterrupted telemetry but defensible measurement meaning: a raw observation must retain its measurand, units, calibration lineage, time context, uncertainty and revision history or be declared untrustworthy. The work combines three mother research architectures while respecting their evidential limits. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 65–80, contributes distributed robotics, fault-tolerant task allocation, remote servicing, resource limits and field operations. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, particularly chapters 43–49 and 58–82, contributes bounded autonomy, fleet metrology, human override, classical fallback, recovery and successor handoff. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 33–56 and 79–82, contributes network fault isolation, calibration lineage, replayable evidence and common-mode drift detection. Their intersection motivates proposed experiments but does not demonstrate mature planetary quantum–nano observatories. The central three-coupling is Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance. The candidate mission-continuity heuristic R mission = R energy × R reference × R comm × R recovery × R data represents a useful checklist of necessary capabilities but is not a validated physical law.
evidence_items.title: PLANETARY AND EXTREME-ENVIRONMENT QUANTUM–NANO OBSERVATORY NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT  Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance  This exploratory research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for quantum-enabled and classical sensor networks operating in extreme terrestrial and possible off-world environments. It asks how a distributed observatory can remain scientifically useful under contact loss, power scarcity, reference aging, thermal and radiation stress, material degradation, ambiguous physical changes, delayed commands and difficult maintenance. The central criterion is not uninterrupted telemetry but defensible measurement meaning: a raw observation must retain its measurand, units, calibration lineage, time context, uncertainty and revision history or be declared untrustworthy.  The work combines three mother research architectures while respecting their evidential limits. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 65–80, contributes distributed robotics, fault-tolerant task allocation, remote servicing, resource limits and field operations. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, particularly chapters 43–49 and 58–82, contributes bounded autonomy, fleet metrology, human override, classical fallback, recovery and successor handoff. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 33–56 and 79–82, contributes network fault isolation, calibration lineage, replayable evidence and common-mode drift detection. Their intersection motivates proposed experiments but does not demonstrate mature planetary quantum–nano observatories.  The central three-coupling is Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance. The candidate mission-continuity heuristic R_mission = R_energy × R_reference × R_comm × R_recovery × R_data represents a useful checklist of necessary capabilities but is not a validated physical law. A product of stage reliabilities requires additional independence assumptions. Joint mission survival must account for correlated failures, shared environmental stresses, time-varying hazard rates, depleted resources and common calibration chains. A highly sensitive quantum sensor is not necessarily preferable to a more durable classical instrument once mass, power, packaging, cryogenic or optical stabilization, calibration, data transport and lifecycle cost are included.  The monograph contains 82 research chapters with 12 individually paginated study units per chapter, 30 physical and mathematical derivation plates, a distinct candidate research model and spatial network geometry for each chapter, 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each of the 233 research entrances is paired with a numbered mathematical or physical equation egg. These eggs identify known scientific relationships and interpretation boundaries; they are not newly discovered physical laws. The derivation plates are concise research derivation sketches, not complete mathematical monographs.  The experimental program proposes chamber and field-analog comparisons across thermal cycling, vibration, pressure, salinity, contamination, radiation-relevant exposure and delayed or interrupted communications. It challenges independent versus common-mode reference failures, expired calibration artifacts, clock desynchronization, partial network partitions, compromised firmware, cold starts, long no-contact intervals and station retirement. Classical-only, frozen-calibration and manual-reviewed workflows are mandatory comparators where appropriate. Bench tests, field qualification and actual lunar, Martian or deep-ocean deployments are distinct evidence levels. This volume does not claim that the integrated system is currently mission-qualified.  A 200-Gate research atlas and related spreadsheets support independent laboratories. Gate records specify questions, controlled experiments, independent acceptance and veto criteria, measurement and reference histories, source lineage, energy-data budgets, communication outage tests, fault injections, recoverability, and successor reconstruction. The 33 Answer Embryos remain provisional structures that can be rejected, separated into classical-only alternatives, repaired or reborn. Scientific retirement and no-data states are treated as legitimate results, not failures of intelligence.  SCIENTIFIC BOUNDARY. This is a large-scale, partly template-assisted hypothesis and research-design atlas, not a report of completed physical experiments, qualified space hardware, peer-reviewed validation or guaranteed quantum advantage. A high numerical consensus cannot substitute for a reliable external reference. A robust communication protocol cannot repair a lost measurand or improperly calibrated instrument. Any field deployment would require environment-specific engineering qualification, safety review, lawful mission authority, suitable environmental stewardship and independent verification. Background guidance includes BIPM/JCGM evaluation of measurement uncertainty and NASA documentation of Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking; neither validates the novel integrated platform. evidence_items.summary: Abstract Text embedding models are routinely compared using a single aggregate score on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), yet an aggregate conceals whether a model performs uniformly across task families or excels narrowly on a subset of them. We revisit the original MTEB English-subset results (30 models, 7 task categories) and ask a question the original benchmark report did not directly quantify: is high aggregate performance associated with high cross-task consistency, and does model scale buy consistency in the same way it buys average performance? Using the publicly released per-model, per-task scores, we compute pairwise task correlations, a z-score-based cross-task profile dispersion index for every model, and a Ward hierarchical clustering of models by task profile. We find that profile dispersion is negatively associated with average score (Pearson r = − 0.48, p = 0.008), indicating that top-performing models tend to be more uniformly competent rather than narrowly optimized, but dispersion is essentially uncorrelated with parameter count (r = − 0.003, p = 0.99), indicating that scale alone does not confer cross-task balance. Clustering recovers four qualitatively distinct groups, including a "retrieval-and-reranking specialist" cluster with a pronounced summarization deficit and a fifteen-model "balanced generalist" cluster spanning multiple architectures. These findings reframe model-selection guidance for practitioners and motivate reporting dispersion alongside average score in future embedding leaderboards. All data, code and derived tables are made available for reproducibility [1].
evidence_items.title: Beyond the Leaderboard Average: Cross-Task Consistency, Model Scale, and Specialization Structure in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents increasingly control robots using VLA policies, perception models, and procedural knowledge. These modules are difficult to reuse because their interfaces, embodiment assumptions, and conditions of use differ, and their benefits on physical tasks remain unclear. We package them as embodied skills that extend agent skills with explicit embodiment assumptions and conditions of use, building 250 action, perception, and experience skills from 1,052 resources. On this basis we introduce EmbodiedSkillBench, which runs an agent in a closed observation-action loop and records success, actions, tokens, and wall-clock time. It supports three modes: native control, skill-only execution, and Agent-Directed Reuse (ADR), a mode we propose in which the agent keeps its native controls and decides for each skill whether to invoke, modify, or ignore it. Across four agents on 100 perturbed LIBERO-Pro tasks, we find that skills help an agent only as far as they exceed what it can already do. Skill-only execution lifts GPT-5.6-Sol from 11% to 63% and Kimi-K3 and Claude-Opus-5 by about 20 points, while cutting their token usage by 58% to 85%. Yet all four agents then end up between 61% and 64%, and GPT-6-Astra falls from 92% under native control to 61%. This suggests that as agents grow stronger, the role of embodied skills shifts from supplying missing capability to reducing cost: GPT-6-Astra already solves most tasks through native control, so restricting it to skills removes more than it adds. Under ADR, which lets it keep native control and call skills selectively, GPT-6-Astra recovers to 85%, within 7 points of native control, while using 14.1% fewer tokens and 11.9% less time. With Jev as a skill choosing motion directions and gripper actions, it reaches 81% with 50% fewer tokens and 57% less time. The code is available at https://github.com/HanZhi306/EmbodiedSkill-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Embodied Skill Bench: Benchmarking How Well Agents with Embodied Skills Perform on Physical Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. While tool-augmented medical agents can supply such evidence via external modules, they often lack explicit mechanisms for learning when auxiliary evidence is needed and for preventing inapplicable quantitative evidence from entering diagnostic reasoning. To address this, we propose X-Ragent, a post-training framework for tool-augmented reinforcement learning that decouples learned auxiliary-evidence seeking from validity-gated quantitative measurement acquisition for evidence-grounded CXR reasoning. We construct Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus combining causally ordered tool-augmented trajectories with report-style diagnostic reasoning, and use it to initialize Qwen3-VL-8B via agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We then optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an accuracy-gated reward that applies process-level terms for measurement consistency and auxiliary-tool cost only to correct trajectories, preventing plausible process behavior from compensating for an incorrect diagnosis. Across three CXR benchmarks, X-Ragent achieves the strongest results, including an 8.6-point improvement on the fully held-out ChestAgentBench. By seeking evidence selectively and admitting only valid measurements, X-Ragent supports more faithful and evidence-grounded CXR reasoning.
evidence_items.title: X-Ragent: Tool-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Chest X-Ray Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language navigation requires agents to follow natural-language instructions to reach target locations, making high-quality language supervision essential. Since human annotation is costly, prior work has explored scalable data synthesis methods. However, existing methods typically either use separate models for navigation and instruction generation or couple the two tasks through task-specific components; most also annotate the full trajectory corpus with a fixed model before updating, which can cause generated supervision to lag behind the evolving policy. Therefore, we introduce RSI-Nav, a data-centric recursive self-improvement framework for navigation via policy-synchronized language-action dual bootstrapping, which unifies vision-language-to-action instruction following and vision-action-to-language instruction generation within a shared model. Specifically, after supervised fine-tuning establishes fundamental capabilities, RSI-Nav progressively processes unlabeled trajectories in small shards. The current model generates instructions for these trajectories, executes them to evaluate goal completion and path efficiency, retains qualified samples, and immediately updates itself before processing the next shard. This shard-wise update keeps newly generated supervision aligned with the evolving policy. We also incorporate spatial understanding data, since stronger spatial reasoning benefits navigation. Extensive experiments show that RSI-Nav reaches 68.6% SR on R2R-CE and 72.4% SR on RxR-CE, while providing stronger instruction-generation utility and modestly improved spatial understanding after recursive evolution.
evidence_items.title: Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement for Navigation via Policy-Synchronized Language-Action Dual Bootstrapping

evidence_items.summary: Reusable skills improve multimodal agents without updating model weights, but their effectiveness depends on both the evidence presented and the procedure used to read it. We introduce ViewCraft, which jointly evolves an executable evidence interface and its reading procedure. The interface selects, transforms, and organizes observations; the reader interprets the resulting views. Failure traces guide revisions, replay and paired evaluation retain useful changes, and interface projection recovers visual edits from eligible rejected joint proposals. Across eight benchmarks, ViewCraft improves over direct execution by an average of 6.1 points in task score, with gains on every benchmark. The advantage persists at a matched input-token budget. On all five multi-source tasks, the learned interface uses 8%-15% fewer input tokens than Initial skill. The learned skills also transfer across executors and outperform direct execution in every evaluated transfer, supporting evidence construction and reading as a coupled, reusable skill.
evidence_items.title: VIEWCRAFT: Evolving What Multimodal Agents See and How They Read It

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions. Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments. The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences. We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task. Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting. On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate. These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.
evidence_items.title: Agent Sociodrama: Social-Dynamics-Guided Persona Recasting for LLM Agent Teams

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.
evidence_items.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World

evidence_items.summary: Creativity benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) vary widely in task and metric design. This raises the question of whether they capture a common notion of creativity. We propose that this shared target can be formalized as task-specific performance in the long tail of a reference input-output distribution, which describes how common input-output pairs are relative to a chosen source of text. We ground this proposition in the novelty-quality product formulation and evaluate it empirically across 15 benchmarks and 26 open-weight models, using n-gram absence from the pretraining data as a novelty proxy. Our results show that creativity benchmarks lie further in the tail regions than standard benchmarks. Moreover, on both creativity and standard benchmarks, model rankings from higher-tail subsets of each benchmark align more closely with human creativity judgments in LM-Arena. Building on these findings, we introduce q@Tail(α), a lower-cost creativity diagnostic that measures mean task quality on the tail fraction of an existing benchmark. Applying it to creativity-promoting methods reveals substantial room to improve LLM creativity through stronger tail performance.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating LLM Creativity through Long-Tail Performance

evidence_items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories, but a single trajectory realizes only one continuation at each decision, limiting supervision coverage under a finite sampling budget. We propose BranchOPD (Branching On-Policy Distillation), which selects informative decision points using student uncertainty and teacher-student disagreement, resamples student-policy continuations from shared prefixes, and applies token-level teacher supervision to both main trajectories and branches. BranchOPD operates at token-level decisions in mathematics and within-turn decisions in agent tasks. Shared-prefix reuse reduces student-generated token costs by approximately 19% on ALFWorld and 31% on WebShop relative to seven independent trajectories. We also introduce protocol-boundary repair (PBR), which uses targeted supervision under protocol constraints to mitigate repetition and wasted generation. BranchOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD and Multi-Rollout OPD (n=7) across all evaluated benchmarks, with gains over Vanilla OPD of 18.55 percentage points in mean mathematics accuracy over 16 sampled answers (avg@16) and 13.8 points in mean ALFWorld ID/OOD success. Mechanistic analyses and selection ablations show that branching at uncertain decisions expands subsequent behavior coverage and outperforms random selection and turn-initial branching.
evidence_items.title: Branching On-Policy Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Recent work on language-model adaptation has shown that single models can obtain informative training signals by evaluating their behavior in demonstrationor feedback-augmented contexts, with the help of a teacher network, which is driven by the student's learned parameters. Inspired by this internal-reference principle, we investigate how diffusion models can identify self-referenced training signals without external demonstrations or teacher networks. We introduce SALD, a self-referenced training framework that evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels using the same model. The easier, lower-noise path is evaluated without gradient tracking to provide a reference, while the harder, higher-noise path provides the training gradient. Rather than directly distilling the easy-path prediction, SALD uses the difference between two path errors to adapt the hardpath objective. The proposed Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts this relative error into a differentiable sample-level weight. Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) accumulates relative difficulty across training and adapts the future gap between the two noise levels. Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) further compares the residual power spectra of the two paths and constructs a differentiable, frequency-derived latent-element weight. All components share a single set of model parameters, requiring neither an external teacher network nor additional trainable parameters during training or inference, and no modification to the inference procedure. Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in generation quality, while component-wise ablations quantify the contributions of the proposed components.
evidence_items.title: SALD: Self-Referenced Advantage Learning for Diffusion Models

evidence_items.summary: As text-to-SQL systems move beyond demonstrations toward real-world deployment, ambiguity in user questions becomes a primary source of errors. Such ambiguities are often subtle, domain- or data-specific, and can silently cause system outputs to deviate from the user's true intent. Ambiguity is traditionally addressed through conversational clarification, which is often inefficient, cognitively demanding, and poorly aligned with real-world user workflows. We propose structured disambiguation, a new paradigm in which ambiguity is resolved through explicit, constrained interactions rather than free-form dialogue. We construct ARCS (Ambiguity Resolution Corpus for SQL), the first text-to-SQL benchmark featuring naturally occurring, unconstrained ambiguities over real-world databases, with complete annotations of all valid ambiguity points, interpretations, and SQL queries. Experimental results show that text-to-SQL remains challenging in the presence of ambiguity: gpt-6-sol achieves only 51% end-to-end execution accuracy, and no open-source model exceeds 27%.
evidence_items.title: ARCS: Towards Precise Text-to-SQL via Structured Disambiguation

evidence_items.summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) has largely focused on a single agent following a single instruction, yet many real-world applications require teams of robots to tackle tasks beyond the capabilities of any individual agent. We present Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation, providing, to our knowledge, the first systematic formalization of multi-agent VLN as a constrained coordination problem: each mission consists of subtasks carrying dependency and resource constraints (presence locks and holding chains). A verified four-stage crafting pipeline instantiates the task as MAVLN, comprising 11,724 episodes across 145 scenes with teams of up to four agents under three instruction regimes, accompanied by tailored constraint-aware metrics. We further present TRISS, a coordination-ready navigation system coupling an LLM-based subtask scheduler, a shared topological memory that turns each agent's exploration into team knowledge, and a conflict-aware execution mechanism that realizes simultaneous intentions as collision-free routes. Extensive experiments establish TRISS as a comprehensive baseline and reveal substantial room for improvement across scheduling, planning, and execution, highlighting the challenges of coordinating under MAVLN task constraints. Project page: https://xyz9911.github.io/mavln.
evidence_items.title: Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation: Formulation, Benchmark, and Method

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents relies on purely retrospective training signals: credit is assigned only after observing environmental consequences, leaving the agent's belief at action time invisible to the gradient. We introduce Prospective Hindsight (PH), a self-calibrating training principle that augments any retrospective base method with a signal derived from the gap between the agent's prospective prediction (before feedback) and the retrospective evaluation (after feedback). This per-rollout surprise identifies samples where the agent's self-model is most inaccurate and amplifies their gradient contribution through a stop-gradient surprise-weighted advantage. Since the prospective predictor shares parameters with the policy, the two co-evolve, progressively shifting focus to the agent's remaining blind spots. We connect this principle to a privileged-information gap and show that minimizing the surprise residual provides a descent pathway on the agent's miscalibration rate; calibration thus emerges as a byproduct of optimization rather than from an added objective. On single-turn verifiable tasks and a multi-turn personal-agent task (under GRPO, on-policy distillation, and their combination), PH improves both task performance and calibration, with consistent gains across model scales. Notably, the dominant miscalibration mode shifts structurally between regimes, overconfident failures in single-turn, underconfident successes in multi-turn, yet the same training principle addresses both successfully.
evidence_items.title: Prospective Hindsight: Self-Calibrating Reinforcement Learning via Prediction-Reality Gaps

evidence_items.summary: Autoregressive (AR) grounding models serialize spatial predictions, introducing sequential latency and imposing a causal order on output tokens. We view grounding as visual evidence extraction: objects, locations, and spatial relations are jointly constrained by the image and query, yet their dependencies do not imply an intrinsic left-to-right generation order. This distinction makes bidirectional diffusion a natural fit, allowing spatial hypotheses to emerge in parallel and be jointly refined through iterative denoising. We introduce GroundAnything, a 4B-parameter grounding foundation model that reconciles fast parallel decoding with precise localization through blockwise denoising. Training combines grounding pretraining from public datasets and dedicated data engines, direct AR-to-diffusion conversion with joint AR and diffusion objectives, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO-based reinforcement post-training. Across 30 grounding benchmarks, our autoregressive variant, GroundAnything-VLM, establishes a new overall state of the art among similarly sized models at 72.42%, remaining competitive with GPT-6 Astra (71.35%). With entropy-guided decoding, GroundAnything also surpasses the prior state of the art at this scale, averaging 61.75% versus 53.32% for the fast MTP-based LocateAnything model. We further explore decoding strategies, showing that an optional self-speculative mode achieves a 4.51times speedup over the AR counterpart with a 0.74 percentage-point drop in COCO F1mIoU. Infrastructure experiments show that progressive inference optimizations translate parallel decoding into practical speedups. These support efficient visual grounding in latency-sensitive real-world systems.
evidence_items.title: GroundAnything: Reconciling Parallel Decoding with Precise Visual Grounding at Flash Speed

evidence_items.summary: Historical street-view imagery records urban evolution, but uneven coverage leaves substantial gaps in historical records. Generating plausible past appearances requires restoring changed structures while preserving persistent scene content. We construct VIGOR-his, a decade-spanning cross-view dataset containing 43,653 location-level quadruplets across 11 cities on three continents. Its automated pipeline performs spatial pairing, consistency screening, change classification, and the generation and validation of satellite-based change descriptions and local editing instructions. Based on VIGOR-his, we propose CrossTimeEdit, a model that reformulates historical street-view generation as editing, using recent street views to constrain viewpoint and unchanged appearance and temporal satellite differences as change evidence. Starting from FLUX.2 [Klein] 4B, we train CrossTimeEdit through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by online reinforcement learning (RL). We design three street-view editing criteria, namely Instruction Alignment (IA), Background Preservation (BP), and Quality and Physical Plausibility (QP), as both RL reward dimensions and evaluation metrics. We optimize this multi-reward objective using Within Group Relative Policy Optimization for flow-matching models (Flow-GRPO) with Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO), which normalizes each reward dimension before aggregation. CrossTimeEdit improves overall performance across the three editing criteria by 17.12\% over the pretrained baseline and outperforms cross-view generation models in scene consistency, visual realism, and perceptual quality. The implementation code, dataset, and model weights are available at https://luhanwen67.github.io/CrossTimeEdit-release/.
evidence_items.title: CrossTimeEdit: A Decade-Spanning Cross-View Dataset and Reward-Guided Editing for Historical Street-View Generation

evidence_items.summary: Modern AI models are aligned through post-training to adapt them to downstream tasks. Recent work shows that fine-tuning language models on narrow tasks can induce emergent misalignment (EM), causing broadly harmful behaviors beyond the training task. However, EM has been studied almost entirely in text-only tasks, leaving its manifestation in multimodal models unclear. In this paper, we define and analyze EM in the context of vision-language models. We first induce EM via fine-tuning on narrow multimodal tasks targeting vulnerable code, careless household-object use, and conspiratorial interpretations of ordinary scenes. Across fifteen commercial and open-source models with different scales, we find that narrow multimodal fine-tuning can induce coherent and broadly misaligned behavior that transfers to unrelated tasks, including misaligned opinions, visual factual dishonesty, unsafe image generation, vulnerability to visual jailbreaks, and risky agentic actions. We further find that multimodal EM does not depend on the apparent harmfulness of training data but is sensitive to training-evaluation modality alignment. EM can arise under both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization and can propagate through intermediate reasoning. Finally, we explore several mitigation strategies, including prompt inoculation, benign continued training, and activation-level steering, which can partially reduce EM. Overall, our findings suggest that multimodal EM reflects a behavioral shift rather than a general loss of capability, extending beyond text to the visual modality.
evidence_items.title: Narrow Multimodal Fine-Tuning Can Induce Emergent Misalignment

organizations: Department of Occupational Disease, Istanbul University-Cerrahpasa, Cerrahpasa Faculty of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey
Department of Occupational Disease, Izmir City Hospital, Izmir, Turkey
Department of Public Health, Istanbul University-Cerrahpasa, Cerrahpasa Faculty of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey
evidence_items.summary: Background Inadequate or misleading health information about silicosis can delay diagnosis, reporting, and exposure removal, potentially affecting risk communication and timely occupational health interventions. Objective This study evaluates the reliability, quality, and readability of Large Language Models (LLMs) including ChatGPT (GPT-5), Gemini (2.5 Flash), and Copilot (Smart GPT-5), in answering patient-oriented silicosis questions, focusing on risk communication rather than clinical decisions. Methods Silicosis-related questions were collected from online forums (September 1–7, 2025), and 25 frequently asked, clinically relevant questions were selected and submitted to the LLMs (September 8–14, 2025). Two occupational medicine specialists/pulmonologists independently evaluated responses (September 15–30, 2025) for reliability, quality, and readability using modified DISCERN, Global Quality Scale, and readability indices. Analyses used SPSS version 31.0. Results The LLM-generated responses demonstrated fair reliability. Median (min–max) scores were 23 (12–27) for ChatGPT, 21.5 (14–29) for Gemini, and 26 (17.5–31) for Copilot. Copilot scored significantly higher than ChatGPT and Gemini (p = 0.014). GQS scores were similar across models (p = 0.102), with median scores of 4 (3–5) for ChatGPT and Copilot and 4 (2–5) for Gemini. Readability levels corresponded predominantly to secondary or tertiary education, with no significant differences between the models (all p > 0.05). Conclusion LLMs may enhance worker awareness but have limitations in accuracy and readability. They should complement, not replace, expert-supervised occupational health services. Future studies should align LLMs with international standards, improve accessibility, and establish governance frameworks for transparent and equitable AI use in occupational health.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of the reliability, quality, and readability of multiple large language model responses (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) on silicosis

organizations: Zhengzhou University
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models are increasingly used in healthcare. Nursing students need to strengthen academic writing with such technologies, but existing qualitative evidence is fragmented. To synthesize qualitative evidence on nursing students' experiences using large language models for academic writing to inform future education. Methods PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, and SinoMed were searched for relevant qualitative studies from database inception to January 22, 2026. The JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research was used to evaluate study quality, and findings were synthesized using the JBI meta-aggregation approach. Results A total of 11 studies were included. Thirty-nine findings were extracted, grouped into 13 categories, and further synthesized into 5 synthesized findings: perceived usefulness; perceived ease of use and usage practices; perceived risks and limitations; external factors; and the formation of behavioral intention. Conclusion Nursing students generally hold positive attitudes toward using large language models for academic writing, while expressing concerns about content quality and ethical risks. Future efforts should include systematic training and standardized usage guidelines, as well as measures to emphasize the irreplaceable role of humanistic care and clinical judgment in nursing.
evidence_items.title: Nursing Students' Experiences with Large Language Models in Academic Writing: A Qualitative Systematic Review Based on the Technology Acceptance Model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) systems, especially large language models (LLMs), face growing constraints related to energy use, power delivery, memory traffic, experimentation, and infrastructure capacity. These pressures are often studied separately, which makes it difficult to understand how they interact across the full AI lifecycle. This review develops a cross-layer framework that brings these constraints together and examines whether resource-allocation strategies observed in human cognition can inform more sustainable AI design. We compare human and artificial systems by function rather than anatomy, focusing on how each allocates limited resources to learning, search, memory, external support, optimization, and inference. Using a systematized narrative-review approach, we identified 6284 records, screened 898 at the full-text stage, and selected an initial set of 150 focal studies for detailed synthesis. We organize the evidence into seven interacting regimes covering scaling, experimentation, hardware power limits, data movement, infrastructure, evaluation incentives, and inference allocation. The framework extends Green AI by linking these layers and translating insights from human cognition into testable design hypotheses and measurable evaluation criteria. The strongest near-term opportunities include data selection, energy-aware experimentation, hardware-supported low-precision computation, and demand-adaptive inference. However, most reported gains are based on proxy measures such as operations, memory, latency, or data volume rather than direct end-to-end energy measurements. Near- and in-memory computing show longer-term promise, while retrieval, tool use, distributed experts, and multi-agent systems may shift or increase energy costs through communication and repeated inference. These findings support cross-layer co-design and end-to-end evaluation at matched capability, reliability, latency, and service quality.
evidence_items.title: Energy constraints in large scale artificial intelligence and insights from human cognition for efficient large language models

organizations: School of Foreign Languages, Northeast Normal University, Changchun, China
evidence_items.summary: This study examines translation style variation across registers in English Chinese outputs from TencentMT, DeepSeek, and ArkLLM. Using an aligned corpus of public speech, legal-diplomatic texts, and news, it compares length ratio, mean sentence length, and connective density through mixed-effects modelling and qualitative analysis. ArkLLM generally produced longer outputs, while TencentMT produced shorter sentences and used more explicit connectives. Register also shaped these patterns, showing that AI translation style varies across systems and communicative contexts.
evidence_items.title:
Translation Style Variation across Registers in Machine Translation and Large Language Model Outputs
 A Corpus-Based Study of English-to-Chinese Translation

organizations: School of Computer Science Northwestern Polytechnical University  Xi'an China
